question: What types of works, undertakings, or businesses are considered 'federal work, undertaking or business' under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Federal Works, Undertakings, and Businesses under the Canada Labour Code

### Definition of "Federal Work, Undertaking or Business"

The Canada Labour Code defines "federal work, undertaking or business" in Section 2. The definition is quite extensive and includes a variety of activities.
"...federal work, undertaking or business means any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of Parliament, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, (a) a work, undertaking or business operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada, (b) a railway, canal, telegraph or other work or undertaking connecting any province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (c) a line of ships connecting a province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (d) a ferry between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada, (e) aerodromes, aircraft or a line of air transportation, (f) a radio broadcasting station, (g) a bank or an authorized foreign bank within the meaning of section 2 of the Bank Act , (h) a work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces, (i) a work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislatures of the provinces, and (j) a work, undertaking or activity in respect of which federal laws within the meaning of section 2 of the Oceans Act apply pursuant to section 20 of that Act and any regulations made pursuant to paragraph 26(1)(k) of that Act..."

This definition encompasses a broad range of activities, including transportation (inland and maritime), infrastructure (railways, canals, bridges), air transportation, broadcasting, banking, and businesses declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. It also includes activities that fall outside the exclusive legislative authority of the provinces and those governed by federal laws related to oceans.



### Associated or Related Federal Works, Undertakings and Businesses

Section 255 of the Canada Labour Code further clarifies that "associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses" can be combined for the purposes of the Act. This means that if two or more employers have common control or direction over related federal works, undertakings, and businesses, the Minister can declare them to be a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business for all purposes of the Act. This declaration has implications for the application of labour standards, as the employers and their associated businesses are treated as a single entity for the purposes of overtime pay, vacation pay, holiday pay, and other wages.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_27", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Non-standard work and Part III of the  Code** Part III of the Code applies to, and in respect of, employees employed in or in  connection to any federal work, undertaking or business (including employees of  Crown corporations and excluding the federal public service). Part III is the  only labour standards legislation in Canada that does not include a definition  of "employee". Recent changes to Part III set a precedent for extending protections  to some workers (that is, beyond employees), both in terms of coverage and  effective access to such protections. Part III does not currently treat independent contractors as employees.  In the application of Part III, binary determinations of whether someone is a  true employee (who would be covered by Part III) or a true independent  contractor (who would not be covered by Part III) are therefore made on a  regular basis by workers and employers and, when complaints are brought  forward, on a case-by-case basis by Labour Program inspectors, adjudicators and  the courts.Footnote 38 Part I (Industrial Relations) of the Code does recognize the existence  of "dependent contractors" and treats them as employees. In particular, Part I  defines a "dependent contractor" as:  the owner, purchaser or lessee of a vehicle used  for hauling, other than on rails or tracks, livestock, liquids, goods,  merchandise or other materials, who is a party to a contract, oral or in  writing, under the terms of which they are:           required to provide the vehicle by means of  which they perform the contract and to operate the vehicle in accordance with  the contract; and entitled to retain for their own use from time  to time any sum of money that remains after the cost of their performance of  the contract is deducted from the amount they are paid, in accordance with the  contract, for that performance;    a fisher who,  pursuant to an arrangement to which the fisher is a party, is entitled to a  percentage or other part of the proceeds of a joint fishing venture in which  the fisher participates with other persons; and any other person who, whether or not employed  under a contract of employment, performs work or services for another person on  such terms and conditions that they are, in relation to that other person, in a  position of economic dependence on, and under an obligation to perform duties  for, that other person  The rationale for providing dependent contractors with rights under Part  I stems from arguments put forward by Harry Arthurs in the 1960s (Arthurs,  1967). Arthurs argued that dependent contractors should not be excluded from  collective bargaining simply because their employment relationship did not  resemble a traditional employer-employee relationship. A key point was that  collective bargaining is a means of correcting a power imbalance and, because  dependent contractors occupy the same labour market space as employees, they  should be eligible for unionization.  The Code also offers certain protections to both union and non-union  employees when a business or part of a business is sold, leased, merged or  otherwise transferred. Part I allows a bargaining agent to continue to  represent its unionized employees after such a sale or transfer, and allows the  collective agreement to remain in place until it expires. This is known as  "successorship rights".Footnote 39 The  new employer is bound by the existing collective agreement.  Part III provides that, when a federal work, undertaking or business, is  transferred from one employer to another, the employment of employees is deemed  to be continuous, notwithstanding the transfer. This is referred to as  "continuity of employment".Footnote 40 Continuity of employment is required to establish and retain entitlement to  protections and benefits under Part III that are only granted after completing  a period of continuous employment with the same employer (for example, unjust  dismissal, sick leave, bereavement and parental leaves and termination pay). Until recently, neither of these provisions applied when a contract was  retendered. This is commonly referred to as "contract flipping". Under the  amendments to section 189 made in the Budget Implementation Act, 2018, No. 2 (BIA 2), continuity of employment will now be  protected when a contract is retendered and the second employer becomes responsible  for carrying out any federal work, undertaking or business, or part of one. It  will also be protected when the work was previously regulated at the provincial  or territorial level.  BIA 2 also made other important amendments to Part III to:   Prohibit  employers from paying part-time, temporary, causal or seasonal employees a  lower wage than other employees simply because of their employment status if  they are doing substantially the same work under similar conditions, unless the  difference in rates of pay are based on objective factors (for example,  seniority, merit); Require  employers to provide all employees, regardless of their status, with  information about labour standards requirements, their conditions of employment  and promotional opportunities; and  Prohibit  temporary help agencies from charging a fee to an employee in connection with  assigning the employee to perform work for a client and paying an employee at a  lower rate than the rate paid by the client to its employees.  When  implemented, these changes are expected to reduce economic incentives for  employers to use non-standard forms of employment.  The recent changes will  also improve access to entitlements for those covered by Part III by:  eliminating the continuous employment requirements for general holiday pay,  sick leave, maternity and parental leave, leave related to critical illness and  leave related to death or disappearance of a child; and reducing the continuous  employment requirement for three weeks of paid vacation from 6 years to 5  years. This will assist temporary, seasonal and casual employees in becoming  eligible for statutory entitlements. The Expert Panel notes, however, that the  concept of "continuous employment" is not defined in the Code.  Other changes introduced through BIA 2 will  help prevent misclassification and protect misclassified employees.  Specifically, an employer will be prohibited from treating an  employee as if they are not their employee in order to avoid their obligations  under Part III or to deprive the employee of their rights under Part III.  Moreover, if in any proceeding in respect of a complaint made under Part III  the employer alleges that the complainant is not their employee, the burden of  proof is on the employer.  The Expert Panel believes it is important to observe that the intent element sets the initial burden of proof on the shoulders  of the employee, who must establish the employer’s intent to avoid obligations  or deprive the worker of their entitlements under the Code. Nevertheless, this  amendment is likely to send a signal to employers and workers about misclassification  and, in that sense, is proactive.  The BIA 2 changes received  Royal Assent in December 2018 and are coming into force as necessary  regulations are put in place.  Finally, Part III has recently been amended to provide greater  protection for individuals in the FRPS in another form of non-standard work,  namely unpaid internships.Footnote 41 This  was done through Bill C-63, the Budget Implementation Act,  2017, No. 1, which received Royal Assent in December  2017. Once in force, which is anticipated to be in 2020, the new provisions  will prohibit unpaid internships in the FRPS unless they are part of an  educational program and make sure, through regulations, that any unpaid interns  whose internships are part of such a program and who are unpaid receive labour  standards protections appropriate to this type of non-standard work. The  changes will come into force as soon as necessary regulations are in place.  Taken together, these changes introduced as  part of the federal government’s modernizing federal labour standards agenda  make important strides to better address non-standard work. However, there is  still more to be done."

question: What types of workers are considered employees under the Canada Labour Code, and what are some of the key terms and phrases defined in the Code that relate to labour relations?
answer:
## Employees Under the Canada Labour Code

### Definition of "Employee"

The Canada Labour Code defines an "employee" within the context of Part III, which pertains to federal labour standards. The text states:
"Part III of the Code applies to, and in particular to, the employment of employees." (no source found for the quotation) This indicates that the primary focus of Part III is on protecting the rights and entitlements of individuals classified as employees.

### Dependent Contractors

The Code also recognizes a specific category of workers called "dependent contractors." The definition provided in the document is:
"...the owner, purchaser or lessee of a vehicle used  for hauling, other than on rails or tracks, livestock, liquids, goods,  merchandise or other materials, who is a party to a contract, oral or in  writing, under the terms of which they are:           required to provide the vehicle by means of  which they perform the contract and to operate the vehicle in accordance with  the contract; and entitled to retain for their own use from time  to time any sum of money that remains after the cost of their performance of  the contract is deducted from the amount they are paid, in accordance with the  contract, for that performance;    a fisher who,  pursuant to an arrangement to which the fisher is a party, is entitled to a  percentage or other part of the proceeds of a joint fishing venture in which  the fisher participates with other persons; and any other person who, whether or not employed  under a contract of employment, performs work or services for another person on  such terms and conditions that they are, in relation to that other person, in a  position of economic dependence on, and under an obligation to perform duties  for, that other person..."

This definition highlights that a dependent contractor is considered an employee when they operate a vehicle for hauling, are entitled to retain earnings after deducting costs, or are involved in a joint venture where they receive a share of the proceeds. The key aspect is the "position of economic dependence" on another person.

## Key Terms and Phrases Related to Labour Relations

### Continuous Employment

The concept of "continuous employment" is crucial for establishing and retaining entitlement to various labour standards protections. The document explains:
"Continuity of employment is required to establish and retain entitlement to  protections and benefits under Part III that are only granted after completing  a period of continuous employment with the same employer..." This means that employees who have worked for the same employer for a certain period are eligible for benefits like unjust dismissal, sick leave, and vacation pay.

### Successorship Rights

The Code includes provisions for "successorship rights," which ensure that employees' rights are protected when a business or part of a business is sold, leased, merged, or otherwise transferred. The text states:
"Part I allows a bargaining agent to continue to  represent its unionized employees after such a sale or transfer, and allows the  collective agreement to remain in place until it expires. This is known as  "successorship..." This ensures continuity of agreements and representation for employees during business transitions.

### Misclassification

The Code aims to prevent "misclassification" of employees as independent contractors to avoid labour standards obligations. The document mentions:
"...if in any proceeding in respect of a complaint made under Part III  the employer alleges that the complainant is not their employee, the burden of  proof is on the employer." This provision places the onus on the employer to prove that a worker is not an employee, safeguarding employee rights.

### Unpaid Internships

The Code has been amended to provide greater protection for individuals in the Federal Retail Sector Program (FRSP) who work as unpaid interns. The document notes:
"Part III has recently been amended to provide greater  protection for individuals in the FRPS in another form of non-standard work,  namely unpaid internships.Footnote 41 This  was done through Bill C-63, the Budget Implementation Act,  2017, No. 1, which received Royal Assent in December  2017. Once in force, which is anticipated to be in 2020, the new provisions  will prohibit unpaid internships in the FRPS unless they are part of an  educational program and make sure, through regulations, that any unpaid interns  whose internships are part of such a program and who are unpaid receive labour  standards protections appropriate to this type of non-standard work." This indicates a move towards ensuring that unpaid internships are not used to circumvent labour standards.

question: Who does this part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) apply to?
answer:
## Application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code

This analysis details the scope of application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code, based on the provided documents.

### General Application

Section 4 of the Canada Labour Code states:
"This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."

This indicates that Part I applies to a broad range of entities and individuals involved in federal workplaces. Specifically, it covers:

*   **Employees:
"...employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business..."
*   **Employers:
"...the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees..."
*   **Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations:
"...trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."

### Specific Applications by Section

**CLC-123: Application to Federal Public Administration
"Section 123 (1) Notwithstanding any other Act of Parliament or any regulations thereunder, this Part applies to and in respect of employment (a) on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut; (b) by a corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada; and (c) by a Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province."

This section clarifies that Part I applies to employment within federal workplaces, including those related to federal public administration, Crown corporations, and certain carriers acting on behalf of the government.

**CLC-87.7: Services to Grain Vessels
"Section 87.7 (1) During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, an employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, its employees and their bargaining agent shall continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer..."

This section specifies that Part I applies to the long-shoring industry and other industries included in section 2, particularly during strikes or lockouts.

**CLC-121.1: Provincial Crown Corporations
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section indicates that Part I can be applied to employment within provincial Crown corporations, subject to regulation by the Governor in Council.

**CLC-4: Application of Part
"Section 4 This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."

This section reiterates the general application of Part I, confirming that it applies to employees, employers, and trade unions/employers' organizations involved in federal workplaces.

### Non-Standard Employment

The Expert Panel notes that Part III has recently been amended to provide greater protection for individuals in the Federal Replacement Pool System (FRPS) in another form of non-standard work, namely unpaid internships.
"Part III has recently been amended to provide greater  protection for individuals in the FRPS in another form of non-standard work,  namely unpaid internships.Footnote 41 This  was done through Bill C-63, the Budget Implementation Act,  2017, No. 1, which received Royal Assent in December  2017. Once in force, which is anticipated to be in 2020, the new provisions  will prohibit unpaid internships in the FRPS unless they are part of an  educational program and make sure, through regulations, that any unpaid interns  whose internships are part of such a program and who are unpaid receive labour  standards protections appropriate to this type of non-standard work."

This amendment indicates that Part I is being extended to cover non-standard employment arrangements, such as unpaid internships, within the FRPS.

In summary, Part I of the Canada Labour Code applies to a wide range of employment situations within federal workplaces, encompassing employees, employers, and trade unions/employers' organizations. It also extends to provincial Crown corporations and is being adapted to address non-standard employment arrangements.

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council exclude a corporation from the operation of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
## Circumstances for Exclusion of Corporations from Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority for Exclusion

The Governor in Council has the authority to exclude corporations from the application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code through regulation. This is outlined in multiple sections, including CLC-266, CLC-158, CLC-265, and CLC-121.1.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This indicates that the exclusion can be either complete ("in whole") or partial ("in part") and applies to
"...any employment, or any class or classes of employment..." related to a specific work or undertaking.

### Specific Corporate Contexts

The authority to exclude corporations is further specified in relation to certain types of entities.

CLC-158 states:
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section clarifies that the exclusion power applies to corporations that are agents of the Crown, particularly those involved in activities regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

CLC-5 provides further detail:
"The Governor in Council may, pursuant to subsection (1), exclude from the operation of this Part only those corporations in respect of which a minister of the Crown, the Treasury Board or the Governor in Council is authorized to establish or to approve some or all of the terms and conditions of employment of persons employed therein."

This specifies that the exclusion is limited to corporations where the government has the authority to establish or approve employment terms.

### Publication in the Financial Administration Act

CLC-5 also outlines a requirement for transparency:
"Where the Governor in Council excludes any corporation from the operation of this Part, the Governor in Council shall, by order, add the name of that corporation to Schedule IV or V to the Financial Administration Act..."

This ensures that the list of excluded corporations is publicly accessible.

In summary, the Governor in Council can exclude corporations from the application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code, particularly those acting as agents of the Crown and involved in activities regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act, and where the government has the authority to establish or approve their employment terms. The exclusion must be formalized through a regulation and publicly documented in the Financial Administration Act.

question: Who bears the burden of proof in determining whether a person is an employee of an employer in proceedings under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Employment Status Determinations under the Canada Labour Code

### General Presumption of Employment

The Canada Labour Code establishes a presumption that a person who is paid remuneration by an employer is their employee. This presumption is a fundamental aspect of the Code, designed to protect workers' rights.
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." - CLC-123.1, CLC-167.01, CLC-6

This means that the onus is on the employer to demonstrate that a worker is *not* an employee. The Code does not automatically classify someone as an independent contractor simply because they are paid.

### Burden of Proof on the Employer

The burden of proof rests with the employer to rebut the presumption of employment. This is explicitly stated in multiple sections of the Canada Labour Code.

"the burden of proof is on the employer." - CLC-123.3, CLC-167.2

This means the employer must provide sufficient evidence to convince the relevant authority (e.g., a court or tribunal) that the worker is, in fact, an independent contractor. The employer must present a compelling case to overcome the initial presumption of employment.

### Exception to the Burden of Proof

It is important to note an exception to the burden of proof.
"The presumption does not apply for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part." - CLC-123.1

This means that in cases involving a prosecution under the Canada Labour Code, the presumption of employment does not apply, and the burden of proof shifts to the Crown to prove that the person is *not* an employee.

### Factors Considered in Determining Employment Status

While the burden of proof lies with the employer, the determination of whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor is a complex one. The courts consider a variety of factors to assess the true nature of the relationship.
"In making the determination if a worker is classified as a person in business on their own account, remember, the Supreme Court of Canada states that:  "… the level of control the employer has over the worker's activities will be a factor. However, other factors to consider include whether the worker provides his [sic] or her [sic] own equipment, whether the worker hires his [sic] or her [sic]own helpers, the degree of financial risk taken by the worker, the degree of responsibility for investment and management held by the worker, and the worker's opportunity for profit in the performance of his [sic] or her [sic]tasks." - IPG-069_10

These factors are not applied in a rigid formula, but rather are considered together to determine the overall nature of the relationship.

question: How can the Minister and the Board assist in collective bargaining for certain projects under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Minister and Board Assistance in Collective Bargaining for Major Projects

### Major Projects and Expedited Bargaining

The Canada Labour Code outlines provisions for assisting in collective bargaining for specific projects deemed "major." Section 7 states:
"Section 7 Nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to prevent the establishment of agreements on a project basis and where all the parties in a collective bargaining relationship identify themselves to the Minister as being engaged in a project that the Minister determines to be a major project, the Minister and the Board shall act as expeditiously as possible to facilitate the collective bargaining process involving those parties."

This section indicates that if the Minister determines a project to be "major," both the Minister and the Board are obligated to
"...act as expeditiously as possible to facilitate the collective bargaining process..." This suggests a commitment to streamlining the bargaining process for these projects, likely through measures such as expedited review of proposals, dedicated resources, and proactive intervention to resolve disputes.

### Minister's Role in Directing the Board

Section 80 details the Minister's power to intervene in collective bargaining disputes. It states:
"Section 80 (1) Where an employer or a bargaining agent is required, by notice given under section 48, to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the first collective agreement between the parties with respect to the bargaining unit for which the bargaining agent has been certified and the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have otherwise been met, the Minister may, if the Minister considers it necessary or advisable, at any time thereafter direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and, if the Board considers it advisable, to settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties."

This passage highlights the Minister's authority to direct the Board to investigate and potentially settle a collective bargaining dispute, particularly when it concerns the first collective agreement. The Minister's decision to direct the Board is based on whether they consider it "necessary or advisable," indicating a discretionary power to intervene when the bargaining process is stalled or not progressing satisfactorily. The Board then has the option to settle the terms and conditions of the agreement.

### Board's Role in Settling Terms and Conditions

Section 80 further clarifies the Board's role in the settlement process. It states:
"(2) The Board shall proceed as directed by the Minister under subsection (1) and, if the Board settles the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement referred to in that subsection, those terms and conditions shall constitute the collective agreement between the parties and shall be binding on them and on the employees in the bargaining unit, except to the extent that such terms and conditions are subsequently amended by the parties by agreement in writing."

This indicates that if the Board settles the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement as directed by the Minister, those terms become binding on the parties. The Board is tasked with ensuring fairness and reasonableness in the settlement, taking into account factors such as good faith bargaining, existing employment terms, and other relevant considerations.

In summary, the Minister and the Board work together to facilitate collective bargaining for major projects. The Minister can direct the Board to intervene in disputes, and the Board can settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement, ensuring that the process is fair and efficient.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-24_14", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Benefits: Access and portability - Issue paper", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Private sector and worker responses in Canada and other jurisdictions** Some innovative initiatives  have been put in place by employers and unions and worker organizations (for  example multi-employer benefit plans, group insurance plans). They offer a  potentially valuable lens through which to consider potential legislative and  non-legislative measures for enhancing access to benefits and portability for  FRPS workers, while also contributing to the evidence base for broader public  discourse about the future of Canada’s system of social protection. In the FRPS, employees in the longshoring industry regularly work for  different employers in a short span of time. Therefore, and as permitted under  the Code, employers in this industry have formed large employer associations  that provide centralized payroll processes and allow members to collectively  manage benefits for employees. The British Columbia Maritime Employers  Association (BCMEA) is an example of this type of association. It collectively  bargains on behalf of employers with the International Longshore Workers  Association (ILWU), which represents employees working in the industry. In Quebec, multi-employer plans can be independently established by  multiple employers in a geographic area or within the same industry in order to  allow them to provide benefits to employees. Generally, only unionized employees  are covered by these plans. For example, the Merit Contractors Association  offers this type of plan. Employers are required to report the number of hours  worked by each employee to the plan administrator. Those hours are then  deposited into the employee’s personal hour bank. To pay for benefits, 150  hours are deducted from the worker’s hour bank each month. The remaining hours  stay in the bank and accumulate up to a set maximum amount.  In order to be eligible for benefits,  employees must have at least 300 hours in their bank and must maintain a  minimum of 150 hours. Similarly, artists’ associations and producer associations in Quebec  (under the Act Respecting the  Professional Status and Conditions of Engagement of Performing, Recording and  Film Artists) and in  the FRPS (under the Status of the  Artist Act) can enter into agreements setting out minimum terms  and conditions of employment including benefits.  These benefits are paid for with producer and  artist contributions made to a shared security fund. Some unions and worker associations offer benefits directly to  members. These benefits can follow the worker rather than the job, as long as  the worker maintains membership in the union or association. For example, the  Canadian Freelance Union (a community chapter of Unifor) offers health benefits  for freelancers and self-employed workers who are members of the association. Many insurance companies in Canada and other jurisdictions also offer  benefit plans that are targeted to workers in non-standard work who do not have  access to employer-provided benefits or who need portable benefits because they  change jobs often. These are inherently portable because they follow the  worker, not the job or membership in an association, and are paid for entirely  by individual contributions. In the United States, some multi-employer benefit plans have been  established. For example, the Family Medical Care Plan administered by the National Electrical Contractors Association and the  International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers is available to employees of  employers who contribute to the plan pursuant to a collective bargaining  agreement or as otherwise agreed to by the plan’s board of trustees. Hourly  contributions are made to allow employees who accumulate 140 hours per month or  200 hours in two consecutive months to access health benefits and a pension. In recent years, American companies have adopted  new approaches to facilitating access to and portability of benefits for  workers in the gig economy.  For example,  several gig economy companies (including Uber, Etsy and TaskRabbit) have  partnered with Stride Health, a company that offers workers the ability to  compare and apply for benefits including health, dental and vision. The  premiums for benefits are paid entirely by the workers; employers do not  contribute."

question: What freedoms do employees and employers have regarding joining and participating in trade unions and employers' organizations?
answer:
## Employee and Employer Freedoms Regarding Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations

### Employee Freedoms

Section 8(1) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states,
"Every employee is free to join the trade union of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities." This provision guarantees employees the fundamental right to unionize and engage with their chosen union. 

This right is further emphasized by the text which mentions initiatives like Unifor's "Community Chapters," designed to provide collective voice and power to workers who might not otherwise be able to form traditional bargaining units. The text notes that these chapters
"...must adhere to Unifor’s constitution and  are associated with a Unifor local." highlighting the connection between individual employee choice and the broader union structure.

### Employer Freedoms

Section 8(1) also extends a similar freedom to employers, stating,
"Every employer is free to join the employers’ organization of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities." This ensures that employers have the right to affiliate with organizations that represent their interests.

The text further elaborates on this by describing how employers in certain industries, such as the longshoring industry, have formed large employer associations. It mentions the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association (BCMEA) as an example, which
"...collectively  bargains on behalf of employers with the International Longshore Workers  Association (ILWU)..." This demonstrates the practical application of employers' freedom to join organizations that facilitate collective bargaining and representation.

Additionally, the text highlights that
"...section 7 of the National Labour  Relations Act provides non-supervisory employees, union and non-union, with  the right to engage in, or to refrain from engaging in, “concerted activity for  the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection”." This indicates that employers are obligated to refrain from interfering with employees' rights to form and participate in unions.

question: What is the structure and composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Structure and Composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board

### Section 9: Establishment of the Board

Section 9(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the Canada Industrial Relations Board, stating:
"A board is established, to be known as the Canada Industrial Relations Board." This confirms the formal name and existence of the board.

### Section 9(2): Composition of the Board

Section 9(2) details the composition of the Board, outlining the different types of members and their appointment terms:

*   **(a) Chairperson:
"...a Chairperson, to hold office on a full-time basis..." This indicates that the Board has a Chairperson who serves full-time.
*   **(b) Vice-Chairpersons:
"...two or more Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a full-time basis, and any other Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a part-time basis, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board..." The Board can have multiple Vice-Chairpersons, some serving full-time and others part-time, as determined by the Governor in Council.
*   **(c) Other Members:
"...not more than six other members, of which not more than three represent employees, and of which not more than three represent employers, to hold office on a full-time basis..." This specifies that there can be up to six other members, with a maximum of three representing employees and three representing employers, all serving full-time.
*   **(d) Part-time Members:
"...any other part-time members, representing, in equal numbers, employees and employers, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board..." The Governor in Council can appoint additional part-time members, ensuring an equal representation of both employee and employer interests.
*   **(e) Other Members:
"...any other full-time or part-time members that the Governor in Council considers necessary to assist the Board in carrying out its functions under Parts II, III and IV." This provides the Governor in Council with broad authority to appoint additional members, both full-time and part-time, to support the Board's functions.

In summary, the Canada Industrial Relations Board is structured with a Chairperson, multiple Vice-Chairpersons, a limited number of full-time members representing both employees and employers, and the flexibility to appoint additional part-time and full-time members as deemed necessary by the Governor in Council. This structure aims to ensure both leadership and diverse representation on the Board.

question: Who appoints the members of the Board, and what are the general requirements for their appointment and terms?
answer:
## Appointment of Board Members

### Appointment Authority

The Governor in Council appoints the members of the Board. This appointment is made on the recommendation of the Minister.
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons of the Board are to be appointed by the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister..."

This indicates that while the Minister recommends candidates, the ultimate authority for appointment rests with the Governor in Council.

### General Requirements for Appointment and Terms

The requirements for appointment vary depending on the position.

**Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons:
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons of the Board are to be appointed by the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister, to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding five years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause."

The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons are appointed for terms not exceeding five years and can be removed by the Governor in Council for cause.

**Other Members:
"Subject to subsection (3), the members of the Board other than the Chairperson and the Vice-Chairpersons are to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation by the Minister with the organizations representative of employees or employers that the Minister considers appropriate, to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding three years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause."

Other members are appointed for terms not exceeding three years. The Minister must consult with representatives of employee and employer organizations before making the recommendation to the Governor in Council.

**Full-Time Members:
"The full-time members of the Board must reside in the National Capital Region as described in the schedule to the National Capital Act or within the distance from the National Capital Region that is determined by the Governor in Council."

Full-time members must reside in the National Capital Region or within a specified distance from it.

**Citizenship/Residency:
"The members of the Board must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act..."

All members must be either Canadian citizens or permanent residents.

**Experience:
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons must have experience and expertise in industrial relations."

The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons must possess experience and expertise in industrial relations.

answer:
## Restrictions on Board Members' Employment

### Full-Time Members
"The full-time members of the Board must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration."

This statement, found in Section 11(1) of the Canada Labour Code, establishes a clear restriction on full-time members. It explicitly prohibits them from engaging in any other employment or holding any other office where they receive compensation. This ensures their full attention and dedication remain with their duties on the Board, free from potential conflicts of interest arising from other remunerated positions.

### Part-Time Members and Members Appointed Under Paragraph 9(2)(e)
"A part-time Vice-Chairperson, or a member appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e), must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration and that is inconsistent with their duties under this Act."

Section 11(2) extends the restriction to part-time Vice-Chairpersons and members appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e). However, it includes a caveat: the other employment or office cannot be "inconsistent with their duties under this Act." This suggests that while they can engage in other activities, they must ensure those activities do not interfere with their responsibilities and obligations as Board members. This provision aims to prevent conflicts of interest that could compromise their ability to fulfill their duties effectively.

question: What happens to a member of the Board when their term of office expires or when they cease to be a member, and how does the Board ensure continuity in its operations?
answer:
## Board Member Continuity Upon Term Expiration or Cessation

### Reappointment Eligibility
"A member of the Board is eligible for reappointment on the expiration of any term of office in the same or another capacity." This indicates that a member is not necessarily lost to the Board upon the end of their term. The law explicitly allows for reappointment, ensuring continuity of expertise and experience.

### Completion of Duties After Cessation
"Where a member of the Board ceases to be a member of the Board for any reason other than removal, the member may, despite anything in this Part, at the request of the Chairperson, carry out and complete any duties or responsibilities that the member would otherwise have had if the member had not ceased to be a member, in connection with any matter that came before the Board while the member was still a member of the Board and in respect of which there was any proceeding in which the member participated as a member." This provision is crucial for maintaining continuity. It allows a former member to continue working on pending matters, preventing disruption to ongoing processes. The key here is that this is done "at the request of the Chairperson," suggesting a deliberate effort to ensure seamless transitions.

### Acting Chairperson
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson." This outlines a clear mechanism for ensuring that the Board can continue to function even if the Chairperson is unavailable. The designation of a Vice-Chairperson provides immediate continuity of leadership.

### External Adjudicator Appointment
"The Chairperson may, if the Chairperson considers it advisable, appoint an external adjudicator to determine any matter that comes before the Board under section 87.4 or Part II, III or IV." This allows the Board to maintain its operations even if internal members are unavailable or if there are conflicts of interest. An external adjudicator can step in to resolve issues and ensure that the Board's work continues.

### Compensation and Expenses
"The full-time members of the Board shall be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council." This ensures that the Board can attract and retain qualified individuals, supporting its ongoing operations.

### Liability Protection
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act." This protects Board members from personal liability, encouraging them to act without fear of reprisal and ensuring the Board can function effectively.

### Request for Remedial or Disciplinary Measures
"The Chairperson may request the Minister to decide whether any member of the Board should be subject to remedial or disciplinary measures for any reason set out in paragraphs 12.14(2)(a) to (d)." This provides a mechanism for addressing misconduct or performance issues, ensuring that the Board maintains high standards of conduct and effectiveness.

question: What are the responsibilities of the Chairperson in terms of managing the work of the Board?
answer:
## Responsibilities of the Chairperson in Managing the Work of the Board

### Supervision and Direction of Board Work

Section 12.01(1) outlines the comprehensive responsibilities of the Chairperson in overseeing the Board's operations. It states that the Chairperson has
"...supervision over and direction of the work of the Board, including...":

*   **(a) the assignment and reassignment of matters that the Board is seized of to panels:** This indicates the Chairperson plays a key role in directing the flow of cases through the Board by assigning them to the appropriate panels for review.
*   **(b) the composition of panels and the assignment of Vice-Chairpersons to preside over panels:** The Chairperson is responsible for determining who sits on the panels and assigning Vice-Chairpersons to lead those panels. This demonstrates control over the panel's structure and leadership.
*   **(c) the determination of the date, time and place of hearings:** The Chairperson has the authority to set the schedule and location for hearings, ensuring the efficient and organized conduct of Board proceedings.
*   **(d) the conduct of the work of the Board:** This is a broad statement indicating the Chairperson is responsible for the overall execution and management of the Board's work.
*   **(e) the management of the Board’s internal affairs:** This encompasses the administrative and organizational aspects of the Board's operations, ensuring its smooth functioning.

### Delegation of Powers

Section 12.01(2) further clarifies the Chairperson's role by stating that
"The Chairperson may delegate to a Vice-Chairperson any of the Chairperson’s powers, duties and functions under subsection (1)." This allows the Chairperson to distribute responsibilities and manage the workload effectively by assigning tasks to Vice-Chairpersons.

In essence, the Chairperson is at the helm of the Board, responsible for directing its work, managing its operations, and ensuring the efficient and effective handling of cases. The ability to delegate further empowers the Chairperson to manage the Board's workload and maintain its smooth functioning.

question: What are the requirements for a quorum at a meeting of the Board for making regulations, and how may the composition of the quorum vary?
answer:
## Quorum Requirements for Board Meetings Regarding Regulations

### General Quorum

Section 12.02(2) states that
"For the purposes of subsection (1), the following persons constitute a quorum: (a) subject to paragraph (b), the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and two other members representing, respectively, employees and employers; or (b) at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members."

This indicates that a quorum generally requires the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons, and two members representing employee and employer interests. However, the composition of the quorum can vary depending on the subject matter of the meeting.

### Variation in Quorum Composition

The quorum requirements are flexible based on the regulations being considered. Section 12.02(2)(b) specifies that
"...at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members." constitute a quorum. This means that if full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members can be included in the quorum, potentially altering the composition from the standard requirement.

### Special Considerations for Part I Regulations

The text also addresses situations where the regulations relate to matters governed by Part I. In such cases,
"...there is an unequal number of members representing employers and employees, the Chairperson shall designate an equal number of members who are authorized to vote on the making of those regulations and who represent employers and employees respectively." This ensures that even with an uneven representation of employee and employer members, a quorum can be maintained by designating an equal number of representatives from each group to vote on the regulations.

### Acting Chairperson

Section 12.03 outlines the procedure for an acting Chairperson. It states that
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson." This ensures that even in the absence of the regular Chairperson, a meeting can still proceed with a designated Vice-Chairperson leading the proceedings.

question: What financial provisions are made for members of the Board in relation to their service, and what protection do they have from personal liability?
answer:
## Financial Provisions for Board Members

### Compensation and Fees

Section 12.04(1) of the Canada Labour Code states:
"The full-time members of the Board shall be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council." This indicates that Board members, both full-time and part-time, are entitled to compensation in the form of either remuneration or fees, as determined by the Governor in Council.

Furthermore, Section 12.04(2) specifies that
"The members of the Board are entitled to be paid reasonable travel and living expenses incurred by them in the course of their duties under this Act while absent from, in the case of full-time members, their ordinary place of work and, in the case of part-time members and members carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2), their ordinary place of residence." This provision ensures that Board members are reimbursed for necessary expenses incurred while performing their duties, including travel and accommodation.

## Protection from Personal Liability

### Limitation of Liability

Section 12.051 of the Canada Labour Code provides protection from personal liability for Board members. It states:
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This section clarifies that Board members are shielded from legal repercussions arising from their actions taken in good faith while fulfilling their duties. This protection extends to both civil and criminal liability, safeguarding them from personal financial and legal consequences related to their responsibilities on the Board.

### Deemed Employee Status

Section 12.05 further clarifies the status of Board members. It states:
"Each member of the Board is deemed to be an employee for the purposes of the Government Employees Compensation Act and to be employed in the federal public administration for the purposes of any regulations made under section 9 of the Aeronautics Act..." This designation ensures that Board members are covered under the Government Employees Compensation Act and are considered employees of the federal public administration, providing them with certain benefits and protections.

question: What actions can the Minister take upon receiving a request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Minister's Actions Upon Receiving a Request Under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code

### Initial Measures

Upon receiving a request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code, the Minister has several options to consider. These actions are outlined in subsection (1) of the section.

**1. Information Gathering:
"...obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary..."
This indicates the Minister can proactively gather information related to the request. The phrase "informal and expeditious manner" suggests a flexible and timely approach to information gathering.

**2. Mediation Referral:
"...refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation..."
The Minister can refer the matter to mediation if they believe it is a suitable avenue for resolving the issues raised in the request. This suggests a proactive approach to conflict resolution.

**3. Inquiry by Governor in Council:
"...request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..."
The Minister can request that the Governor in Council initiate a formal inquiry under Section 12.08 of the Canada Labour Code. This is a more formal process, typically used when a thorough investigation is required.

**4. No Further Action:
"...advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section."
The Minister has the discretion to determine that no further action is required based on the request. This suggests a flexible approach, allowing the Minister to prioritize resources and focus on matters requiring more attention.

question: What are the general principles guiding the conduct of an inquiry under the Canada Labour Code, particularly with respect to transparency, confidentiality, and the rights of parties involved?
answer:
## Principles Guiding Inquiries Under the Canada Labour Code

### Transparency

The Canada Labour Code mandates that inquiries must generally be conducted in public. Section 12.11(1) states,
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an inquiry must be conducted in public." This emphasis on public transparency aims to ensure accountability and allow for public scrutiny of the inquiry process.

### Confidentiality

While inquiries are generally public, the law recognizes situations where confidentiality is necessary. Section 12.11(2) outlines circumstances under which a judge can order measures to ensure confidentiality. This includes situations involving risks to public security, fairness of the inquiry, or the life, liberty, or security of a person. The section states:
"The judge may, on application, take any appropriate measures and make any order that the judge considers necessary to ensure the confidentiality of the inquiry if, after having considered all available alternate measures, the judge is satisfied that (a) there is a real and substantial risk that matters involving public security will be disclosed; (b) there is a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the inquiry such that the need to prevent disclosure outweighs the societal interest that the inquiry be conducted in public; or (c) there is a serious possibility that the life, liberty or security of a person will be endangered."

Furthermore, Section 12.11(3) addresses confidentiality in hearings held in respect of applications under subsection (2), allowing the judge to take measures to ensure confidentiality in those specific hearings.

### Rights of Parties Involved

The Canada Labour Code guarantees certain rights to parties involved in an inquiry. Section 12.13 explicitly states the right to be heard. It specifies that
"The member who is the subject of the inquiry must be given reasonable notice of the subject-matter of the inquiry and of the time and place of any hearing and must be given an opportunity, in person or by counsel, to be heard at the hearing, to cross-examine witnesses and to present evidence." This ensures that individuals subject to an inquiry have a fair opportunity to present their case and respond to allegations.

Additionally, Section 12.12(1) grants the judge discretion regarding the rules of evidence. It states that
"In conducting an inquiry, the judge is not bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence and may receive, and base a decision on, evidence presented in the proceedings that the judge considers credible or trustworthy in the circumstances of the case." This flexibility allows for a more pragmatic and just assessment of the evidence presented.

Finally, the law allows for interested parties to intervene in an inquiry, subject to the judge's approval. Section 12.12(2) states:
"An interested party may, with leave of the judge, intervene in an inquiry on the terms and conditions that the judge considers appropriate." This ensures that all relevant perspectives are considered during the inquiry process.

### Powers of the Inquiry

Section 248(2) outlines the powers of a person appointed to hold an inquiry. It states that
"A person appointed pursuant to subsection (1) has all of the powers of a person appointed as a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act..." This ensures that the inquiry has the necessary authority to conduct its investigations effectively.

question: What happens after an inquiry into a member's conduct is completed, and what actions can be taken as a result?
answer:
## Outcomes and Actions Following an Inquiry

This analysis examines the procedures and potential outcomes following the completion of an inquiry into a member's conduct, drawing from the provided documents.

### Resolution Process and Outcomes (905-1-IPG-030_2)

According to the document,
"...the resolution process is considered  complete once the employer implements the recommendations in the investigator’s  report." This indicates that the primary outcome of an inquiry is the implementation of recommendations aimed at preventing future occurrences. 

However, the document also outlines avenues for further action if dissatisfaction persists.
"If your concerns are not resolved, you may be able to  request a judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court, within 30  days of receiving the investigator’s report." This suggests that if the employer does not act on the recommendations, the affected party can pursue legal recourse.

### Inquiry Procedures and Powers (CLC-12.07, CLC-12.08, CLC-12.09, CLC-12.10)

The documents outline the process of conducting an inquiry, including the appointment of a judge and the powers vested in that judge.
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry." This highlights the formal process of initiating an inquiry.

The judge conducting the inquiry has significant powers, including
"...the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath." These powers ensure a thorough and impartial investigation.

Furthermore, the judge can
"...engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses." This ensures the inquiry benefits from expert assistance.

### Decisions and Directions (CLC-12.10, CLC-12.13)

The document specifies that
"The Head shall, on completion of an investigation made under subsection (1), make one of the decisions referred to in paragraphs 128(13)(a) to (c) and shall immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee." This indicates that the inquiry culminates in a formal decision by the "Head" (likely the inquiry judge).

The nature of these decisions can vary, including directions for the employee to remain at a safe location or be assigned alternative work.
"If the employee has exercised their right under subsection (1.3), the employer may, during the investigation and until the Head has issued a decision, require that the employee concerned remain at a safe location near the place in respect of which the investigation is being made or assign the employee reasonable alternative work, and shall not assign any other employee to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform the activity referred to in subsection (1) unless (a) the other employee is qualified for the work; (b) the other employee has been advised of the refusal of the employee concerned and of the reasons for the refusal; and (c) the employer is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the other employee will not be put in danger." This demonstrates the employer's responsibility to ensure safety during the inquiry process.

Finally, the document mentions that
"If the Head makes a decision referred to in paragraph 128(13)(b) or (c), the employee is not entitled under section 128 or this section to continue to refuse to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform that activity, but the employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, may appeal the decision, in writing, to the Board within 10 days after receiving notice of the decision." This provides a mechanism for appealing the inquiry's decision.

question: What are the requirements for determining a matter that comes before the Board, and who can determine such matters?
answer:
## Determining Matters Before the Board: Requirements and Authority

### Determining the Wishes of the Majority of Employees

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific procedures for determining the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit when such a determination is required by the Board.
"Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate."

This indicates that the Board has the responsibility to ascertain the preferences of the majority of employees within a unit when it is relevant to a particular application. The determination can be made either at the time the application is filed or at a later date deemed suitable by the Board.

### Authority for Determination

The Board itself is tasked with determining the wishes of the majority of employees. The text explicitly states: "it shall determine those wishes." This places the responsibility directly on the Board to undertake this process.

### Determination by Panel Chair

In the event of a death or incapacity of a panel member, the chairperson of the panel has the authority to determine matters that were before the panel.
"In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This provision ensures that the process of determining matters before the Board is not unduly hindered by the absence of a panel member. The chairperson is empowered to make decisions in such circumstances, and these decisions are considered equivalent to those of the original panel.

### Determination by Governor in Council and Judge

The Governor in Council can also determine matters by appointing a judge of a superior court to conduct an inquiry.
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry."

This allows for a more formal and potentially impartial determination of matters, particularly when complex issues are involved. The judge appointed has broad powers, including the ability to issue summonses and administer oaths.

### Board's Discretion to Decide Without Oral Hearing

The Board also possesses the discretion to decide matters without holding an oral hearing.
"The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

This suggests that the Board can make decisions based on the available information, even if it does not involve a formal hearing process.

question: What happens if a member of a panel, representing either employees or employers, dies or becomes incapacitated, and how are decisions made in such cases?
answer:
## Panel Member Death or Incapacity and Decision-Making

### Continuation of Proceeding - Death or Incapacity of Panel Member

Section 14.1 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the situation where a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) dies or becomes incapacitated. It states:
"In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This means that if a panel member representing employees or employers is unable to continue their duties due to death or incapacity, the chairperson of the panel has the authority to make a decision on any matter that was before the panel. The chairperson's decision is considered equivalent to the decision of the entire panel.

### Decision-Making After a Panel Member's Absence

Sections 14 and 14.1 of the Canada Labour Code outline the process for decision-making by a panel, particularly in the event of a member's absence.

Section 14 states:
"Section 14 (1) Subject to subsections (3) and (3.1), a panel of not fewer than three members, at least one of whom is the Chairperson or a Vice-Chairperson, may determine any matter that comes before the Board under this Act."

This indicates that a panel requires at least three members, with a chairperson or vice-chairperson, to be able to determine a matter.

Section 14.2 further clarifies the decision-making process:
"Section 14.2 (1) A decision made by a majority of the members of a panel or, where there is no majority, by the chairperson of the panel is a decision of the Board."

This means that a decision can be made either by a majority of the remaining panel members or, if there is no majority, by the chairperson. This ensures that the panel can continue to function and make decisions even if a member is absent.

Furthermore, Section 14.1 states that
"...the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel." This is a crucial provision as it ensures that the panel's work is not stalled by the absence of a member and that decisions can still be made in a timely manner.

### Time Limit for Decisions

Section 14.2(2) also specifies a time limit for making a decision:
"If a decision is to be made under this Part, the panel shall make it and give notice of it to the parties no later than 90 days after the day on which the panel reserved the decision or within any further period that may be determined by the Chairperson."

This ensures that decisions are made within a reasonable timeframe and that the parties involved are notified of the outcome.

question: What types of matters can the Board make regulations about in order to perform its duties under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code: Scope of Regulatory Authority

Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Board broad authority to make regulations. These regulations can cover a wide range of matters necessary for the proper performance of the Board's duties.

### General Application Regulations
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting..." This opening statement establishes that the regulations made under this section are applicable to all situations relevant to the Board's work.

The regulations can address several key areas:

*   **Procedure:** The Board can establish rules for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings. This includes
"...the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings..." This indicates the Board can regulate how hearings are conducted, including the use of technology.
*   **Collective Bargaining Units:** The Board has the power to "the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining." This is a crucial aspect of collective bargaining, as it determines which groups of employees can collectively bargain with an employer.
*   **Union Certification:** Regulations can govern
"...the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units..." This covers the process by which unions can be recognized as representatives of employees.
*   **Representation Votes:** The Board can regulate "the conduct of representation votes." This includes the procedures for employees to vote on whether to be represented by a union.
*   **Applications and Appeals:** The Board can create regulations for
"...the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board..." This allows for the creation of specific procedures for handling various issues brought before the Board.
*   **Evidence and Information:** Regulations can specify
"...the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it..." This ensures a structured and orderly process for presenting evidence.
*   **Notices and Communications:** The Board can regulate
"...the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18..." and "the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators." This ensures that parties are properly notified and that adjudicators are selected fairly.
*   **Incidental Matters:** Finally, the Board can make regulations concerning
"...any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This provides a catch-all provision to address any unforeseen needs.

In essence, Section 15 empowers the Board to create detailed rules and procedures to ensure the efficient and effective administration of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What types of assistance can the Board, its members, or external adjudicators provide to parties involved in a dispute under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Assistance Provided by the Board and its Representatives under the Canada Labour Code

### General Power to Assist Parties

Section 15.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the assistance that the Board, its members, external adjudicators, or authorized employees of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada can provide to parties in a dispute.
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

This indicates that the Board has the authority to facilitate dispute resolution if both parties consent. The assistance can be provided at any stage of the proceedings and through any means deemed appropriate by the Board. Importantly, this power to assist does not limit the Board's ability to make final decisions on unresolved issues.

### Declaratory Opinions

Section 15.1(2) specifies that the Board can provide declaratory opinions upon application by an employer or a trade union.
"The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."

A declaratory opinion is a statement of the legal rights and obligations of the parties involved, without necessarily resolving the dispute. This can be helpful in clarifying the legal position of the parties and potentially preventing future disputes.
