question: What powers does the Board have in relation to proceedings before it, particularly in terms of gathering evidence and information?
answer:
## Board Powers Regarding Gathering Evidence and Information

The Canada Labour Code outlines several powers the Board possesses concerning the gathering of evidence and information in relation to proceedings before it. These powers are detailed in Section 16 and related sections.

### Summoning Witnesses and Compelling Evidence

Section 16(a) states that the Board has the power
"...to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce such documents and things as the Board deems requisite to the full investigation and consideration of any matter within its jurisdiction that is before the Board in the proceeding..." This indicates a broad authority to obtain necessary information through witness testimony and document production.

### Administering Oaths and Affirmations

"Section 16(b) to administer oaths and solemn affirmations." This power is crucial for ensuring the reliability and legal validity of the evidence received.

### Receiving Evidence in Various Forms

Section 16(c) specifies that the Board
"...receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the Board in its discretion sees fit, whether admissible in a court of law or not..." This demonstrates flexibility in accepting evidence, acknowledging that evidence may be presented in various forms beyond traditional court-admissible formats.

### Examining Evidence Respecting Union Membership
"...to examine, in accordance with any regulations of the Board, such evidence as is submitted to it respecting the membership of any employees in a trade union seeking certification..." This power is specifically directed towards verifying union membership, a critical aspect of certification proceedings.

### Examining Union Documents
"...to examine documents forming or relating to the constitution or articles of association of (i) a trade union or council of trade unions that is seeking certification, or (ii) any trade union forming part of a council of trade unions that is seeking certification..." This allows the Board to scrutinize the foundational documents of unions seeking certification to assess their legitimacy and structure.

### Compelling Information and Documents
"...to compel, at any stage of a proceeding, any person to provide information or produce the documents and things that may be relevant to a matter before it, after providing the parties the opportunity to make representations..." This is a powerful tool for ensuring the Board has access to all relevant information, with a provision for fairness to the parties involved.

### Entering Employer Premises
"...to enter any premises of an employer where work is being or has been done by employees and to inspect and view any work, material, machinery, appliances or articles therein and interrogate any person respecting any matter that is before the Board in the proceeding..." This allows the Board to conduct site visits and gather information directly from the workplace.

### Representation Votes
"...to order, at any time before the proceeding has been finally disposed of by the Board, that (i) a representation vote or an additional representation vote be taken among employees affected by the proceeding in any case where the Board considers that the taking of such a vote would assist the Board to decide any question that has arisen or is likely to arise in the proceeding, whether or not such a representation vote is provided for elsewhere in this Part, and (ii) the ballots cast in any representation vote ordered by the Board pursuant to subparagraph (i) or any other provision of this Part be sealed in ballot boxes and not counted except as directed by the Board..." This power enables the Board to gather the views of employees through representation votes, which can be crucial for resolving disputes.

### Authorizing Others to Gather Information
"...to authorize any person to do anything that the Board may do under paragraphs (a) to (h), (j), or (m) and to report to the Board thereon..." This allows the Board to delegate the task of gathering information to others, such as external adjudicators or staff.

In summary, the Board has extensive powers to gather evidence and information, including summoning witnesses, compelling document production, examining union records, conducting site visits, and ordering representation votes. These powers are designed to ensure the Board has access to all necessary information to make informed decisions in labour disputes.

question: How does the Board determine the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit when an application is made under this Part?
answer:
## Determining the Wishes of the Majority of Employees

### Section 17: General Rule for Determining Majority Wishes
"Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate."

This section establishes the fundamental principle for the Board's determination. It states that the Board must assess the majority wishes as of a specific date: either the date the application is filed or another date the Board deems suitable. This provides a clear starting point for the Board's analysis.

### Section 16.1: Board's Authority to Decide Without Oral Hearing
"The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

While not directly detailing *how* the Board determines majority wishes, this section is relevant because it implies the Board has the authority to make decisions regarding the wishes of the majority without necessarily requiring a formal hearing. This suggests the Board can rely on available evidence and information to reach a determination.

### Section 31: Evidence of Majority Opinion
"A vote by the majority of the employees voting in a representation vote is evidence that a majority of employees in the unit in respect of which the vote was ordered are of the opinion expressed in the vote of the majority of employees voting."

This section clarifies that a successful representation vote serves as strong evidence of the majority's opinion. It explicitly states that
"A vote by the majority of the employees voting in a representation vote is evidence that a majority of employees in the unit in respect of which the vote was ordered are of the opinion expressed in the vote..." This means that if a majority of employees vote in favor of a particular union, the Board can reasonably infer that the majority of the employees in the unit share that opinion.

### Section 18.1: Review of Bargaining Unit Structure and Party Agreement
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement."

This section is relevant as it outlines the Board's power to review bargaining unit structures. If the Board reviews the structure of bargaining units, it must allow the parties to come to an agreement on the determination of bargaining units. This implies that the Board will consider the wishes of the majority of employees in the unit when determining the structure of the bargaining units.

In summary, the Board determines the wishes of the majority of employees by considering the situation as of the application date or another date it deems appropriate, relying on evidence such as the outcome of representation votes. The Board also has the authority to review bargaining unit structures and consider the parties' agreements to determine the appropriate bargaining units.

question: Can the Board change its previous decisions or orders, and if so, what is the scope of this authority?
answer:
## Board's Authority to Review, Rescind, Amend, or Vary Orders and Decisions

### Section 18: General Authority for Review and Amendment
"Section 18 The Board may review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it, and may rehear any application before making an order in respect of the application."

This section explicitly grants the Board the authority to modify its own prior actions. The phrase "review, rescind, amend, alter or vary" indicates a broad scope of power. 

*   **Review:** This suggests the Board can re-examine existing orders and decisions.
*   **Rescind:** This implies the Board can cancel or revoke a previous order or decision.
*   **Amend:** This means the Board can make changes to an existing order or decision.
*   **Alter:** Similar to amend, this indicates the Board can make modifications.
*   **Vary:** This suggests the Board can make changes to an order or decision.

The provision
"...and may rehear any application before making an order in respect of the application." further supports the Board's ability to revisit and potentially change its decisions. This implies a process for reconsideration and modification.

### Section 156: Finality of Orders and Decisions
"Section 156 (1) Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

While Section 18 grants the Board the power to change its own orders, Section 156 establishes the finality of orders and decisions made under this Part. This means that once an order or decision is made, it is generally not subject to judicial review. 

However, Section 18 provides the mechanism for the Board to change its own orders and decisions, effectively circumventing the finality established in Section 156. This suggests that the Board's authority to review, rescind, amend, alter or vary its orders and decisions is a significant exception to the general rule of finality.

### Section 18.1: Review of Bargaining Unit Structure
"Section 18.1 (1) On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining."

This section provides a specific instance where the Board can review and potentially alter its previous decisions regarding bargaining unit structure. The Board can "review" the structure of bargaining units, which could lead to changes in existing certification orders or descriptions of bargaining units. 

The Board's authority in this area is limited to cases where it determines that the existing bargaining unit structure is no longer appropriate. The Board must also allow the parties to come to an agreement regarding the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review. If the parties do not agree, the Board can determine any question that arises and make any orders it considers appropriate.

In summary, the Board has the authority to review, rescind, amend, alter or vary its own orders and decisions, as stated in Section 18. This authority is a significant exception to the general rule of finality established in Section 156. Section 18.1 provides a specific example of this authority in the context of reviewing and amending bargaining unit structures.

question: What is the process for the Board to review the structure of bargaining units if it is deemed that they are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining, and what actions can the Board take if the parties do not reach an agreement?
answer:
## Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

### Initiation of Review

Section 18.1(1) outlines the process for initiating a review of bargaining unit structures. It states that
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that either the employer or a bargaining agent can request the Board to examine the current structure of bargaining units. The Board's decision to review is based on its assessment of whether the existing units are still suitable for collective bargaining.

### Process When Parties Reach an Agreement

Section 18.1(2) details the process when the Board undertakes a review and the parties reach an agreement. It specifies that
"...the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This means the Board will facilitate negotiations between the parties to reach a mutually acceptable solution regarding the bargaining unit structure. If an agreement is reached, the Board can then issue orders to implement that agreement.

### Board Action When Parties Do Not Reach an Agreement

Section 18.1(3) addresses the situation where the parties fail to reach an agreement within the timeframe deemed reasonable by the Board. It states that
"If the Board is of the opinion that the agreement reached by the parties would not lead to the creation of units appropriate for collective bargaining or if the parties do not agree on certain issues within the period that the Board considers reasonable, the Board determines any question that arises and makes any orders it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This signifies that if the parties cannot agree, the Board has the authority to make its own determinations and issue orders.

### Scope of Board Orders

Section 18.1(3) further clarifies the scope of the orders the Board can make. These include:

*   Determining which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each bargaining unit that results from the review.
*   Amending any certification order or description of a bargaining unit contained in any collective agreement.
*   Deciding which collective agreement is in force if multiple agreements apply to employees in a bargaining unit.
*   Amending provisions of collective agreements relating to expiry dates or seniority rights.
*   Deciding which terms and conditions of employment apply to employees in a bargaining unit until a collective agreement becomes applicable or until certain conditions are met.
*   Authorizing a party to a collective agreement to give notice to bargain collectively.

These powers allow the Board to ensure that the bargaining unit structure is appropriate for collective bargaining, even if the parties themselves cannot agree on the details.



## Successor Rights and Obligations

### Board's Role in Successor Situations

Section 45 outlines the Board's role in situations involving a sale or change of activity. It states that
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board can review the bargaining unit structure when a business is sold or undergoes a significant change in activity.

### Determining Appropriate Units

The Board's determination is based on whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining. This allows the Board to ensure that the bargaining unit structure remains appropriate even when the business changes hands.

question: What flexibility does the Board have when making decisions or issuing orders under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Flexibility of the Board in Decision-Making and Orders

The Canada Labour Code outlines several aspects of the Board's flexibility when making decisions and issuing orders. This analysis will explore these aspects, drawing upon the provided sections.

### Scope of Orders and Decisions

Section 251.12 states that
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal; (c) award costs in the proceedings; and (d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board."

This demonstrates significant flexibility. The Board isn't limited to simply upholding or rejecting a previous decision. It can
"...confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..." This allows the Board to tailor the outcome to the specific circumstances of the appeal. Furthermore, the Board can address various aspects related to the appeal, including financial matters like directing payment of wages or awarding costs. The power to order a party to pay for expenses incurred due to undue delay also provides a mechanism to ensure efficient proceedings.

### Finality of Orders and Decisions

Sections 243 and 156 both emphasize the finality of the Board's orders and decisions. Section 243 states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." Similarly, Section 156 asserts,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This finality is crucial. It means that once an order is issued, it cannot be challenged in the courts. This provides stability and certainty to the resolution of labour disputes. The language used is strong: "shall not be questioned or reviewed." This indicates a deliberate intention to prevent judicial interference with the Board's decisions.

### Limitations on Judicial Review

The finality of the Board's orders is reinforced by the explicit prohibition of judicial review. Both Section 243 and Section 156 include the phrase,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section..."

This is a powerful statement limiting the ability of courts to intervene in the Board's proceedings. It underscores the importance of respecting the Board's authority in resolving labour disputes.

### Flexibility in Appeals

Section 251.11 outlines the process for appeals, stating that
"...a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served."

This indicates that the Board allows for appeals, providing a mechanism for review of its decisions. However, it also includes an exception, limiting the scope of appeals to certain types of decisions. This demonstrates a degree of control over the appeal process, ensuring that it is used appropriately.

In summary, the Board possesses considerable flexibility in making decisions and issuing orders, particularly in the context of appeals. However, this flexibility is balanced by the finality of its orders and the limitations on judicial review, ensuring stability and preventing undue interference from the courts.

question: Can the Board issue a decision on some issues in a proceeding while still having jurisdiction over other issues?
answer:
## CLC-20: Powers and Duties: Interim decision

### Partial Decisions and Reserved Jurisdiction

The Canada Labour Code, Section 20, outlines a scenario where the Board can issue a partial decision. It states:
"Where, in order to dispose finally of an application or complaint, it is necessary for the Board to determine two or more issues arising therefrom, the Board may, if it is satisfied that it can do so without prejudice to the rights of any party to the proceeding, issue a decision resolving only one or some of those issues and reserve its jurisdiction to dispose of the remaining issues."

This passage directly addresses the question. It explicitly permits the Board to
"...issue a decision resolving only one or some of those issues and reserve its jurisdiction to dispose of the remaining issues." This means the Board can make a decision on certain aspects of a case while retaining the authority to rule on other outstanding matters. The condition is that this is done
"...without prejudice to the rights of any party to the proceeding..." ensuring fairness to all involved.



## CLC-156: Orders, Decisions and Directions of Board: Decision final

### Finality of Partial Decisions

Section 156 of the Canada Labour Code confirms the finality of decisions made by the Board, including partial decisions. It states:
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This confirms that a decision issued under Section 20, which resolves only some issues, is also considered a final decision and cannot be challenged in court. This reinforces the ability of the Board to issue partial decisions with reserved jurisdiction, as the partial decisions themselves are legally binding.

question: What are the general responsibilities of The Board in relation to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Responsibilities of The Board under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code outlines several general responsibilities for The Board. These responsibilities encompass a wide range of activities aimed at facilitating fair labour practices, resolving disputes, and ensuring compliance with the Act.

### Section 15: Making Regulations
"...any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act."

This section grants the Board the authority to create regulations that govern its operations. This is a broad power, allowing the Board to establish detailed rules and procedures for various aspects of its work. This includes areas like
"...the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings..." "the conduct of representation votes," and
"...the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board..." This demonstrates the Board's responsibility to create a structured and orderly process for handling matters brought before it.

### Section 15.1: Assisting Parties and Giving Declaratory Opinions
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."
"The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."

This section highlights the Board's role in facilitating dispute resolution. It empowers the Board to assist parties in reaching settlements and to provide declaratory opinions on legal questions. The Board's ability to
"...assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute..." underscores its commitment to promoting amicable solutions and preventing unnecessary conflict.

### Section 15.1: Compensation and Liability
"The members of the Board are entitled to be paid reasonable travel and living expenses incurred by them in the course of their duties under this Act while absent from, in the case of full-time members, their ordinary place of work and, in the case of part-time members and members carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2), their ordinary place of residence."
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This section outlines the compensation and liability of the Board's members. It ensures that members are adequately compensated for their duties and are protected from personal liability when acting in good faith. This reinforces the Board's commitment to maintaining a fair and impartial decision-making process.

### Section 15: Inquiry and Evidence
"...the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it..."

This section emphasizes the Board's responsibility to conduct thorough inquiries and consider all relevant evidence. It empowers the Board to establish procedures for hearing and determining applications, complaints, and appeals. It also ensures that the Board has access to the necessary information to make informed decisions.

In summary, the Board's general responsibilities, as outlined in the Canada Labour Code, are multifaceted. They include establishing rules and procedures, facilitating dispute resolution, providing declaratory opinions, ensuring fair compensation and liability for its members, and conducting thorough inquiries with consideration of all relevant evidence. These responsibilities collectively contribute to the Board's role in upholding labour standards and promoting a fair and equitable workplace.

question: Under what conditions can an order or decision made by the Board be reviewed or questioned in a court?
answer:
## Review and Questioning of Board Orders and Decisions in Court

Based on the provided documents, the general rule is that orders and decisions made by the Board are final and cannot be questioned or reviewed in any court. However, there are specific exceptions to this rule.

### General Finality of Board Orders and Decisions

Several sections explicitly state the finality of Board orders and decisions. For example, CLC-243 states:
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This indicates a strong presumption against judicial review. Similarly, CLC-22 states,
"...every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This reinforces the principle of finality.

CLC-156 also emphasizes this point, stating:
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

### Exceptions to the General Rule

CLC-22 outlines the specific circumstances under which a Board order or decision *can* be challenged in court. It specifies that review is permitted
"...except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." While the exact grounds are not detailed in these documents, it indicates that judicial review is possible based on the grounds outlined in the Federal Courts Act.

The documents also state that
"...shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground, including the ground that the order, decision or proceeding is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board to make or carry on or that, in the course of any proceeding, the Board for any reason exceeded or lost its jurisdiction." This means that a court can intervene if the Board acted outside its legal authority.

### No Court Proceedings to Prevent Board Action

Furthermore, the documents clarify that no court proceedings can be initiated to prevent or restrain the Board from carrying out its functions. CLC-22 states:
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Part." This ensures the Board's autonomy in its decision-making processes.

question: What is the purpose of filing a copy of an order or decision of the Board in a court, and what are the implications of such registration?
answer:
## Purpose of Filing in Court

### Section 23: Filing in Federal Court
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This section outlines that the primary purpose of filing a copy of a Board order or decision in Federal Court is to provide a mechanism for ensuring compliance and establishing the legal force of the decision. The requirement for filing "on the request in writing" ensures that the filing is initiated by those directly affected by the order. The exception clause allows the Board to withhold filing if it deems it unnecessary or futile, considering factors like the likelihood of compliance.

### Section 23.1: Filing in Provincial Superior Court
"The Board may, on application by a person or organization affected by an order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the superior court of a province. Section 23 applies, with any modifications that the circumstances require, to an order or decision filed in such a superior court."

This section provides an alternative to filing in the Federal Court, allowing the Board to file in a provincial superior court upon application. It also indicates that the same principles and requirements outlined in Section 23 apply to such filings, with necessary adjustments for the provincial court system.

## Implications of Registration

### Section 23: Effect of Registration
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court."

This passage highlights the significant legal implications of registering a Board order or decision in court.  It states that the registered order or decision has the
"...same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court..." This means it becomes legally binding and enforceable, similar to a court judgment. 

Furthermore, "all proceedings may be taken thereon" which implies that legal actions can be initiated based on the registered order or decision, just as they could be based on a judgment from a court. This provides a powerful tool for enforcing the Board's decisions and ensuring compliance.

### Section 22: No Review in Court
"Except as permitted by subsection (1), no order, decision or proceeding of the Board made or carried on under or purporting to be made or carried on under this Part shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground, including the ground that the order, decision or proceeding is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board to make or carry on or that, in the course of any proceeding, the Board for any reason exceeded or lost its jurisdiction."

This section reinforces the finality of Board orders and decisions. It explicitly states that such orders and decisions cannot be challenged or reviewed in court, except under very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act. This underscores the importance of the registration process, as it solidifies the legal standing of the order and prevents attempts to overturn it.

question: What are the rules and restrictions surrounding the timing of a trade union's application for certification as a bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
answer:
## Timing of Trade Union Certification Applications

### Section 24(1) - General Application Process
"A trade union seeking to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining may, subject to this section and any regulations made by the Board under paragraph 15(e), apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the unit."

This section establishes the fundamental right of a trade union to apply for certification. It states that a union can apply to the Board if it believes a unit of employees is appropriate for collective bargaining. The application is subject to certain conditions and regulations set by the Board.

### Section 24(2) - Application Timing Based on Collective Agreements

This section outlines the specific times when a trade union can make an application for certification, depending on the existence and duration of a collective agreement.

*   **(a) No Collective Agreement:
"...where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, at any time..."
    This means a union can apply at any time if there is no existing collective agreement covering the unit and no other union is already certified.

*   **(b) Collective Agreement in Force, After 12 Months:
"...where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time..."
    If a union has previously been certified but the collective agreement has expired, it can apply for certification again after a period of twelve months, or earlier with the Board's consent.

*   **(c) Collective Agreement Term of Up to Three Years:
"...where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation..."
    If a collective agreement is in effect for a term of up to three years, a union can only apply for certification during the final three months of the agreement's term.

*   **(d) Collective Agreement Term of More Than Three Years:
"...where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."
    For collective agreements lasting longer than three years, the timing of the application is more restricted. The union can apply only during specific periods: from the 34th to the 37th month of the agreement's operation, and during the three months immediately preceding the end of each year after the third year of the agreement.

### Section 24(3) - Restrictions During Strikes or Lockouts
"An application for certification under subsection (2) in respect of a unit must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part and that involves employees in the unit."

This section prohibits applications for certification during a strike or lockout, unless the Board grants permission. This is to avoid disrupting the collective bargaining process during a period of industrial action.

### Section 24(4) - Employer Actions After Notification of Application
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board."

This section restricts employers from making changes to employees' terms and conditions of employment after being notified of a certification application. The restriction lasts until the application is withdrawn or dismissed, or until 30 days have passed after the Board certifies the union as the bargaining agent, unless a collective agreement is in place or the Board consents to the changes.

question: Can a trade union that has entered into a collective agreement but is not certified apply for certification under certain circumstances?
answer:
## Application for Certification: Exception - Section 24.1

### General Rule Regarding Certification Applications
"Section 24 (1) A trade union seeking to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining may, subject to this section and any regulations made by the Board under paragraph 15(e), apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the unit."

This section establishes the general process for a trade union to apply for certification. However, Section 24.1 provides an exception to this general rule.

### Exception for Unions with Existing Collective Agreements
"Section 24.1 A trade union that is not certified but has entered into a collective agreement the term of which has not expired may, despite paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d), make an application for certification at any time, in respect of the unit to which the collective agreement applies or substantially the same unit."

This section explicitly states that a trade union, even if it hasn't yet been officially certified, can still apply for certification if it has a collective agreement in place. The key is that the term of the collective agreement has not expired. This allows the union to seek certification even while a collective agreement is already in effect, potentially streamlining the process and ensuring the union's representation continues. The phrase "despite paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d)" indicates that the usual restrictions on application timing do not apply in this situation.

question: Under what conditions may the Board refuse to certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
answer:
## Section 26: Prohibition on Certification for Dual Units

### Dual Bargaining Units
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific condition under which the Board is prohibited from certifying a trade union as the bargaining agent for two separate bargaining units. The prohibition applies when the union seeks to represent both a unit of private constables and a unit of other employees, and if any or all of the employees in both units are employed by the same employer. 

This rule is in place to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure fair representation. It prevents a union from effectively representing two distinct groups of employees when those groups are linked by a common employer, which could compromise the union's ability to bargain effectively for either group. The law aims to maintain clarity and avoid situations where a single union could potentially disadvantage one group of employees in favor of the other due to the shared employer relationship.

question: Can a trade union act as the bargaining agent for both private constables and other employees if they are employed by the same employer?
answer:
## Analysis of Section 26 of the Canada Labour Code

### Prohibition on Dual Representation

Section 26 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly addresses the situation where a trade union might seek to represent both private constables and other employees who are employed by the same employer. The section states:
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This passage directly answers the question. It unequivocally prohibits a trade union from acting as the bargaining agent for both groups of employees when they are employed by the same employer. The prohibition applies to both the certification process by the Board and the union's actual role as bargaining agent.

### Rationale Behind the Prohibition

The rationale behind this prohibition is to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure fair representation. The law aims to avoid situations where a union might be divided in its loyalties or unable to effectively advocate for the distinct interests of private constables versus other employees within the same workplace. The section ensures that each group has a dedicated representative to safeguard their specific rights and concerns.

The phrase
"...if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer." is crucial. It clarifies that the prohibition applies specifically when there is a shared employer. This prevents a union from potentially creating artificial bargaining units to circumvent the rules and potentially dilute its ability to represent employees effectively.

question: What factors influence the Labour Board's decision when determining a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining?
answer:
## Factors Influencing the Labour Board's Determination of an Appropriate Bargaining Unit

The Labour Board's determination of an appropriate bargaining unit is influenced by several factors, as outlined in the provided documents. These factors encompass the trade union's application, the composition of the workforce, and the overall suitability of the unit for collective bargaining.

### Trade Union Application and Board Review

Section 27(1) states,
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board shall determine the unit that, in the opinion of the Board, is appropriate for collective bargaining." This highlights that the Board's initial decision is based on the trade union's proposed unit, but the Board retains the authority to review and potentially modify it.

Section 18.1(2) further elaborates on this process. It indicates that
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This suggests that the Board considers the input of both the employer and the union during the review process and can issue orders to resolve any disputes.

### Composition of the Workforce

Section 27(2) specifies that
"In determining whether a unit constitutes a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board may include any employees in or exclude any employees from the unit proposed by the trade union." This demonstrates the Board's flexibility in adjusting the unit's composition.

Section 27(3) addresses the specific case of units comprised of professional employees. It states,
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including professional employees, the Board, subject to subsections (2) and (4), shall determine that the unit appropriate for collective bargaining is a unit comprised of only professional employees, unless such a unit would not otherwise be appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that while the Board generally aims for units consisting solely of professional employees, it can deviate from this if it deems necessary for appropriate collective bargaining.

Section 27(4) provides further detail on the composition of the unit, stating that
"In determining that a unit is appropriate for collective bargaining under subsection (3), the Board may include in the unit (a) professional employees of more than one profession; and (b) employees performing the functions, but lacking the qualifications, of a professional employee." This shows that the Board can broaden the unit to include employees who, while not formally classified as professionals, perform similar duties.

Section 27(5) addresses units including employees with supervisory duties, stating that
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including employees whose duties include the supervision of other employees, the Board may, subject to subsection (2), determine that the unit proposed in the application is appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board considers supervisory roles when determining the appropriate unit.

Finally, Section 27(6) specifies an exclusion:
"The Board shall not include a private constable in a unit with other employees." This highlights a specific factor that the Board considers when determining unit composition.



### Overall Suitability for Collective Bargaining

The overarching theme throughout these sections is that the Board assesses the "appropriateness" of the unit for collective bargaining. This is a broad criterion that encompasses the workforce's composition, the trade union's proposal, and the potential for effective collective bargaining. The Board has the discretion to adjust the unit to ensure that it is suitable for collective bargaining, considering the needs of both the employees and the employer.

question: What are the requirements for a trade union to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
answer:
## Requirements for Trade Union Certification under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 28: General Certification Requirements

Section 28 outlines the general conditions under which the Board must certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit. It states that the Board must certify if three conditions are met:
"(a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit..." This indicates that the process begins with a formal application from the trade union.
"(b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining..." The Board must first determine the appropriate bargaining unit.
"(c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent." This is a crucial requirement, as the Board must be satisfied that a majority of employees in the unit desire the union's representation.

### Section 29: Representation Vote Requirement

Section 29 elaborates on the requirement for demonstrating employee support. It states that
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This means that if the Board is not certain about the employees' desire for union representation, it can order a vote to determine their preference.

Furthermore, Section 29 specifies a threshold for triggering a representation vote:
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This indicates that a union needs to demonstrate a certain level of membership within the unit to trigger a vote.

### Section 33: Certification for Units with Multiple Employers

Section 33 addresses a specific scenario where employees are employed by multiple employers who have formed an employers' organization. It states that
"...the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part." This allows for a single employer designation when an employers' organization exists, simplifying the certification process.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification

Section 36 outlines the consequences of a trade union being certified as the bargaining agent. It states that
"...the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..." This means that once certified, the union is the sole representative of the employees in collective bargaining. It also specifies that the union is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects the employees in the bargaining unit.

In summary, a trade union must meet the requirements outlined in Section 28, including submitting a formal application, determining an appropriate bargaining unit, and demonstrating that a majority of employees in the unit wish to be represented by the union. If the Board is uncertain about employee support, it may order a representation vote. Specific rules apply when employees are employed by multiple employers who have formed an employers' organization, as outlined in Section 33. Once certified, the union gains exclusive bargaining authority, as stated in Section 36.

question: Under what circumstances may or must the Board order a representation vote among employees in a unit to determine their bargaining agent?
answer:
## Representation Votes: Board Authority and Requirements

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific circumstances under which the Board may order a representation vote among employees to determine their bargaining agent. These circumstances are detailed in sections 29, 30, and 31.

### General Authority to Order a Vote

Section 29(1) grants the Board the authority to order a representation vote
"...for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent..." This indicates that the Board can initiate a vote whenever it deems necessary to ascertain the employees' preference for a specific union.

### Vote When Union Membership Threshold is Met

Section 29(2) specifies a particular scenario where the Board *must* order a representation vote. It states:
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This provision establishes a threshold of union membership (35% to 50%) that triggers a mandatory vote.

### Vote When Union Membership Practice is Established

Section 29(3) provides another circumstance where the Board may order a vote. It states:
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union." This allows the Board to order a vote even if the union's formal membership requirements are not being strictly followed, as long as there is a demonstrated practice of admitting members.

### Vote on Application for Certification

Section 31(1) outlines that the Board can review the structure of bargaining units
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent..." This review may lead to a determination of an appropriate bargaining unit, which could necessitate a representation vote if the existing unit is deemed inappropriate.

### Choice on Ballot

Section 30(2) specifies that when a Board orders a representation vote on an application for certification, the ballot must include an option for employees to indicate they do not wish to be represented by any union listed on the ballot. This ensures that employees have the freedom to choose not to affiliate with any union.

### No Choice in Subsequent Votes

Section 30(3) clarifies that if a representation vote results in no union receiving a majority of the votes, and a second or subsequent vote is required, the option to not be represented is not included on the ballot. This is to avoid unnecessary complexity in repeated voting processes.

question: What are the responsibilities of the Board when ordering a representation vote among employees in a unit, and what choices must be included on the ballots?
answer:
## Responsibilities of the Board When Ordering a Representation Vote

**Section 30(1)(a) - Determining Eligible Voters
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote..."

This indicates the Board's initial responsibility is to identify and verify the eligibility of employees within the unit to participate in the vote. This involves establishing who is entitled to cast a ballot.

**Section 30(1)(b) - Arranging for Proper Conduct
"...and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

The Board is responsible for the logistical aspects of conducting the vote. This includes ensuring the ballots are prepared correctly, establishing a clear procedure for casting and counting ballots, and maintaining the security of the ballots throughout the process.

**Section 30(2) - Inclusion of a "No Representation" Choice
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots."

When a union seeks certification, the Board must provide employees with the option to abstain from union representation. This ensures that employees have a genuine choice regarding union affiliation. This is a crucial aspect of ensuring the fairness and legitimacy of the vote.

**Section 30(3) - No "No Representation" Choice in Subsequent Votes
"Notwithstanding subsection (2), where the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote."

This section clarifies that if a union fails to achieve a majority of the vote in the initial representation vote, the "no representation" option is not included in subsequent votes. This is likely intended to encourage unions to gain majority support in the initial vote rather than repeatedly offering a "no representation" option.



## Choices Included on the Ballots

Based on Section 30(2), the ballots must include a
"...choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots." This provides employees with the option to decline union representation. The ballots will also present the employees with the trade unions seeking certification as bargaining agents.

question: Under what conditions does the Board consider a representation vote valid and how does it determine the outcome?
answer:
## Validity and Outcome of Representation Votes under the Canada Labour Code

### Determining Validity

The validity of a representation vote is primarily determined by the number of eligible employees who participate in the vote. Section 31(2) states:
"Where, on considering the result of a representation vote, the Board determines that less than thirty-five per cent of the employees who are eligible to vote have voted, the Board shall determine that the representation vote is void." This indicates that a minimum turnout of 35% of eligible voters is required for the vote to be considered valid.

### Determining the Outcome

Section 31(1) clarifies how the Board determines the outcome of a valid representation vote:
"Subject to subsection (2), the Board shall determine the result of a representation vote on the basis of the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting." This means that if the turnout meets the 35% threshold, the Board will assess the ballots cast and declare the outcome based on which union receives the most votes.

### Additional Considerations

Section 30 outlines the Board's responsibilities in conducting the vote, including determining eligible voters and ensuring proper procedures are in place. Section 30(2) also specifies that ballots must include an option for employees to indicate they do not wish to be represented by any union on the ballots.

### The Significance of Majority Support

Section 31(3) further clarifies that a vote where the majority of employees voting support one union is considered evidence that a majority of employees in the unit are of the opinion expressed in the vote. This reinforces the importance of a majority vote in determining the outcome and reflects the principle of majority rule in collective bargaining representation.

question: What are the implications for a council of trade unions and its member trade unions when the council is certified as the bargaining agent for a unit?
answer:
## Implications of Certification for a Council of Trade Unions

### Collective Agreement and Legal Standing
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."

This section clearly outlines the significant implications of certification.  Firstly, it establishes that the council and its member unions are legally bound by any collective agreement negotiated on their behalf. This means the agreement has the full force and effect of a traditional trade union collective agreement. Secondly, the law treats the certified council as if it were a single trade union for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code. This provides the council with the same rights and protections as a traditional union, including the ability to bargain collectively and be included as a party to collective agreements.

### Scope of Representation
"Section 32 (1) Where two or more trade unions have formed a council of trade unions, the council so formed may apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in the same manner as a trade union."

This indicates that a council of trade unions can seek certification just like a single trade union.  This is important because it allows multiple unions to pool their resources and bargaining power, potentially leading to stronger outcomes for the employees represented.

### Membership and Authority
"Membership in any trade union that forms part of a council of trade unions is deemed to be membership in the council of trade unions."

This provision clarifies the relationship between individual unions and the council.  Any union that is part of the council is automatically considered part of the council itself. This ensures that the council has a unified voice and authority when bargaining with employers.

### Obligation to Bargain
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."

This reinforces the obligation to bargain collectively. The council, acting as the certified bargaining agent, is legally obligated to bargain with the employer on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit. This is a fundamental aspect of the Canada Labour Code and ensures that employees have a voice in their working conditions.

question: What happens when an employers' organization is designated as the employer for a unit of employees of two or more employers in the context of collective bargaining under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Designation of Employers' Organization as Employer

### Section 33(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

This section outlines the circumstances under which the Labour Code Board can designate an employers' organization as the employer for collective bargaining purposes. The key condition for this designation is that each employer within the organization must have granted the organization the authority to act on their behalf. This ensures that the designation reflects a genuine agreement and consent from the individual employers.

### Section 33(1)(1) and (1.1) - Implications of Designation
"The Board may, on application by the employers’ organization, include in the designation referred to in subsection (1) any employer that becomes a member of the employers’ organization if it is satisfied that that employer has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable the employers’ organization to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer and that such an inclusion would ensure the fulfilment of the objectives of this Part."

This subsection clarifies that the designation can be extended to new employers who join the organization, provided they also grant the necessary authority. This ensures that the collective bargaining unit remains comprehensive as the organization grows.

### Section 33(1)(2) - Rights and Obligations of Designated Employers' Organization
"Where the Board designates an employers’ organization as an employer pursuant to subsection (1), (a) the employers’ organization and each employer forming the employers’ organization is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the employers’ organization were an employer."

This is a crucial aspect of the designation. It means that the designated employers' organization becomes legally responsible for any collective agreements negotiated with the trade union.  Furthermore, the Labour Code applies to the entire unit as if the employers' organization were a single employer. This ensures that the union can bargain with a single entity, simplifying the collective bargaining process.

### Section 33(1)(3) - Consequences of Employer Ceasing Membership
"Where an employer ceases to be a member of an employers’ organization or withdraws the authority referred to in subsection (1) or (1.1) that the employer granted to the employers’ organization, the employer (a) continues to be bound by any collective agreement applicable to the employer’s employees that was entered into by the employers’ organization; and (b) may be required to commence collective bargaining in accordance with section 48."

Even if an employer withdraws their authority, they remain bound by any collective agreements negotiated by the employers' organization. However, they may still be required to participate in collective bargaining under certain circumstances, as outlined in section 48 of the Labour Code. This ensures that the collective bargaining process remains fair and inclusive.

question: What is the process for determining a bargaining unit for employees in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries, and what is the role of the employer representative in collective bargaining?
answer:
## Determining Bargaining Units in Long-Shoring and Designated Industries

### Section 34(1) - Board's Authority to Determine Unit
"Where employees are employed in (a) the long-shoring industry, or (b) such other industry in such geographic area as may be designated by regulation of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Board, the Board may determine that the employees of two or more employers actively engaged in the industry in the geographic area constitute a unit appropriate for collective bargaining and may, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit."

This section outlines the process for determining a bargaining unit in long-shoring and other designated industries. It grants the Board the authority to determine if employees of two or more employers, actively engaged in a specific industry and geographic area, form an appropriate bargaining unit. The Board can then certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for that unit. The key here is the Board's role in assessing whether the employees constitute an "appropriate" unit for collective bargaining.

### Section 34(2) - Board's Inquiry and Recommendation
"No recommendation under paragraph (1)(b) shall be made by the Board unless, on inquiry, it is satisfied that the employers actively engaged in an industry in a particular geographic area obtain their employees from a group of employees the members of which are employed from time to time by some or all of those employers."

This subsection specifies the criteria the Board must consider when determining if a unit is appropriate in industries other than long-shoring. The Board must conduct an inquiry to ensure that the employers in the industry draw their workforce from a common pool of employees. This ensures that the bargaining unit truly represents all employees within the industry, regardless of which employer they are currently employed by.

### Section 34(3) - Employer Representative's Role
"Where the Board, pursuant to subsection (1), certifies a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, (a) require the employers of the employees in the bargaining unit (i) to jointly choose a representative, and (ii) to inform the Board of their choice within the time period specified by the Board; and (b) appoint the representative so chosen as the employer representative for those employers."

This section details the role of the employer representative. After the Board certifies a union as the bargaining agent, the Board orders the employers to jointly select a representative. The Board then formally appoints this representative as the employer representative for all employers within the bargaining unit. This ensures a unified voice for the employers in collective bargaining.

### Section 34(5) - Powers and Responsibilities of the Employer Representative
"An employer representative shall be deemed to be an employer for the purposes of this Part and, by virtue of having been appointed under this section, has the power to, and shall, discharge all the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part on behalf of all the employers of the employees in the bargaining unit, including the power to enter into a collective agreement on behalf of those employers."

This subsection clarifies the scope of the employer representative's authority. The representative is essentially deemed an employer for the purposes of the Act, granting them the power to negotiate and enter into collective agreements on behalf of all employers within the bargaining unit. This ensures a cohesive and unified approach to collective bargaining.

### Section 34(5.1) - Costs and Responsibilities
"The employer representative may require each employer of employees in the bargaining unit to remit its share of the costs that the employer representative has incurred or estimates will be incurred in fulfilling its duties and responsibilities under this Part and under the terms of the collective agreement."

This subsection addresses the financial aspect of the employer representative's role. The representative can recover costs associated with their duties from the employers within the bargaining unit, ensuring that the representative is adequately funded to perform their responsibilities.

### Section 34(6) - Duty of Impartiality
"In the discharge of the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part, an employer representative, or a person acting for such a representative, shall not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith in the representation of any of the employers on whose behalf the representative acts."

This subsection emphasizes the importance of impartiality. The employer representative must act fairly and without bias in representing the interests of all employers within the bargaining unit. This ensures that the collective bargaining process is conducted equitably.

In summary, the process for determining a bargaining unit in long-shoring and other designated industries involves the Board assessing whether employees of multiple employers form an appropriate unit. The Board then appoints an employer representative to negotiate collective agreements on behalf of all employers within that unit, ensuring a unified and impartial approach to collective bargaining.

question: Under what circumstances can the Board declare multiple employers and their federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes?
answer:
## Section 255: Combining Federal Works, Undertakings and Businesses - Declaration of Single Employer

### Circumstances for Declaration

Section 255(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the conditions under which the Minister can declare multiple employers and their associated federal works, undertakings, and businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes.
"Where associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Minister may, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This indicates that the declaration is triggered when multiple employers share "common control or direction" over associated or related federal works, undertakings, and businesses. The Minister must provide these employers with a "reasonable opportunity to make representations" before making such a declaration.

### Section 35: Board's Authority to Declare Single Employer

Section 35(1) grants the Board the authority to make a similar declaration.
"Where, on application by an affected trade union or employer, associated or related federal works, undertakings or businesses are, in the opinion of the Board, operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Board may, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This section mirrors the conditions outlined in Section 255(1), requiring the Board to determine if the associated or related federal works, undertakings, and businesses are operated by multiple employers with "common control or direction." It also mandates that the Board must provide an opportunity for representations from affected employers and trade unions before making the declaration.

In essence, both Section 255 and Section 35 empower either the Minister or the Board to declare multiple employers and their associated federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes when those employers share common control or direction. question: What happens to the collective bargaining authority and existing collective agreements when a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit?
answer:
## Section 36: Effect of Certification

### Exclusive Authority to Bargain
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

This indicates that upon certification, the trade union gains sole power to engage in collective bargaining with the employer(s) representing the bargaining unit's employees. This means that other unions or entities cannot bargain on behalf of those employees.

### Revocation of Prior Certifications
"...the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees..."

This passage clarifies that any previous certifications of other unions for the same bargaining unit are automatically cancelled. The new certification takes precedence, effectively ending the authority of the previously certified union.

### Substitution in Collective Agreements
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

This is a crucial point. When a collective agreement exists, the certified union steps into the shoes of the previous bargaining agent.
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..." This means the certified union assumes all rights and obligations under the existing collective agreement.

### Designation for Purposes of Section 50
"...the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This confirms that the certification has implications beyond collective bargaining agreements. The certified union is recognized as the primary representative for purposes outlined in paragraph 50(b) of the Canada Labour Code.

### Requirement to Commence Collective Bargaining
"...the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This passage outlines the certified union's right to initiate negotiations for a new or revised collective agreement. It provides a timeframe of three months following certification to formally request the employer to begin bargaining. This ensures a timely process for updating or establishing a collective agreement.
