question: What are the main responsibilities of a policy health and safety committee that an employer is required to establish under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Responsibilities of a Policy Health and Safety Committee under the Canada Labour Code

### Establishment and Membership
"For the purposes of addressing health and safety matters that apply to the work, undertaking or business of an employer, every employer who normally employs directly three hundred or more employees shall establish a policy health and safety committee and, subject to section 135.1, select and appoint its members."

This indicates that the Canada Labour Code mandates the establishment of a policy health and safety committee for employers with 300 or more employees. It also specifies the employer's responsibility to select and appoint the committee members.
"An employer who normally employs directly more than twenty but fewer than three hundred employees may also establish a policy committee." This provides an exception for employers with fewer than 300 employees.

### Core Duties and Functions

The policy committee has a broad range of responsibilities, as outlined in section 134.1(4):

*   **Policy and Program Development:
"...shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..." This means the committee plays a key role in shaping the overall health and safety framework within the workplace.
*   **Matter Disposal:
"...shall consider and expeditiously dispose of matters concerning health and safety raised by members of the committee or referred to it by a work place committee or a health and safety representative..." This highlights the committee's function as a forum for addressing health and safety concerns.
*   **Hazard Prevention Program:
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..." This emphasizes the committee's role in proactively preventing workplace hazards and promoting safety awareness.
*   **Inquiries, Investigations, Studies, and Inspections:
"...shall participate to the extent that it considers necessary in inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to occupational health and safety..." This indicates the committee's involvement in examining and addressing health and safety issues.
*   **Personal Protective Equipment:
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials..." This highlights the committee's role in ensuring appropriate PPE is available and used.
*   **Cooperation with the Head:** "shall cooperate with the Head." This suggests a collaborative relationship with senior management.
*   **Data Monitoring:
"...shall monitor data on work accidents, injuries and health hazards..." This indicates the committee's responsibility to track and analyze health and safety data.
*   **Implementation of Changes:
"...shall participate in the planning of the implementation and in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures." This highlights the committee's role in adapting to changes and ensuring safety is maintained.

### Information Access and Meetings
"A policy committee may request from an employer any information that the committee considers necessary to identify existing or potential hazards with respect to materials, processes, equipment or activities in any of the employer’s..." This gives the committee the right to request information to identify hazards.
"A policy committee shall meet during regular working hours at least quarterly and, if other meetings are required as a result of an emergency or other special circumstances, the committee shall meet as required during regular working hours or outside those hours." This outlines the requirement for regular meetings to ensure ongoing engagement and effectiveness.

"...every employer who normally employs directly three hundred or more employees shall establish a policy health and safety committee and, subject to section 135.1, select and appoint its members." The responsibilities of a policy health and safety committee are outlined in section 134.1 (4). These responsibilities include:

#### Policy and Program Development
"...shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..." This signifies that the committee plays a crucial role in shaping the overall health and safety framework of the workplace.
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..." This highlights the committee's involvement in proactively preventing hazards and ensuring employees are adequately informed.

#### Hazard Management and Investigation
"...shall consider and expeditiously dispose of matters concerning health and safety raised by members of the committee or referred to it by a work place committee or a health and safety representative..." This demonstrates the committee's duty to address health and safety concerns promptly.
"...shall participate to the extent that it considers necessary in inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to occupational health and safety..." This indicates the committee's involvement in investigating incidents and assessing workplace hazards.

#### Program Implementation and Monitoring
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials..." This shows the committee's role in ensuring appropriate resources are available for employee safety.
"...shall monitor data on work accidents, injuries and health hazards..." This highlights the committee's responsibility to track and analyze workplace safety data.
"...shall participate in the planning of the implementation and in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures." This indicates the committee's involvement in implementing safety improvements.

### Committee Operations
"A policy committee shall meet during regular working hours at least quarterly and, if other meetings are required as a result of an emergency or other special circumstances, the committee shall meet as required during regular working hours or outside those hours." This outlines the minimum meeting frequency for the committee.

### Limitations
"Despite paragraph (4)(d), a policy committee shall not participate in an investigation, other than an investigation under section 128 or 129, relating to an occurrence of harassment and violence in the..." This specifies a limitation on the committee's involvement in harassment and violence investigations.

### Information Access
"A policy committee may request from an employer any information that the committee considers necessary to identify existing or potential hazards with respect to materials, processes, equipment or activities in any of the employer’s..." This ensures the committee has access to the information needed to effectively fulfill its responsibilities.
"A policy committee shall have full access to all of the government and employer reports, studies and tests relating to the health and safety of employees in the work place, or to the parts of those reports, studies and tests that relate to the health and safety of employees, but shall not have access to the medical records of any person except with the person’s consent." This guarantees the committee has access to relevant safety-related data.

question: What are the requirements for the composition of a policy committee or a work place committee in terms of employee representation and selection?
answer:
## Requirements for Composition of Policy and Workplace Committees

### Minimum Membership and Employee Representation
"Section 135.1 (1) Subject to this section, a policy committee or a work place committee shall consist of at least two persons and at least half of the members shall be employees who (a) do not exercise managerial functions; and (b) subject to any regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), have been selected by (i) the employees, if the employees are not represented by a trade union, or (ii) the trade union representing employees, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented."

This section outlines the fundamental requirements for committee composition. It mandates a minimum of two members, with a crucial stipulation that at least half of the members must be employees who do not hold managerial positions. The selection process for these employee members depends on whether employees are represented by a trade union. If not represented, employees themselves are responsible for selection. If a trade union represents employees, the union must select the members in consultation with non-unionized employees.

### Exceptions for Policy Committees
"(2) Despite subsection (1) and if provided in a collective agreement or other agreement, the members of a policy committee may include persons who are not employees."

This exception allows for the inclusion of non-employee members on a policy committee, provided this is stipulated in a collective agreement or other agreement. This provides flexibility for incorporating expertise or perspectives beyond the employee base.

### Additional Members for Workplace Committees
"(3) If there is no policy committee, a work place committee may, when dealing with an issue that would have come within the responsibilities of a policy committee, select two additional members. Unless otherwise provided in a collective agreement or other agreement, one of the additional members shall be an employee who meets the criteria set out in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b)."

Workplace committees, lacking a policy committee counterpart, have the option to add two members when addressing issues typically handled by a policy committee. At least one of these additional members must be an employee meeting the criteria of not exercising managerial functions and being selected according to the established process.

### Selection Process and Trade Union Involvement
"...have been selected by (i) the employees, if the employees are not represented by a trade union, or (ii) the trade union representing employees, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented."

This part of the section details the selection process for employee members. It emphasizes that if employees are not represented by a trade union, they are responsible for selecting the members. Conversely, if a trade union represents employees, the union must select the members in consultation with non-unionized employees. This ensures a collaborative and inclusive selection process.

### Alternate Members
"(6) The employer and employees may select alternate members to serve as replacements for members selected by them who are unable to perform their functions. Alternate members for employee members shall meet the criteria set out in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b)."

To ensure continuity, committees can designate alternate members who can step in when regular members are unavailable. These alternate members must meet the same criteria as the primary employee members, ensuring that the committee maintains a consistent composition of non-managerial employees.

question: What are the rules surrounding the provision of information that could reveal the identity of a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a policy committee or a workplace committee?
answer:
## Information and Policy/Workplace Committees Regarding Identity Disclosure

### Canada Labour Code Section 135.11

Section 135.11 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the restrictions on providing information that could reveal the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence occurrence to policy or workplace committees.

**Restriction on Disclosure Without Consent
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a policy committee or a work place committee with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place. Neither a policy committee nor a work place committee shall have access to that information without the person’s consent."

This section clearly states that employers and heads are prohibited from sharing information with committees if it could identify someone involved in a harassment or violence incident, unless that person has given their consent. This provision aims to protect the privacy of individuals who have experienced or witnessed such events.

**Exceptions to the Rule
"Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to (a) information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections; or (b) a decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2)."

This section specifies two exceptions to the general rule. The first exception applies to information shared under sections 128 or 129, or related to the application of those sections. The second exception applies to decisions, reasons, or directions made under subsection 146.1(2). These exceptions suggest that certain types of information sharing are permissible even without the individual's consent, likely to facilitate the committee's function and the resolution of the issue.

### Implications for Employers

Employers must be mindful of the information they share with policy and workplace committees. They must obtain consent from individuals before disclosing information that could reveal their identity. Failure to do so could violate the Canada Labour Code. Employers should also be aware of the exceptions outlined in Section 135.11, which may permit information sharing in certain circumstances.

question: What are the primary responsibilities of a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees, and how are they selected?
answer:
## Primary Responsibilities of a Health and Safety Representative in a Workplace with Fewer Than 20 Employees

### Selection Process

According to Section 136(1) of the Canada Labour Code, the health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than twenty employees is selected as follows:
"...the employees at the work place who do not exercise managerial functions shall select from among those employees the person to be appointed..."

This indicates that employees who are not in managerial roles have the responsibility of choosing the health and safety representative from among themselves. If the employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union selects the representative in consultation with any employees who are not represented, and subject to any regulations made under subsection (11).

### Core Duties and Functions

Section 136(5) outlines the key responsibilities of a health and safety representative. These duties are extensive and encompass a wide range of activities aimed at protecting employee health and safety. Some of the primary responsibilities include:

*   **Complaint Handling:
"...shall consider and expeditiously dispose of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees..." This highlights the representative's role in addressing and resolving employee concerns regarding safety issues.
*   **Record Keeping and Monitoring:
"...shall ensure that adequate records are maintained pertaining to work accidents, injuries, health hazards and the disposition of complaints related to the health and safety of employees and regularly monitor data relating to those accidents, injuries, hazards and complaints..." This emphasizes the importance of tracking safety data and identifying trends.
*   **Collaboration with Employer:
"...shall meet with the employer as necessary to address health and safety matters..." This underscores the representative's role as a liaison between employees and management.
*   **Program Implementation and Monitoring:
"...shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c)..." This refers to a program for the prevention of hazards, including employee education.
*   **Hazard Prevention:
"...shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of those hazards that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters related to those hazards..." This highlights the representative's role in proactively preventing hazards.
*   **Inquiries and Investigations:
"...shall participate in all of the inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to the health and safety of employees, including any consultations that may be necessary with persons who are professionally or technically qualified to advise the representative on those matters..." This indicates the representative's involvement in safety investigations.
*   **Policy Development and Implementation:
"...shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..." This emphasizes the representative's role in shaping safety protocols.
*   **Information Access:
"...shall have full access to all of the government and employer reports, studies and tests relating to the health and safety of employees, or to the parts of those reports, studies and tests that relate to the health and safety of employees, but shall not have access to the medical records of any person except with the person’s consent." This ensures the representative has the necessary information to fulfill their duties.
*   **Time and Compensation:
"...is entitled to take the time required, during their regular working hours, (a) to perform any of the representative’s functions; and (b) for the purposes of preparation and travel, as authorized by both chairpersons of the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, as authorized by the employer." and
"...shall be compensated by the employer for the functions described in paragraphs (8)(a) and (b), whether performed during or outside the representative’s regular working hours, at the representative’s regular rate of pay or premium rate of pay, as specified in the collective agreement or, if there is no collective agreement, in accordance with the employer’s policy." This ensures the representative is adequately compensated for their duties.

In summary, the health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees plays a crucial role in safeguarding employee well-being through a combination of employee selection, proactive hazard prevention, investigation, policy development, and information access.

question: Under what conditions can the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident be revealed to a health and safety representative?
answer:
## Identity Disclosure to Health and Safety Representatives

### General Rule: Consent Required
"Section 136.1 (1) Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place. A health and safety representative shall not have access to that information without the person’s consent."

This section clearly establishes the general rule: disclosure of information that could reveal the identity of someone involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident requires the individual's consent. The law prioritizes protecting the privacy of those involved.

### Exceptions to the Rule

However, there are specific exceptions to this rule outlined in the same section:

*   **(a) Information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections:** This exception allows for the disclosure of information if it is provided under specific sections of the Canada Labour Code (sections 128 and 129) or if it relates to a direction or report concerning the application of those sections.
*   **(b) A decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2):** This exception permits the disclosure of a decision, the reasons for that decision, or a direction related to subsection 146.1(2).

These exceptions are narrowly defined, suggesting that the law aims to balance the need for transparency with the protection of individual privacy.

### "Persons Involved" and Consent
"For this purpose, the “persons involved” are the  complainant, respondent, and witnesses who have provided information to either  the employer or the CP."

The employer must obtain consent from the "persons involved" before disclosing any identifying information to the CP, the WPHSC, or the Representative. This includes the complainant, respondent, and witnesses.

### Consent Form
"...it is recommended  the employer obtain consent in writing; a template “consent form” is found at Appendix B."

The employer should obtain consent in writing to demonstrate that the required consent was obtained from the persons involved. A template consent form is available in Appendix B.

question: Under what circumstances may an employer need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives?
answer:
## Circumstances Requiring Multiple Health and Safety Committees or Representatives

### Section 135 and 137 of the Canada Labour Code

Both Section 135 and Section 137 of the Canada Labour Code address the establishment of workplace health and safety committees and the appointment of health and safety representatives. These sections outline scenarios where an employer may need to establish multiple committees or appoint multiple representatives.

### Employer Controlling Multiple Workplaces
"Section 137 Despite sections 135 and 136, if an employer controls more than one work place..."

This indicates that if an employer oversees more than one workplace, the employer is required to establish a health and safety committee or appoint a health and safety representative for each workplace. This is to ensure that health and safety matters are addressed appropriately in each work environment.

### Size or Nature of Operations
"...the size or nature of the operations of the employer or those of the work place precludes the effective functioning of a single work place committee or health and safety representative..."

This provision addresses situations where a single committee or representative would be insufficient to effectively address the health and safety needs of the workforce. This could occur due to the size of the workforce, the complexity of the operations, or other factors that make it difficult for one committee or representative to adequately serve all workplaces.

### Approval or Direction of the Head
"...employer shall, subject to the approval or in accordance with the direction of the Head, establish or appoint..."

This section clarifies that the establishment of multiple committees or representatives requires the approval or direction of the Head. This ensures that the decision is made in the best interest of workplace health and safety.

In summary, an employer may need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives when they control multiple workplaces, or when the size or nature of their operations makes it impractical for a single committee or representative to effectively address health and safety matters. The establishment of these additional committees or representatives requires the approval or direction of the Head.

question: What is the purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission and how is it structured?
answer:
## Purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

The primary purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission is to ensure the health and safety of employees in coal mines. This is achieved through several key functions:

*   **Approval of Plans and Procedures:** The Commission has the authority to approve mining methods, machinery, and equipment to ensure they meet safety standards. This includes approving the use of equipment where prescribed safety standards do not exist, provided that the protection of employee health and safety is not diminished.
"The Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)."
    This indicates that the Commission plays a crucial role in reviewing and authorizing safety measures within coal mines.
*   **Investigation and Inquiry:** The Commission investigates matters referred to it by the Minister, particularly those involving disputes or differences between employers and employees. This involves inquiring into the matters referred to it and endeavoring to carry out its terms of reference.
"(a) shall inquire into the matters referred to it by the Minister and endeavour to carry out its terms of reference..."
*   **Exemptions and Substitutions:** The Commission can grant exemptions from certain regulations or substitute them with alternative provisions, as long as it doesn't negatively impact employee safety.
"...employer, the Commission may, if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, by order, (a) exempt the employer from compliance with any provision of the regulations in the operation of coal mines controlled by the employer, subject to any conditions contained in the order; or (b) substitute for any provision of the regulations, so far as it applies to coal mines controlled by the employer, another provision having substantially the same purpose and effect."
*   **Recommendations for Amendments:** The Commission can recommend amendments or revocations of regulations related to coal mines to the Minister.

## Structure of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

The Commission is structured as follows:

*   **Membership:** The Commission consists of no more than five members, appointed by the Minister.
"There is hereby established a Coal Mining Safety Commission, in this section referred to as the “Commission” consisting of, subject to subsection (2.1), not more than five members to be appointed by the Minister to hold office during pleasure."
*   **Chairperson:** One member is designated as Chairperson by the Minister.
"One member of the Commission shall be designated chairperson of the Commission by the Minister and the others shall be equally representative of the non-supervisory employees employed in coal mines and of the employers of those employees."
*   **Representation:** The remaining members are equally representative of non-supervisory employees and employers in coal mines.
*   **Alternate Chairperson:** The Minister may appoint an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the Chairperson.
"The Minister may appoint, by order, and under the terms and conditions specified in the order, any person as an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the chairperson. An alternate chairperson, while acting as chairperson, has all of the powers, duties and immunity of the chairperson."
*   **Quorum:** A quorum for the Commission consists of the Chairperson or alternate Chairperson, one member representative of non-supervisory employees, and one member representative of employers.
"A quorum of the Commission consists of the chairperson or alternate chairperson, one member representative of non-supervisory employees and one member representative of employers."
*   **Staff and Assistance:** The Minister can provide the Commission with necessary staff and other assistance to carry out its functions.
"The Minister may, at the request of the Commission, make available to the Commission such staff and other assistance as are necessary for the proper conduct of its activities."

question: What is the primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions?
answer:
## Primary Goal of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

The primary goal that the Coal Mining Safety Commission (Commission) considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions, is the **protection of the health and safety of employees.**

### Approval of Plans, Procedures, Methods, Machinery, and Equipment

Section 137.2(2) explicitly states:
"On the application of an employer, the Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, (a) approve in writing the use by the employer in coal mines of mining methods, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable; or (b) approve in writing, notwithstanding anything in this Part, the use by the employer in coal mines, for a specified time and subject to specified conditions, of any mining method, machinery or equipment that does not meet prescribed safety standards applicable in respect of it."

This indicates that the Commission's approval hinges on a careful assessment of whether the proposed plans, procedures, methods, machinery, or equipment will maintain or enhance employee safety. The phrase
"...if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..." highlights this central consideration.

### Exemptions and Substitutions for Regulatory Provisions

Similarly, Section 137.2(3) reinforces this priority. It states:
"On the application of an employer, the Commission may, if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, by order, (a) exempt the employer from compliance with any provision of the regulations in the operation of coal mines controlled by the employer, subject to any conditions contained in the order; or (b) substitute for any provision of the regulations, so far as it applies to coal mines controlled by the employer, another provision having substantially the same purpose and effect."

Here, the Commission's decision to grant exemptions or substitutions is contingent upon the assurance that employee health and safety will not be compromised. The requirement that the substituted provision "having substantially the same purpose and effect" further underscores the Commission's commitment to maintaining a level of safety equivalent to that mandated by the original regulation.

In essence, the Commission operates under a principle of balancing the needs of employers with the paramount importance of safeguarding the well-being of coal mine employees. The "protection of the health and safety of employees" serves as the guiding principle in all its decisions related to approving activities and modifying regulatory requirements.

question: What actions can the Minister take to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies?
answer:
## Minister's Role in Promoting Occupational Health and Safety

The Canada Labour Code grants the Minister significant authority to promote and ensure occupational health and safety. This authority is outlined in Section 138 of the Code, which details various actions the Minister can undertake.

### Establishing Special Committees
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies."

This indicates the Minister can establish committees to provide advice and assistance on occupational health and safety matters. These committees can help inform the Minister's decisions and contribute to the development of policies and programs.

### Conducting Inquiries
"The Minister may cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning occupational health and safety in any employment to which this Part applies and may appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."

The Minister has the power to initiate inquiries into occupational health and safety issues. This allows for a thorough investigation of specific concerns and the identification of necessary improvements.

### Undertaking Research
"The Minister may undertake research into the cause of and the means of preventing employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake such research in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or with any organization undertaking similar research."

The Minister can directly undertake research to understand the causes of workplace injuries and illnesses and to develop preventative measures. Furthermore, the Minister can collaborate with other government bodies, provinces, and organizations to enhance research efforts.

### Publishing Information and Disseminating Data
"The Minister may publish the results of any research undertaken under subsection (4) and compile, prepare and disseminate data or information bearing on health or safety of employees obtained from that research or otherwise."

The Minister is empowered to share research findings and relevant data to inform the public and stakeholders about occupational health and safety issues. This promotes transparency and facilitates the implementation of effective safety measures.

### Undertaking Programs
"The Minister may undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs."

The Minister can initiate programs aimed at preventing workplace injuries and illnesses. This includes the ability to collaborate with other entities to expand the reach and effectiveness of these programs.

### Head of Compliance and Enforcement
"The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement."

This provision allows the Minister to designate a specific individual to oversee compliance with the occupational health and safety provisions of the Canada Labour Code. This ensures effective enforcement of the regulations.

### Preventive Measures
"Preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, all with the goal of ensuring the health and safety of employees."

This outlines the hierarchy of controls that the Minister should prioritize when implementing preventive measures. It emphasizes eliminating hazards first, followed by reducing them, and finally providing personal protective equipment as a last resort.

question: What is the role of the Minister in relation to medical surveillance, examination programs, and reporting on harassment and violence in workplaces under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## The Minister's Role in Medical Surveillance, Examination Programs, and Reporting on Harassment and Violence

### Medical Surveillance and Examination Programs

The Canada Labour Code grants the Minister significant authority concerning medical surveillance and examination programs related to occupational health and safety.
"The Minister may undertake medical surveillance and examination programs with respect to occupational health and safety and may, if the Minister considers it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all of the provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs."

This indicates that the Minister has the power to initiate and oversee such programs, either independently or in collaboration with other entities. This includes the authority to appoint medical practitioners qualified in occupational medicine to carry out these programs.

### Reporting on Harassment and Violence

The Minister is mandated to produce and publish annual reports detailing statistical data related to harassment and violence in workplaces covered by the Canada Labour Code.
"The Minister shall prepare and publish an annual report that contains statistical data relating to harassment and violence in work places to which this Part applies. The report shall not contain any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence."

Furthermore, the Minister is required to conduct a review of the provisions of the Code pertaining to harassment and violence every five years.
"Five years after the day on which this section comes into force and every five years after that, the Minister shall commence a review of the provisions of this Part relating to harassment and violence. At the conclusion of the review, the Minister shall prepare a report on the review."

This report must be tabled in both Houses of Parliament within the first 15 days of their sitting after completion. The statistical data included in these reports must be categorized according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act.
"The statistical data contained in the report shall include information that is categorized according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act..."

question: Who can the Minister and the Head delegate their powers, duties, or functions to, and under what conditions?
answer:
## Delegation Authority of the Minister and the Head

### Who Can Be Delegated To?

Both the Minister and the Head can delegate their powers, duties, or functions "to any qualified person or class of persons." This indicates a broad scope of potential delegates.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part."

### Conditions for Delegation

The delegation is subject to certain conditions.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."

This means the Minister and the Head can impose terms and conditions on the delegation, and these conditions can be specified by the Minister.
"...the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with any province or any provincial body specifying the terms and conditions under which the Minister may delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body the powers, duties or functions that the Minister or the Head is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

The delegation can also be subject to terms and conditions outlined in agreements with provinces or provincial bodies, subject to approval from the Governor in Council.

question: What are the powers and responsibilities of the Head in carrying out duties related to workplace health and safety, particularly in terms of entering workplaces, conducting examinations, and issuing directions?
answer:
## Powers and Responsibilities of the Head in Workplace Health and Safety

### Entering Workplaces

The Head possesses the power to enter any workplace controlled by an employer "at any reasonable time" while carrying out their duties. This is outlined in Section 141(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"...the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may..."

This broad authority allows the Head to access workplaces as needed to fulfill their responsibilities related to health and safety.

### Conducting Examinations, Tests, Inquiries, Investigations, and Inspections

A key aspect of the Head's responsibilities is the ability to conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations, and inspections. This power is explicitly stated in Section 141(1).
"...may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them..."

The Head can undertake these activities directly or delegate the task to the employer. This ensures a proactive approach to identifying and addressing potential health and safety hazards.

### Issuing Directions

The Head has the authority to issue directions related to workplace health and safety, even when not physically present at the workplace. This is detailed in Section 141(1).
"Section 141 (1) ...may direct the employer to conduct them..." (no source found for the quotation)

This power allows the Head to mandate specific actions by the employer to improve workplace safety. The directions can cover a wide range of issues, including ensuring that places or things are not disturbed during investigations.
"(f) direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing..."

### Additional Powers

Beyond the core activities of entering workplaces, conducting examinations, and issuing directions, the Head has several other powers:

*   **Taking Samples:** The Head can take or remove samples of materials or substances for analysis.
*   **Bringing Equipment:** The Head can bring any equipment deemed necessary to carry out their duties.
*   **Obtaining Documents and Information:** The Head can direct the employer to produce documents and information related to workplace health and safety.
*   **Requiring Statements:** The Head can require employers or employees to make statements regarding working conditions and equipment.
*   **Witnesses:** The Head can direct someone to accompany them while they are in the workplace.
*   **Private Meetings:** The Head can meet with individuals in private or with legal counsel or union representatives present.

These additional powers provide the Head with a comprehensive toolkit to address workplace health and safety concerns effectively.



### Inspections

Section 141.1 outlines the conditions under which the Head can conduct inspections.
"Section 141.1 (1) If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer."

This ensures that inspections are conducted with appropriate representation to facilitate communication and address concerns. The Head can proceed with an inspection even if those representatives are not present, if they choose not to be.

question: What are the consequences and prohibitions related to interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and providing information to authorities?
answer:
## Interference with Powers and Duties under Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 143: Obstruction and False Statements

Section 143 of the Canada Labour Code outlines prohibitions against obstructing or hindering, or making false statements to authorities exercising powers and duties under Part II.
"No person shall obstruct or hinder, or make a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions, under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This section clearly states that any individual who intentionally obstructs or provides false information to the Head, external adjudicators, Board members, or delegated authorities is in violation of the law. This prohibition aims to ensure that investigations and oversight related to occupational health and safety can be conducted effectively and without interference.

### Section 143.1: Preventing the Provision of Information

Section 143.1 specifically prohibits actions that prevent an employee from providing information to authorities.
"No person shall prevent an employee from providing information to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This provision is crucial for ensuring that employees can freely and openly communicate relevant information regarding workplace health and safety concerns. It protects employees from being intimidated or prevented from cooperating with investigations or inquiries.

## Provision of Information to Authorities

### Section 141: Head's Powers Regarding Workplace Inspections and Investigations

Section 141 grants the Head broad powers to conduct inspections, investigations, and inquiries related to occupational health and safety.
"Section 141 (1) Subject to section 143.2, the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them; (b) take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent; (c) be accompanied or assisted by any person and bring any equipment that the Head deems necessary to carry out the Head’s duties; (d) take or remove, for testing, material or equipment if there is no reasonable alternative to doing so; (e) take photographs and make sketches; (f) direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (g) direct any person not to disturb any place or thing specified by the Head for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (h) direct the employer to produce documents and information relating to the health and safety of the employer’s employees or the safety of the work place and to permit the Head to..."

This section empowers the Head to gather information necessary to ensure workplace safety. It also outlines the Head's authority to investigate deaths and accidents, and to obtain relevant documents and information from employers.

### Section 143: Consequences for Interference

As highlighted earlier, Section 143 outlines the consequences for interfering with these powers and duties. Specifically, it states that
"No person shall obstruct or hinder, or make a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions, under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This means that anyone who attempts to impede an investigation, provide false information, or prevent an employee from sharing information with authorities faces legal repercussions. The purpose of this provision is to safeguard the integrity of the investigation process and ensure that workplace safety concerns are addressed effectively.

question: Under what condition can a person carrying out a duty under this Part enter a workplace that is situated in an employee's residence?
answer:
## Analysis of Access to Employee Residence

### Section 143.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 143.2 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the issue of access to an employee's residence. 

**Permission Requirement:
"No person who carries out a duty under this Part shall enter a work place that is situated in an employee’s residence without the employee’s permission."

This section clearly states that access to an employee's residence is **prohibited** unless the employee provides explicit permission. This provision is designed to protect the privacy and personal space of employees. 

**Scope of the Section:**

The section applies to
"...person who carries out a duty under this Part..." This implies that anyone performing duties related to the Canada Labour Code, such as health and safety inspections or investigations, must obtain the employee's consent before entering their home. 

**No Exceptions:**

The section does not outline any exceptions to the permission requirement. Therefore, unless the employee explicitly grants permission, access to their residence is not permitted.

question: What are the general rules regarding the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals, such as the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and others, in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Rules Regarding Disclosure of Information under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 144(3) - Non-Disclosure of Information
"Subject to subsection (4), the Head, an external adjudicator or a member of the Board who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 — or a person who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 that are delegated to them under subsection 140(1.1) or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2) — and any person accompanying them, shall not disclose to any person any information obtained in the work place by the Head, external adjudicator or member or person with regard to any secret process or trade secret, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law."

This section outlines a fundamental principle: individuals working under the authority of the Head, external adjudicators, or members of the Board are generally prohibited from disclosing information obtained while performing their duties. This protection extends to "secret process or trade secret," highlighting the importance of confidentiality in their roles. The exception to this rule is when disclosure is necessary for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code or is required by law.

### Section 144(5) - Restrictions on Publication or Disclosure
"No person shall, except for the purposes of this Part or for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part or unless the Head is satisfied that the publication or disclosure is in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest, publish or disclose any information obtained as a result of activities carried out under section 141."

This provision places a restriction on the general rule of non-disclosure. While information obtained under the authority of the Canada Labour Code is generally protected, it can be disclosed under specific circumstances. These circumstances include:

*   For the purposes of the Canada Labour Code itself.
*   In connection with a prosecution under the Canada Labour Code.
*   If the Head is satisfied that the publication or disclosure is in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest.

### Section 144(6) - Confidential Communication and Informant Protection
"No person to whom information obtained under section 141 is communicated in confidence shall divulge the name of the informant to any person except for the purposes of this Part, and no such person is competent or compellable to divulge the name of the informant before any court or other tribunal."

This section specifically addresses the protection of informants. It states that if information is received in confidence, the identity of the informant must be protected. No one is allowed to reveal the informant's name unless it is necessary for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code, and individuals who receive confidential information are legally bound not to disclose the informant's identity in court or other legal proceedings.

### Section 144(4) - Privileged Information
"All information that, under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , an employer is exempt from disclosing under this Act or the Hazardous Products Act and that is obtained in a work place under section 141 is privileged and, notwithstanding the Access to Information Act or any other Act or law, shall not be disclosed to any other person except for the purposes of this Part."

This section provides a specific form of protection for information related to hazardous materials. It states that information exempt from disclosure under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act is considered privileged and cannot be disclosed to anyone, even under general access to information laws, except for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What actions can the Head take if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened, and what are the requirements for documenting and communicating these actions?
answer:
## Head's Actions Upon Suspected Contravention

Based on the provided documents, the Head has several actions available to them if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened. These actions primarily revolve around investigation, documentation, and communication.

### Establishing Notices of Violation

Section 271 outlines the Head's ability to "establish the form of notices of violation." This indicates a formal process for communicating that a violation has occurred. 

>
"Section 271 The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation..."

This suggests that the Head is responsible for creating a standardized format for notifying the parties involved about the violation.

### Delegation of Authority

Section 271 also allows the Head to
"...designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation..." This implies that the Head can delegate the responsibility of issuing these notices to others, potentially streamlining the process.

>
"Section 271 The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation; (b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation..."

### Investigation and Evidence Gathering

Section 249 grants the Head broad powers to investigate potential violations. This includes the ability to:

*   Inspect and examine records.
*   Take extracts from records.
*   Require statements from employers and employees.
*   Require proof of insurance for long-term disability plans.
*   Require disclosure of information from employees.
*   Enter premises for inspection.
*   Request reasonable assistance from those within the workplace.

>
"For the purposes of this Part and the regulations, the Head may (a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee; (b) take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a); (c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment..."

These powers enable the Head to gather evidence to determine if a violation has occurred.

### Documentation and Communication Requirements

The documents emphasize the importance of documentation and communication.

*   **Informing the Head of Appeals:** Section 286(1) mandates that the Board must inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide a copy of the request. This ensures the Head is aware of any challenges to decisions.
>
"Section 286 (1) The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for..."

*   **Certificate of Authority:** Section 249(1.1) requires the Head to furnish a certificate of authority to anyone to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated. This provides a clear record of delegated authority.

>
"The Head shall furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated under subsection (1) a certificate of authority..."

*   **Record Keeping:** The Head is empowered to require employers to make and furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment. This ensures that records are maintained.

>
"(c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment..."

*   **Witness Protection:** Section 249(6) protects individuals who provide information to the Head from being required to testify in civil suits or proceedings, unless they have the Head's written permission. This encourages open communication and information sharing.

>
"...or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions..."

In summary, the Head can take actions to investigate potential violations, establish a formal process for notifying parties of violations, delegate authority to issue notices, and ensure proper documentation and communication throughout the process.

question: What are the powers, duties, and functions of the Board in relation to certain sections of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Powers, Duties, and Functions of the Board under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code grants the Board a wide range of powers, duties, and functions, as outlined in several sections. These can be broadly categorized as follows:

### 84. Powers of the Board

Section 84 details the Board's authority in relation to proceedings before it. It states:
"Section 84 A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board (a) may determine their own procedure; (b) has, in relation to any proceeding before them, the powers conferred on the Board, in relation to any proceeding before the Board, by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), (f) and (h); and (c) may authorize any person to do anything described in paragraph 16(b) or (f) that the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board may do and to report to the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board..."

This section essentially grants conciliators and conciliator boards the power to determine their own procedures and to exercise many of the same powers as the Board itself. Specifically, it mentions paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), (f), and (h) of section 16, indicating a significant delegation of authority. This suggests that the Board's powers are not limited to its own proceedings but can be extended to those conducted by conciliators and conciliator boards.

### 15. Powers and Duties: Regulations

Section 15 outlines the Board's power to make regulations of general application. This is a broad power that allows the Board to create rules and procedures governing various aspects of its operations.
"Section 15 The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings; (b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit; (f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit; (g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board..."

This section demonstrates the Board's extensive regulatory power. It covers a wide array of topics, including procedural rules, collective bargaining unit determination, certification of unions, conduct of representation votes, and the handling of evidence. The breadth of these regulations highlights the Board's role in shaping the entire process of labour dispute resolution.

### 16. Determination without oral hearing

Section 16 grants the Board the power to authorize individuals to perform certain functions on its behalf.
"(k) to authorize any person to do anything that the Board may do under paragraphs (a) to (h), (j), or (m) and to report to the Board..."

This section allows the Board to delegate its powers to others, enabling it to manage its workload efficiently. It specifically mentions the power to perform actions related to procedures, inquiries, and the handling of evidence.

In summary, the Board's powers, duties, and functions are extensive, encompassing procedural rules, collective bargaining, union certification, dispute resolution, and regulatory oversight. Sections 84, 15, and 16 collectively illustrate the breadth of authority granted to the Board under the Canada Labour Code.

question: What happens to a direction issued by the Head when an appeal is made, and what are the requirements for making the appeal?
answer:
## Appeal Process and Direction Status

### Appeal Process

The Canada Labour Code outlines the process for appealing a direction issued by the Head.
"An employer, employee or trade union that feels aggrieved by a direction issued by the Head under this Part may appeal the direction to the Board, in writing, within 30 days after the day on which the direction was issued or confirmed in writing."

This indicates that any party feeling aggrieved by a direction has 30 days from the date the direction was issued or confirmed to file a written appeal with the Board.

### Status of Direction During Appeal

The appeal of a direction does not automatically stop the direction from being in effect.
"Unless otherwise ordered by the Board on application by the employer, employee or trade union, an appeal of a direction does not operate as a stay of the direction."

This means that unless the Board specifically orders otherwise, the direction remains in force while the appeal is being processed.

### Head's Involvement

The Head is informed of the appeal.
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146 and provide him or her with a copy of the request for appeal."

This ensures the Head is aware of the appeal and receives a copy of the appeal request. The Head also has the opportunity to provide documents relied upon in making the decision or issuing the direction.
"The Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision or issuing the direction being appealed."



### Board's Actions

The Board has the power to review the appeal.
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)."

The Board will conduct a review, potentially modifying, cancelling, or upholding the original direction. They can also issue new directions as part of the appeal process.

question: What happens when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146 of the Canada Labour Code, and what actions can the Board take?
answer:
## Appeals of Decisions and Directions: Board's Role in Appeals

### Section 146.1: Board Inquiry and Actions
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)."

This section outlines the Board's responsibilities when an appeal is filed under either subsection 129(7) or section 146. The Board is mandated to conduct a "summary way and without delay" inquiry into the appeal. This implies a prompt and efficient review process. 

The Board has the authority to take several actions following this inquiry. These include:

*   **Varying, rescinding, or confirming the decision or direction:** The Board can modify the original decision, completely overturn it, or uphold it as is.
*   **Issuing new directions:** The Board can issue additional directions, potentially to clarify the situation or address any shortcomings in the original decision.

### Section 146.5: Employee Rights During Appeal Process
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This section specifies the rights of employees who participate in the appeal process. It states that employees who attend the proceedings, whether voluntarily or summoned by the Board, are entitled to be paid their regular wages for the time spent at the proceedings. This ensures that employees are not financially penalized for participating in the appeal process.

### Section 146. The Board's Reporting to the Head
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146 and provide him or her with a copy of the request for..."

This section details the process of informing the Head of an appeal. The Board is required to notify the Head in writing when an appeal is filed under either subsection 129(7) or section 146, and to provide the Head with a copy of the appeal request. This ensures that the Head is aware of the appeal and can take any necessary action.

### Section 146. The Board's Reporting to the Employer and Employee
"The Board shall provide a written decision, with reasons, and a copy of any direction to the employer, employee or trade union concerned and to the Head, and the employer shall, without delay, give a copy of the decision, the reasons, and any direction to the work place committee or health and safety representative."

This section outlines the process of disseminating the Board's decision and directions. The Board is required to provide a written decision, including the reasons for the decision, to the employer, employee, and any relevant trade union. The employer is then obligated to share this information with the workplace committee or health and safety representative without delay. This ensures transparency and allows all parties to be informed of the outcome of the appeal.

question: What happens to an employee's pay if they attend a proceeding under a specific subsection of the Canada Labour Code, or are summoned by the Board to attend such a proceeding?
answer:
## Employee Pay for Attending Hearings under the Canada Labour Code

### General Entitlement to Pay

Both the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) and the Canada Labour Code (CLC) establish the right of an employee to be paid for their time spent attending a proceeding. 

The Canada Industrial Relations Board's guide states:
"As an employee, if you are summoned by the Canada Industrial Relations Board to attend at an appeal proceeding, you are entitled to be paid at your regular rate of wages. Your employer must pay you your regular rate of wages for time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time spent at work." This indicates a clear entitlement to compensation for time spent at hearings convened by the CIRB.

This right is further reinforced by Section 288 of the Canada Labour Code, which explicitly states:
"An employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at an appeal proceeding under this Part and who attends is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." 

Section 146.5 of the Canada Labour Code provides a similar provision, stating:
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

### Scope of Entitlement

The entitlement to pay extends to time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been considered work time. This means that employees are not expected to forgo their regular wages for attending hearings related to wage recovery appeals or other proceedings under the Canada Labour Code. 

The Labour Standards document further clarifies this by stating that this applies to
"...appeal proceedings related to:  payment orders compliance orders notices of unfounded complaint, or notices of voluntary compliance..." This confirms that the right to be paid applies to a range of proceedings under the Canada Labour Code.

question: What protection does the Canada Labour Code offer to employees who exercise their rights or provide information related to workplace health and safety?
answer:
## Employee Protection under the Canada Labour Code for Health and Safety Rights

### Right to Use Safety Equipment

The Canada Labour Code mandates that employers must provide employees with the necessary safety equipment and clothing. Employees are obligated to use this equipment for their protection. This is explicitly stated in Section 126(1)(a):
"...use any safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing that are intended for the employee’s protection and furnished to the employee by the employer or that are prescribed..." This ensures employees have the tools to mitigate risks in the workplace.

### Duty to Report Hazardous Conditions

Employees have a right and a responsibility to report any workplace hazards. Section 126(1)(g) outlines this:
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer..." This provision empowers employees to proactively identify and address potential dangers before they lead to injuries.

### Protection Against Employer Retaliation for Reporting

The Canada Labour Code protects employees who report workplace hazards. Section 126(1)(g) emphasizes the importance of reporting, and the overall framework of the Code aims to encourage open communication about safety concerns. While not explicitly stated as protection *against* retaliation in this specific section, the broader context of occupational health and safety legislation implies that employers cannot retaliate against employees for fulfilling their duty to report hazards.

### Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

Employees have the right to refuse to perform work that poses a danger to themselves or others. This right is detailed in the "Right to refuse" section of WORKPPLACE-4_1:
"You have the right to refuse to work if you have reasonable cause to believe that:  your workplace presents a danger to you the use or operation of a machine or apparatus presents a danger to you or to another employee, and  the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to you or to another employee..." The text further clarifies that employees must follow proper procedures when exercising this right.

### Protection for Assistance in Emergencies

The Canada Labour Code provides protection for employees who assist in first-aid or other emergency measures. Section 126(3) states:
"No employee is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done in good faith by the employee when the employee is assisting the employer, as requested by the employer, in providing first-aid or in carrying out any other emergency measures." This ensures employees are not held liable for actions taken to help in emergency situations.

### Right to Participate in Health and Safety Committees

Employees have the right to participate in health and safety committees. WORKPPLACE-4_1 mentions that
"...employees have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns." as health and safety representatives or members of health and safety committees. Employers with 300 or more employees are required to establish a health and safety committee.

### Protection Against Contravention of the Code

Employees have the right to report situations they believe to be a contravention of the Canada Labour Code. Section 126(1)(j) states:
"...report to the employer any situation that the employee believes to be a contravention of this Part by the employer, another employee or any other person." This empowers employees to hold others accountable for failing to comply with health and safety regulations.
