question: What happens to an employee's employment status when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased from one employer to another, according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 44: Successor Rights and Obligations: Definitions

### Transfer or Lease of Business

Section 44(2) of the Canada Labour Code addresses the situation when a business is transferred or leased from one employer to another. It outlines several key provisions regarding the continuation of the employees' employment status.
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This passage indicates that upon the sale of a business, the existing trade union remains the bargaining agent for the employees. Furthermore, a trade union that had previously applied for certification for the employees can still be certified. Crucially, the new owner of the business is bound by any existing collective agreement applicable to the employees at the time of the sale. This ensures that the employees' terms and conditions of employment are largely maintained.

### Change of Activity or Sale of a Provincial Business

Section 44(3) further clarifies the situation when a provincial business undergoes a change of activity or is sold to an employer subject to the federal Labour Code.
"Where, as a result of a change of activity, a provincial business becomes subject to this Part, or such a business is sold to an employer who is subject to this Part, (a) the trade union that, pursuant to the laws of the province, is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the provincial business continues to be their bargaining agent for the purposes of this Part; (b) a collective agreement that applied to employees employed in the provincial business at the time of the change or sale continues to apply to them and is binding on the employer or on the person to whom the business is sold; (c) any proceeding that at the time of the change or sale was before the labour relations board or other person or authority that, under the laws of the province, is competent to decide the matter, continues as a proceeding under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party; and (d) any grievance that at the time of the change or sale was before an arbitrator or arbitration board continues to be processed under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party."

This section ensures that the existing collective agreement remains in effect even after a change of activity or sale, and that any ongoing legal proceedings or grievances are transferred to the new employer. This helps to protect the employees' rights and ensures continuity in the resolution of workplace issues.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code aims to protect the employment status and rights of employees when a business is transferred or leased. The existing trade union remains the bargaining agent, the collective agreement continues to be binding, and any ongoing legal proceedings are transferred to the new employer. This helps to ensure a smooth transition and protects the employees' interests.

question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make in relation to employee vacation rights and pay under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Regulations Regarding Employee Vacation Rights and Pay

The Governor in Council has the authority to make regulations concerning employee vacation rights and pay under the Canada Labour Code. These regulations cover a wide range of aspects related to vacation, as outlined in the provided documents.

### Waiver and Postponement of Vacation Rights
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this Division and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) defining the circumstances and conditions under which the rights of an employee under this Division may be waived or the enjoyment thereof postponed..."

### Notification of Vacation Time
"(b) prescribing the notices to be given to employees of the times when vacations may be taken..."

Regulations can mandate how employers must inform employees about the scheduling of their vacations. This ensures transparency and allows employees to plan accordingly.

### Defining Continuity of Employment
"(d) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of..."

This allows for the clarification of situations where absences, such as illness or leave, do not disrupt an employee's eligibility for vacation benefits.

### Determination of Year of Employment
"(e) respecting the determination by the employer of a year of employment in relation to any industrial..."

Regulations can establish the criteria and methods by which employers determine an employee's "year of employment," which is crucial for calculating vacation entitlements.

### Vacation and Vacation Pay for Specific Employees
"(f) for the calculation and determination of vacation and vacation pay in the case of seasonal or temporary employees or in other suitable cases..."

This allows for the creation of specific rules for calculating vacation and vacation pay for employees who do not fit the standard definition of full-time employees.

### Vacation in the Event of Temporary Cessation of Employment
"(g) providing for the granting of vacation or the payment of vacation pay in the event of temporary cessation of..."

Regulations can address the situation where an employee's employment is temporarily suspended, ensuring they still receive their vacation entitlements.

### Application to Employees with Unavoidable Absences
"(h) providing for the application of this Division where, owing to illness or other unavoidable absence, an employee has been absent from his..."

This ensures that employees who are temporarily unable to work due to illness or other unavoidable reasons still receive their vacation benefits.

In summary, the Governor in Council has broad authority to create regulations that govern nearly every aspect of employee vacation rights and pay under the Canada Labour Code, ensuring fairness and clarity for both employers and employees.

question: What types of work operations are considered continuous operations for the purpose of determining holiday entitlement under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Continuous Operations Under the Canada Labour Code

### Definition of Continuous Operations

Section 191 of the Canada Labour Code defines "employed in a continuous operation" as work in any of the following:
"...any industrial establishment in which, in each seven-day period, operations once begun normally continue without cessation until the completion of the regularly scheduled operations for that period; (b) any operations or services concerned with the running of trains, planes, ships, trucks or other vehicles, whether in scheduled or non-scheduled operations; (c) any telephone, radio, television, telegraph or other communication or broadcasting operations or services; or (d) any operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays."

This definition outlines a broad range of work environments that are considered continuous operations for holiday entitlement purposes. It encompasses industrial settings with ongoing operations, transportation services (scheduled and non-scheduled), communication and broadcasting industries, and any work that typically continues regardless of Sundays or public holidays.

### Specific Examples of Continuous Operations

The Canada Labour Code provides specific examples within the definition to clarify what constitutes a continuous operation. These include:

*   **Industrial establishments:** This covers a wide variety of workplaces where operations run continuously, such as factories, manufacturing plants, and other industrial settings.
*   **Transportation services:** This includes operations related to trains, planes, ships, and trucks, whether they operate on a fixed schedule or not.
*   **Communication and broadcasting:** This encompasses industries like telephone, radio, television, and telegraph services.
*   **Operations carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays:** This is a broad category that includes businesses that operate seven days a week, regardless of public holidays.

### Implications for Holiday Entitlement

The designation of a workplace as a continuous operation has significant implications for holiday entitlement. As stated in the Workplace-2_7 document,
"...an employee working in the continuous operations, there are separate general holiday entitlements." This means that employees in continuous operations are entitled to different holiday pay arrangements compared to those in non-continuous operations. Specifically, they are entitled to 1.5 times their regular rate of pay for the actual hours worked on a general holiday, in addition to general holiday pay, or be paid for the actual hours worked on the general holiday at their regular rate of wages. They are also entitled to a holiday with pay at some other time.

question: What is the general entitlement of employees regarding holidays with pay under the Canada Labour Code?

## General Entitlement to Holidays with Pay under the Canada Labour Code

### General Holiday Entitlement
"As an employee working for a federally regulated employer, you are entitled to a day off with pay for the following 10 days, which are called general holidays:  New Year’s Day Good Friday Victoria Day Canada Day Labour Day National Day for Truth and Reconciliation  Thanksgiving Day Remembrance Day Christmas Day Boxing Day..."

This passage from WORKPLACE-2_3 clearly outlines the specific days recognized as general holidays for employees working under federal regulations. It establishes the fundamental right to a paid day off for these designated holidays.

### Holiday Pay Entitlement
"Section 192 Except as otherwise provided by this Division, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on each of the general holidays falling within any period of his employment."

This statement from CLC-192 is a core principle of the Canada Labour Code regarding general holidays. It asserts that every employee is legally entitled to holiday pay for each general holiday that falls within their employment period. This is a broad and encompassing statement of entitlement.

### Pay for Working on General Holidays
"When you work on a general holiday in a “continuous operation” business or sector, you are entitled to:  1.5 times your regular rate of pay for the actual hours worked on the general holiday, in addition to general holiday pay (for information on the general holiday pay entitlement, refer to Calculating general holiday pay), or be paid for the actual hours worked on the general holiday at your regular rate of wages. You must also be provided a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to your annual vacation or on another day that is convenient to both you and your employer, or be paid holiday pay for the first day on which you do not work after the general holiday, if permitted by your collective agreement..."

This section from WORKPLACE-2_7 details the specific compensation an employee receives for working on a general holiday. It states that employees are entitled to at least 1.5 times their regular rate of pay for hours worked, in addition to general holiday pay. Furthermore, it guarantees a substitute paid holiday at a later date.

### Holiday Pay for Employees in Continuous Operations
"An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable."

This passage from CLC-196 clarifies the conditions under which employees in continuous operations are *not* entitled to holiday pay. It emphasizes the requirement to report for work when called and the obligation to be available according to the terms of employment.

### Holiday Pay During Leave
"When you are on leave with pay, your:  employment status does not change, and benefits accumulate as if you were at work  In addition, you continue to earn vacation time and pay during the leave period. When you are on leave without pay, your:  seniority continues to accumulate, and vacation pay is calculated only on your wages earned during the “year of employment”  The leave of absence does not change the date on which you become eligible for:  additional weeks of vacation, and an increase in vacation pay..."

This information from WORKPLACE-2_3 explains that even during a leave of absence, employees continue to accrue benefits and vacation pay. This ensures that the entitlement to holiday pay is not affected by a temporary leave.

### Holiday Pay for Managers and Professionals
"In this instance, there is no additional entitlement to a day off. If you are a manager or professional who is required to work on a general holiday, you are entitled to receive your regular rate of pay. In addition, you must receive a substitute general holiday with pay at another time."

This statement from WORKPLACE-2_6 specifies the pay entitlement for managers and professionals who are required to work on a general holiday, which is their regular rate of pay, along with a substitute paid holiday.

question: If a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, what are the employee's entitlements according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Entitlements for General Holidays Falling on Non-Working Days

### Section 193(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This section clearly outlines the entitlement when a general holiday coincides with a non-working day for an employee. It states that the employee is entitled to a "holiday with pay at some other time." This means the employer must provide the employee with a paid day off, either by adding it to their annual vacation time or granting it as a separate paid holiday at a mutually agreeable time. This ensures the employee receives the benefit of the holiday even if it falls on a day they would normally not be working.

### Section 193(2) - Specific Application to Certain Holidays
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division, when New Year’s Day, Canada Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Remembrance Day, Christmas Day or Boxing Day falls on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on the working day immediately preceding or following the general holiday."

This subsection provides a specific rule for certain holidays that fall on weekends. It specifies that if any of the listed holidays occur on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to a paid holiday on the working day immediately before or after the general holiday. This ensures that employees do not lose out on a holiday simply because it falls on a weekend that is not their regular working day.

question: Are there any exceptions to the application of Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code regarding holidays with pay for employees?
answer:
## Exceptions to Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code

### General Holiday Falling on a Day Off

Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code addresses situations where a general holiday falls on a day that is normally a non-working day for an employee. It states:
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This section outlines the general rule for employees whose scheduled day off coincides with a general holiday. However, it also includes a specific exception outlined in subsection (2).

### Exception for Employees under Collective Agreements

Section 194 provides an exception to Section 193. It states:
"Section 193 does not apply in respect of any employees who are employed under the terms of a collective agreement that entitles those employees to at least nine holidays with pay, exclusive of any annual vacation, in each year."

This means that if an employee is covered by a collective agreement that guarantees them at least nine paid holidays per year (excluding vacation time), Section 193 does not apply to them. This is a significant exception, as it acknowledges that collective agreements can provide employees with greater holiday entitlements than those mandated by the Canada Labour Code.

### Holiday Work for Managers, etc.

Section 199 outlines an exception for employees excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who are required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay. It states:
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This exception applies to specific employees who are excluded from the general rules of the Canada Labour Code, providing them with a holiday with pay at a later date if they are required to work on a general holiday.

question: Under what conditions can an employer substitute a different day for a general holiday for their employees according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Employer Substitution of General Holidays: Conditions Under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific conditions under which an employer can substitute a different day for a general holiday for their employees. These conditions vary depending on whether the employees are covered by a collective agreement or not.

### Substitution for Employees Subject to Collective Agreement (Section 195)

An employer can substitute a day for a general holiday for employees subject to a collective agreement if the substitution is agreed to in writing by both the employer and the trade union.
"An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, substitute any other day for a general holiday if the substitution is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union, and the substituted day shall, for that employee or those employees, be deemed to be a general holiday for the purposes of this Part."

This means that a collaborative agreement between the employer and the union is a prerequisite for any substitution to be valid. The substituted day is then legally considered a general holiday for those employees.

### Substitution for Employees Not Subject to Collective Agreement (Section 195)

For employees not covered by a collective agreement, the conditions for substitution are more stringent. An employer can substitute a day for a general holiday if one of the following conditions is met:

*   **Individual Employee Approval:** The employee provides written approval for the substitution.
*   **Majority Employee Approval:** At least 70% of the affected employees provide written approval for the substitution.
"Subject to subsection (3), an employer may, in respect of one or more employees not subject to a collective agreement, substitute any other day for a general holiday and the substituted day shall, for that employee or those employees, be deemed to be a general holiday for the purposes of this Part, if the substitution has been approved (a) in the case of a substitution that affects one employee, by that employee in writing; or (b) in the case of a substitution that affects more than one employee, by at least 70% of the affected employees."

Furthermore, if a substitution is to be made for employees not subject to a collective agreement, the employer is required to post a notice of the substitution in readily accessible places for at least 30 days before the substitution takes effect.
"If any other day is to be substituted for a general holiday under subsection (2), the employer shall post a notice of the substitution in readily accessible places where it is likely to be seen by the affected employees, for at least 30 days before the substitution takes effect."

There is an exception to the posting requirement: a substitution in respect of one employee following a request made under subsection 177.1(1) is exempt.

### Alternative Day for Holiday Falling on a Day Off (Section 193)

There is a specific provision for when a general holiday falls on a day that is already a non-working day for an employee. In such cases, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time.
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This ensures that employees who would otherwise not be working on a general holiday still receive the benefit of the holiday with pay.

question: How is holiday pay calculated for employees under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Holiday Pay Calculation under the Canada Labour Code

### General Holiday Pay Entitlement

The Canada Labour Code outlines the entitlement to holiday pay for employees working for federally regulated employers. Generally, employees are entitled to
"...no less than 1.5 times your regular rate of wages for the time worked on that day, and general holiday pay for that day..." if they work on a general holiday. This is stated in WORKPLACE-2_6.

### Regular Rate of Wages Calculation

The calculation of regular rate of wages is crucial for determining holiday pay.
"Your regular rate of wages is equal to:  the average daily earnings, excluding overtime pay, for the 20 days you worked immediately before the general holiday, or an amount calculated by a method agreed on in your collective agreement, if applicable..." This average is used when an employee's hours of work vary from day to day or if they are paid on a basis other than an hourly rate.

### Holiday Pay for Employees Paid on Commission

For employees paid in whole or in part by commission, the holiday pay entitlement is calculated differently.
"...your general holiday pay is equal to at least one-sixtieth (1/60th) of the wages, excluding overtime pay, earned in the 12-week period immediately before the week in which the general holiday occurs..." if they have completed at least 12 weeks of continuous employment. If they have not completed 12 weeks of continuous employment, the entitlement is
"...equal to at least one-twentieth (1/20th) of your wages, excluding overtime pay, earned in the 4-week period immediately before the week in which the general holiday occurs..."

### Holiday Pay for Employees in the Longshoring Sector

Employees working in the longshoring sector have a specific holiday pay calculation.
"...your general holiday pay is your basic rate of wages multiplied by at least one-twentieth (1/20th) of the total number of hours worked, excluding overtime hours, during the 4-week period before the week in which the holiday occurs." However, there are exceptions.
"...if you work for an employers’ association and perform work for another employer who is not a member of the association, a different calculation applies. In this case, instead of general holiday pay, the other employer must also pay you, on each payday, an amount equal to 3.5% of your basic rate of wages, multiplied by the number of hours you worked during that pay period."  Furthermore, if an employee is required to work on a general holiday, their employer must pay them
"...at least 1.5 times your basic rate of wages for the time worked on that day."

### Holiday Pay for Part-Time Employees

Part-time employees are entitled to the same 10 general holidays as full-time employees. However, their holiday pay is adjusted based on the number of hours they work. This means that the calculation will be proportional to their regular hours of work. (WORKPPLACE-2_5).

question: What are the requirements for an employee who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Requirements for Employees Working on a General Holiday under the Canada Labour Code

### General Pay Entitlement

The Canada Labour Code stipulates that an employee required to work on a general holiday is entitled to at least 1.5 times their regular rate of wages for the time worked, in addition to general holiday pay. This is explicitly stated in Section 197(1) of the Canada Labour Code:

>
"An employee who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be paid, in addition to the holiday pay for that day, wages at a rate equal to at least one and one-half times their regular rate of wages for the time that they work on that day."

This means that the employee receives a premium rate of pay for working on the holiday, reflecting the fact that it is a day they would otherwise be entitled to holiday pay.

### Alternative Holiday Compensation

Section 197(2) further clarifies the options available to the employer regarding holiday compensation for employees working on a general holiday:

>
"(b) be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer..."

This indicates that if an employee works on a general holiday, they are entitled to a substitute day off with pay. This can be integrated into their annual vacation or scheduled at a mutually agreeable time.

### Continuous Operations Exception

For employees working in continuous operations, there are specific provisions. Section 197(2)(a) states:

> "(a) be paid in accordance with subsection (1);"

This means that employees in continuous operations are entitled to the same premium pay as outlined in subsection (1) when working on a general holiday. Additionally, they are also entitled to either a substitute day off with pay or holiday pay for the first day they do not work after the general holiday, as permitted by their collective agreement.

### Managers and Professionals

For managers or professionals required to work on a general holiday, the requirements are different. Section 199 states:

>
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This means that managers and professionals are entitled to a substitute day off with pay, even if they are excluded from the general holiday pay provisions outlined in Section 197.

### No Entitlement for Non-Reporting

It is important to note that if an employee is scheduled to work on a general holiday but does not report to work, they are no longer eligible to receive pay for the general holiday. This is outlined in Section 196(4):

>
"(4) An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable."

This provision ensures that employees are only compensated for holidays when they actually work.

question: What is the status of the provision regarding holiday work for managers and others under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Holiday Work for Managers and Others under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 199: Holiday Pay for Managers and Others

Section 199 addresses the situation where an employee is excluded from the application of Division I (which deals with general holidays) under subsection 167(2), but is still required to work on a day they are entitled to holiday pay. 

The relevant text states:
"Section 199 Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This provision ensures that even if an employee falls outside the standard holiday pay rules, they are still entitled to a holiday with pay. The provision specifies that this holiday can be granted either by adding it to their annual vacation or by providing it at a mutually convenient time. This ensures fairness and addresses potential inequities that might arise from excluding certain employees from the regular holiday pay provisions.

### Section 197: Conflict with Division I

It is important to note that Section 199 explicitly states "Despite section 197," indicating that it overrides the provisions of Section 197. Section 197 deals with additional pay for holiday work. This suggests that Section 199 provides a specific exception to the general rules outlined in Section 197, particularly for employees excluded from Division I.

### Section 198: Repealed Provision

Section 198 is repealed, meaning it is no longer in effect. The marginal note indicates that it pertained to "Holiday work for managers, etc." This suggests that there was previously a provision addressing holiday work specifically for managers and similar roles, but it has since been removed from the Canada Labour Code.

In summary, the current status of the provision regarding holiday work for managers and others is addressed primarily by Section 199. This section ensures that employees excluded from Division I still receive a holiday with pay if they are required to work on a general holiday. The previous provision in Section 198 has been repealed.

question: What happens when an employee who is excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay?
answer:
## Analysis of Section 199 of the Canada Labour Code

### Exclusion from Division I and Holiday Pay

Section 199 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the specific situation of employees who are excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) and are required to work on a day they are entitled to holiday pay. 

The relevant text states:
"Section 199 Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This indicates that even though these employees are generally excluded from the holiday pay provisions outlined in Section 197, they are still entitled to a holiday with pay if they work on a day they are otherwise entitled to holiday pay. The holiday pay is not provided on the holiday itself, but rather
"...at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer." This ensures that the employee receives the holiday pay they would otherwise be entitled to, while also accommodating the operational needs of the employer.

question: What is the status of holiday pay granted to an employee under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Holiday Pay Under the Canada Labour Code

### General Status of Holiday Pay

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) establishes that
"Holiday pay granted to an employee is for all purposes deemed to be wages." This means that holiday pay is considered part of an employee's total compensation. 

### Holiday Pay for Working on a General Holiday

The CLC outlines specific provisions regarding holiday pay when an employee works on a general holiday.
"The Canada Labour Code does not prohibit work on a general holiday. If you are an employee who works on a general holiday, your wages may need to be adjusted to account for the work performed on the general holiday. If you are entitled to holiday pay and your employer requires you to work on a general holiday, your employer must pay you:  no less than 1.5 times your regular rate of wages for the time worked on that day, and general holiday pay for that day..."

This indicates that employees working on a general holiday are entitled to at least 1.5 times their regular rate of wages, in addition to general holiday pay. 

### Holiday Pay for Managers and Professionals
"In this instance, there is no additional entitlement to a day off. If you are a manager or professional who is required to work on a general holiday, you are entitled to receive your regular rate of pay. In addition, you must receive a substitute general holiday with pay at another time."

Managers and professionals who work on a general holiday are entitled to their regular rate of pay and a substitute paid holiday at a later date.

### Holiday Pay During Leave
"You are entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday takes place while you are on 1 of the following leaves:  personal leave leave for victims of family violence, or bereavement leave medical leave  If a general holiday occurs while you are on a leave with pay, you will only be paid general holiday pay for that day. Your leave with pay may continue the next regular working day without interruption. In this case, because you were only paid for the general holiday and not for the leave with pay, a day of leave with pay will not be subtracted from your entitlement."

Employees on certain types of leave are entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday falls during their leave. The leave with pay does not get reduced for the day the holiday falls on.

### Calculating Regular Rate of Wages
"To calculate your general holiday pay, if you are paid on a basis other than time, or if your hours of work differ from day to day, your employer will need to determine your regular rate of wages. Your regular rate of wages is equal to:  the average daily earnings, excluding overtime pay, for the 20 days you worked immediately before the general holiday, or an amount calculated by a method agreed on in your collective agreement, if applicable..."

The regular rate of wages is calculated based on the average daily earnings over the 20 days preceding the holiday, or as per the terms of a collective agreement.

### Additional Holiday Pay for Continuous Operation Employees
"An employee employed in a continuous operation who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall (a) be paid in accordance with subsection (1); (b) be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer; or (c) be paid holiday pay for the first day on which they do not work after that day, if a collective agreement that is binding on the employer and the employee so provides."

Employees in continuous operation are entitled to holiday pay and either a substitute paid holiday or holiday pay for the first day they do not work after the holiday, depending on the collective agreement.

### Holiday Pay for Employees on Commission
"An employee whose wages are paid in whole or in part on a commission basis and who has completed at least 12 weeks of continuous employment with an employer shall, for each general holiday, be paid holiday pay equal to at least one sixtieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that they earned in the 12-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs."

Employees on commission are entitled to holiday pay equal to at least one-sixtieth of their wages earned in the 12 weeks preceding the holiday, provided they have completed at least 12 weeks of continuous employment.

### Employees Not Entitled to Holiday Pay
"An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable."

Employees in continuous operation are not entitled to holiday pay if they do not report for work after being called to work or if they make themselves unavailable when required to work.

"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This means that the provisions of Section 189 are relevant to the interpretation and application of the rules and regulations outlined in Section 201 regarding General Holidays.

Marginal note: Idem, application (3) Any regulation made pursuant to subsection (2) may be made applicable to all federal works, undertakings or businesses or particularly to one or more such works, undertakings or businesses or such classes thereof or classes of employees thereof as may be specified in the regulations. R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 203 R.S., 1985, c. 9 (1st Supp.), s. 9 2017, c. 33, s. 204"

question: What is the main purpose of the regulations that can be made under section 203 of the Canada Labour Code, and how do they aim to support employees in multi-employer employment?
answer:
## Main Purpose of Regulations under Section 203 of the Canada Labour Code

The main purpose of the regulations that can be made under Section 203 of the Canada Labour Code is to ensure that employees engaged in multi-employer employment have the same rights and benefits as employees employed by a single employer, to the extent that is practicable.

### Defining Multi-Employer Employment

Section 203(1) of the Canada Labour Code defines "multi-employer employment" as
"...employment in any occupation or trade in which, by custom of that occupation or trade, any or all employees would in the usual course of a working month be ordinarily employed by more than one employer." This definition is further elaborated upon by regulations made by the Governor in Council.

### Aiming to Support Employees in Multi-Employer Employment

The regulations aim to support employees in multi-employer employment by:

*   **Modifying Existing Provisions:** The regulations allow the Governor in Council to modify existing provisions of Divisions I, IV, V, VII, VIII, X, XI, XIII, or XIV of the Canada Labour Code. This is to ensure that employees engaged in multi-employer employment will be entitled to the same rights and benefits as employees employed by a single employer,
"...to the extent that the Governor in Council considers necessary..."
*   **Defining Multi-Employer Employment More Specifically:** The regulations provide for a more detailed definition of "multi-employer employment," as outlined in Section 203(2). This allows for a clearer understanding of which employment situations fall under the umbrella of multi-employer employment.
*   **Applying Regulations to Federal Works and Businesses:** The regulations can be made applicable to all federal works, undertakings, or businesses, or to specific ones. This ensures that employees working in these settings, even if they are employed by multiple employers, have access to the protections afforded by the Canada Labour Code.
*   **Ensuring Shared Rights and Benefits:** The overarching goal is to ensure that employees in multi-employer employment are not disadvantaged compared to those employed by a single employer. This includes access to rights and benefits related to wages, holidays, leaves, and other labour standards.

In essence, the regulations under Section 203 are designed to address the complexities of multi-employer employment and to ensure that workers in these situations are afforded the same level of protection and rights as their counterparts in traditional employer-employee relationships.

Reassignment and job modification are provided for in section 204 which states: "(1) An employee who is pregnant or nursing may, during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, request the employer to modify her job functions or reassign her to another job if, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child. (2) An employee's request under subsection (1) must be accompanied by a certificate from a health care practitioner of the employee's choice indicating the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk." The employer's obligations are provided for in section 205 which states: "(1) An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee's job functions or reassign her. (3) The onus is on the employer to show that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate issued under subsection 204(2) is not reasonably practicable. (4) If the employer concludes that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate is not reasonably practicable, the employer shall inform the employee in writing." Return to Work is provided for in subsection 239.1(3) which states: "(3) Subject to the regulations, the employer shall, where reasonably practicable, return an employee to work after the employee's absence due to work-related illness or injury." The above provisions apply to student interns undertaking internships to fulfill the requirements of their educational program. The only exception is if a health care practitioner issues a certificate stating that a student intern is unable to continue performing internship activities, or if the employer informs the student intern in writing that a proposed modification or reassignment is not “Reasonably Practicable”. In such case, it is at the discretion of the employer to give the student intern a leave of absence until they are able to resume their internship."

question: What accommodations can an employee who is pregnant or nursing request from their employer, and what documentation is required to support such a request?
answer:
## Accommodations for Pregnant or Nursing Employees

### Request for Job Modification or Reassignment

An employee who is pregnant or nursing can request their employer to
"...modify her job functions or reassign her to another job..." during the period from the beginning of pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following birth. This is outlined in Section 204(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing may, during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, request the employer to modify her job functions or reassign her to another job if, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."

This provision allows for adjustments to the employee's work to accommodate the physical or health-related challenges associated with pregnancy and nursing.

### Required Documentation

To support this request, the employee must provide the employer with a certificate from a healthcare practitioner of their choice. This certificate must
"...the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk."
"An employee's request under subsection (1) must be accompanied by a certificate from a health care practitioner of the employee's choice indicating the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk."

This documentation is crucial as it provides the employer with medical justification for the requested accommodation and outlines the specific measures needed to ensure the employee's health and safety, as well as the well-being of the fetus or child.

## Employer's Obligations

The employer has an obligation to
"...examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee's job functions or reassign her." This is stated in Section 205(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee's job functions or reassign her."

The employer is also required to demonstrate that a modification or reassignment that would avoid the identified risks is "not reasonably practicable." If the employer concludes this, they must inform the employee in writing.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employer when an employee requests a job modification or reassignment due to a risk indicated in a certificate issued under subsection 204(2), and what are the rights of the employee during this process?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities and Employee Rights Regarding Maternity-Related Job Modifications or Reassignments

This response outlines the employer's responsibilities and the employee's rights when an employee requests a job modification or reassignment due to a risk indicated in a certificate issued under subsection 204(2) of the Canada Labour Code (CLC).

### Employer Obligations

**1. Examination of the Request:
"An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee..." This indicates that the employer is obligated to seriously consider the employee's request. The examination must be done in collaboration with the employee, ensuring their perspective is taken into account.

**2. Modification or Reassignment:
"An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee’s job functions or reassign her." This is a key obligation. The employer must make a reasonable effort to either modify the employee's existing job or assign them to a different one that avoids the risk identified in the certificate.

**3. Determining Reasonableness:
"The onus is on the employer to show that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate issued under subsection 204(2) is not reasonably practicable." This clarifies the burden of proof. The employer must demonstrate why a modification or reassignment is not feasible, rather than the employee having to prove the risk.

**4. Written Communication:
"If the employer concludes that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate is not reasonably practicable, the employer shall so inform the employee in writing." The employer is required to provide written notification if they cannot accommodate the request.

### Employee Rights

**1. Entitlement to Continue in Current Job During Examination:
"An employee who has made a request under subsection 204(1) is entitled to continue in her current job while the employer examines her request..." This ensures the employee is not penalized or disadvantaged while the employer is considering the request.

**2. Leave of Absence if Risk Requires:
"...but, if the risk posed by continuing any of her job functions so requires, she is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence with pay at her regular rate of wages until the employer (a) modifies her job functions or reassigns her, or (b) informs her in writing that it is not reasonably practicable to modify her job functions or reassign her, and that pay shall for all purposes be deemed to be wages." This provides crucial protection. If the employee's health or the health of the fetus or child is at risk, they are entitled to a paid leave of absence while the employer considers the request.

**3. Continued Job Status and Benefits:
"An employee whose job functions are modified or who is reassigned shall be deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time of making the request under subsection 204(1), and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job." This ensures that the employee's employment status and benefits are maintained even after a modification or reassignment.

**4. Entitlement to Leave for Duration of Risk:
"An employee referred to in subsection (4) is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence for the duration of the risk as indicated in the certificate." This guarantees a leave of absence for the entire period specified in the medical certificate.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who is pregnant or nursing in terms of notifying their employer and providing documentation regarding their leave of absence?
answer:
## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Notification and Documentation for Pregnancy or Nursing Leave

### Entitlement to Leave and Initial Notification
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability."

This indicates that an employee must initially inform their employer of their need for leave by providing a medical certificate. The certificate must specify the inability to work due to pregnancy or nursing and the expected duration of the leave. This is a crucial first step to secure the employee's right to leave.

### Ongoing Notification of Changes
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate."

This section outlines the employee's responsibility to keep their employer informed of any changes to their medical situation that might affect their leave. The employee must provide at least two weeks' written notice, along with a new medical certificate, if the duration of their inability to work changes. This ensures the employer has up-to-date information to manage the employee's leave and workplace arrangements.

### Duty to Consult with Healthcare Practitioner
"The employee must consult with a , as defined in section 166, of her choice as soon as possible to establish whether continuing any of her current job functions poses a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."

This highlights the employee's responsibility to seek medical advice and documentation. question: What are the conditions and entitlements for an employee who is pregnant to take a leave of absence from work, and how long can the leave be extended under certain circumstances?
answer:
## Maternity Leave Entitlements and Extensions

### Entitlement to Leave

An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to a leave of absence from work during a specific period. According to Section 206 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 17 weeks, which leave may begin not earlier than 13 weeks prior to the estimated date of her confinement and end not later than 17 weeks following the actual date of her confinement, if the employee provides her employer with a certificate of a health care practitioner certifying that she is pregnant."

Furthermore, Section 205.1 elaborates on this entitlement, stating that an employee must provide a certificate from a healthcare practitioner indicating inability to work due to pregnancy or nursing. This certificate must also specify the duration of that inability.

### Extension of Leave

The duration of the maternity leave can be extended under certain circumstances. 

Section 206.1 outlines the possibility of extending the leave.
"The period referred to in subsection (2) is extended by the number of weeks during which the employee is on leave under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9, is absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1) or is on leave under any of paragraphs 247.5(1)(a), (b) and (d) to (g)." This means that if an employee takes other types of leave during or after their maternity leave, the maternity leave period can be extended.

Additionally,
"If the child referred to in subsection (1) is hospitalized during the period referred to in subsection (2), the period is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized." This ensures that the leave period is extended to cover the hospitalization of the newborn child.

However, these extensions are subject to a limitation.
"An extension under subsection (2.1) or (2.2) must not result in the period being longer than 104 weeks." This means that even with multiple extensions, the total duration of the leave cannot exceed 104 weeks.

### Obligation to Inform Employer

Section 205.1 also specifies the employee's duty to inform the employer of any changes to the duration of the risk or inability, as indicated in the certificate issued by a healthcare practitioner.
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." This ensures that the employer is aware of any changes to the leave period and can make appropriate arrangements.

question: What is the purpose of the leave provided under section 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code, and what life events qualify an employee for this leave?
answer:
## Purpose of Parental Leave under Section 206.1

Section 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code provides a leave of absence from employment to care for a newborn child or a child in adoption. The primary purpose of this leave is to allow employees to bond with and provide care for their new family member during a crucial period.
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 63 weeks to care for a newborn child of the employee or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides."

This quote clearly states the core purpose of the leave: to care for a newborn child or a child who has been adopted. The leave is granted to eligible employees, subject to certain limitations outlined in the subsequent subsections.

## Qualifying Life Events

The following life events qualify an employee for parental leave under Section 206.1:

1.  **Birth of a Newborn Child:
"...to care for a newborn child of the employee..." - This explicitly includes the birth of a child and the subsequent need for parental care.
2.  **Adoption of a Child:
"...or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides." - This extends the leave to employees who adopt a child, recognizing the same need for care and bonding.

The section further clarifies the timeframe during which the leave can be taken, linking it to the period beginning on the day the child is born or comes into the actual care of the employee, or the day the child comes into the actual care of the employee in the case of adoption. The duration of the leave is capped at 63 weeks, with potential extensions based on various factors, including concurrent leave under other sections of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What are the maximum aggregate leave limits for multiple employees and for a single employee in respect of the same birth?
answer:
## Aggregate Parental and Maternity Leave Limits

### Aggregate Leave for Multiple Employees

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) specifies the maximum aggregate leave that can be taken by multiple employees for the same birth.
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by more than one employee under sections 206 and 206.1 in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 86 weeks..." This means that if two or more parents share parental leave, the total amount of leave taken by all of them combined cannot exceed 86 weeks.

### Aggregate Leave for a Single Employee

The CLC also sets a limit on the amount of leave that a single employee can take in respect of the same birth.
"...the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under those sections in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 78 weeks." This indicates that even if a parent takes maternity leave and then parental leave, or takes parental leave alone, the total leave for that parent cannot exceed 78 weeks.

## Additional Considerations

It is important to note that the combined maternity and parental leave periods for one parent cannot exceed 78 weeks.
"Parents who share the parental leave have access to a combined 86 weeks of maternity and parental leave." This is a key provision to consider when parents decide how to distribute their leave.

question: What is the purpose of the leave of absence provided for in the CLC, and under what conditions can an employee take this leave?
answer:
## Purpose of Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force

The primary purpose of the leave of absence provided for in the Canada Labour Code (CLC) is to enable employees who are members of the Reserve Force to participate in military operations and activities. This is explicitly stated in Section 247.5(1), which outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to take leave.

### Conditions for Taking Leave

An employee is eligible for this leave if they meet the following conditions:

*   **Minimum Employment Duration:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities..." This indicates that a minimum of three consecutive months of employment is required to qualify for the leave.
*   **Authorized Activities:** The leave can be taken for a variety of activities, including:
"...an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..." This covers the entire process of deployment, from preparation to return.
    *   "an activity set out in the regulations;" This allows for flexibility in addressing specific needs.
    *   "Canadian Armed Forces military skills training;" This ensures that reservists can participate in training required for their duties.
"...training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act..." This covers mandatory training orders.
"...duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act..." This addresses situations where reservists are activated for specific duties.
"...service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act..." This covers reservists called upon to assist with civil emergencies.
"...treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This provides leave for health-related issues arising from military service.
*   **Maximum Duration:
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period." This sets a limit on the total duration of leave that can be taken for certain activities.
*   **Exceptions:
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..." This indicates that the 24-month limit does not apply to leave taken due to emergencies.
*   **Designation and Delegation:
"The Minister of National Defence may designate an operation for the purposes of paragraph (1)(a) or may authorize another person to do so." This allows for flexibility in designating operations that qualify for leave.
*   **Head's Discretion:
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave." This provides a safeguard to prevent undue disruption to public services or employers.

question: What circumstances entitle an employee to take a leave of absence under section 206.4 of the Canada Labour Code, and what is the maximum duration of such leave?
answer:
## Section 206.4: Leave Related to Critical Illness - Entitlement and Duration

### Entitlement to Leave

Section 206.4 outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence to care for or support a critically ill family member. The section specifies two scenarios:

*   **Critically Ill Child:
"Every employee who is a family member of a critically ill child is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 37 weeks in order to care for or support that child if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that (a) states that the child is a critically ill child and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members; and (b) sets out the period during which the child requires that care or support."
*   **Critically Ill Adult:
"Every employee who is a family member of a critically ill adult is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 17 weeks in order to care for or support that adult if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that (a) states that the adult is a critically ill adult and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members; and (b) sets out the period during which the adult requires that care or support."

The entitlement hinges on a healthcare practitioner issuing a certificate confirming the individual's critical illness and the need for care or support.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

The maximum duration of leave under section 206.4 is dependent on the family relationship and the illness of the family member:

*   **For a critically ill child:** The maximum leave duration is 37 weeks.
*   **For a critically ill adult:** The maximum leave duration is 17 weeks.

The section also includes provisions regarding the aggregate leave amount for employees caring for the same critically ill person, limiting it to 37 weeks for a child or 17 weeks for an adult.

question: What circumstances entitle an employee to a leave of absence under section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code, and what is the maximum duration of such leave?
answer:
## Section 206.5: Leave Related to Death or Disappearance: Entitlement and Duration

### Entitlement to Leave

Section 206.5 outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence. It states:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has died and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child died as a result of a crime. Marginal note: Leave  —  child who has disappeared (3) Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has disappeared and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child disappeared as a result of a crime."

This indicates that an employee is eligible for a leave of absence of up to 156 weeks if their child dies under circumstances suggesting a crime or if their child disappears under similar circumstances. The key factor is the probability that the death or disappearance is linked to a crime.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

The maximum duration of the leave of absence under section 206.5 is explicitly stated in the text:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks..."

This means that an employee can receive a leave of absence for a maximum of 156 weeks if they meet the criteria outlined above.

### Important Considerations

The text also includes important exceptions and clarifications:
"An employee is not entitled to a leave of absence if they are charged with the crime." This means that if the employee is charged with a crime related to the death or disappearance of their child, they are not eligible for the leave.
"Despite paragraph (5)(b), in the case of a child who disappears and who is subsequently found, the period referred to in subsection (5) ends (a) on the 14th day after the day on which the child is found, if the child is found during the 156-week period, but no later than the end of the 156-week period; or (b) 156 weeks after the day on which the disappearance occurs if subsection (2) applies to the child." This clarifies the duration of the leave in cases where the child is later found.
"For greater certainty, a leave under this section ends on the day on which the circumstances are such that it is no longer probable that the death or disappearance was the result of a crime." This provides further clarity on when the leave period concludes.

question: What are the purposes for which an employee is entitled to take a leave of absence of up to five days in a calendar year?
answer:
## Personal Leave Entitlements under the Canada Labour Code

### Personal Leave (Section 206.6)

An employee is entitled to a leave of absence of up to five days in a calendar year for the following purposes:

*   **(b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members.** This indicates that an employee can take leave to attend to the health and care needs of their family.
*   **(c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age.** This provision allows employees to take leave to manage the educational needs of their minor family members.
*   **(d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members.** This is a broad category allowing for leave to handle pressing personal or family issues.
*   **(e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act.** This specifically grants leave for the purpose of participating in the citizenship ceremony.
*   **(f) any other reason prescribed by regulation.** This allows for the possibility of additional reasons for taking personal leave to be defined through regulations.

### Leave for Traditional Aboriginal Practices (Section 206.8)

Aboriginal employees are entitled to a leave of absence of up to five days in a calendar year to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices, including:

*   **(a) hunting;**
*   **(b) fishing;**
*   **(c) harvesting;**
*   **(d) any practice prescribed by regulation.** This demonstrates that the leave is specifically for activities integral to Aboriginal culture and way of life.

### Leave for Members of the Reserve Force (Section 247.5)

While not directly addressing the five-day personal leave entitlement, Section 247.5 outlines specific leave entitlements for employees who are members of the Reserve Force. These leaves are related to military duties and activities, such as:

*   **(a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence;**
*   **(b) an activity set out in the regulations;**
*   **(c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training;**
*   **(d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ;**
*   **(e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ;**
*   **(f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or**
*   **(g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection.**

It is important to note that the total leave taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can not exceed a total of 24 months in any 60-month period.

question: What are the circumstances under which an employee in Canada is entitled to take a leave of absence from work, and what are some of the purposes for which this leave can be used?
answer:
## Entitlement to Leave of Absence in Canada

### General Entitlement and Eligibility

An employee in Canada is entitled to a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code if they have completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer, or a shorter period prescribed for their employment class. This is stated in Section 247.5 of the Canada Labour Code:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment..."

### Purposes for which a Leave of Absence Can Be Used

Section 247.5 outlines several specific purposes for which an employee can take a leave of absence:

*   **Operations and Activities Designated by the Minister of National Defence:
"...an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..." This indicates that employees who are members of the reserve force can take leave for military operations.
*   **Activities Set Out in Regulations:** "an activity set out in the regulations". This suggests that there are specific activities, as defined by regulations, for which leave can be granted.
*   **Canadian Armed Forces Military Skills Training:** "(c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training". This allows for leave to attend training required by the Canadian Armed Forces.
*   **Training Ordered Under the National Defence Act:
"(d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act..." This covers training mandated by the National Defence Act.
*   **Duties Called Out On Service Under the National Defence Act:
"(e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act..." This allows for leave to perform duties when called upon for service.
*   **Service in Aid of a Civil Power:
"(f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act..." This covers leave for service assisting civil authorities.
*   **Treatment, Recovery, or Rehabilitation Due to Service:
"(g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This provides leave for health issues arising from military service.

### Maximum Duration of Leave
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period." This means that the total duration of leave taken for the specified purposes cannot exceed 24 months within a 60-month period.

### Exception to the Maximum Duration
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..." This indicates that the 24-month limit does not apply to leaves taken due to emergencies as defined by the Emergencies Act.

### Designation and Effect of Leave
"The Minister of National Defence may designate an operation for the purposes of paragraph (1)(a) or may authorize another person to do so. Marginal note: Effect (3) A designation takes effect on the day on which it is made or on an earlier or later day that is fixed by the Minister of National Defence or the other person. The Minister of National Defence or the other person may fix the day on which the designation ceases to be in effect." This section explains how operations for which leave can be taken are designated and how those designations are implemented.

### Limitations on Leave
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave." This provides a limitation on the entitlement to leave, allowing the Head to deny leave if it would negatively impact public health, safety, or cause undue hardship to the employer.

answer:
## Leave for Traditional Aboriginal Practices

### Entitlement and Duration

Aboriginal employees who have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer are entitled to a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices.
"Every employee who is an Aboriginal person and who has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year, in order to enable the employee to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices..."

### Included Traditional Practices

The traditional practices that Aboriginal employees can engage in during this leave include:

*   Hunting
*   Fishing
*   Harvesting
*   Any practice prescribed by regulation

These practices are specifically mentioned as activities for which the leave can be used.

### Documentation Requirements

The employer may request documentation demonstrating Aboriginal status, but this request can only be made up to 15 days after the employee's return to work, and only if it is reasonably practicable for the employee to obtain and provide it.
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request the employee to provide documentation that shows the employee as an Aboriginal person. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for him or her to obtain and provide it."
