question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Leave of Absence Entitlements Under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code outlines several circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence. These can be broadly categorized as medical leave, reserve force leave, and personal leave.

### Medical Leave

**Entitlement and Duration:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine."

This indicates that employees are entitled to a medical leave of absence for a variety of health-related reasons, including personal illness or injury, organ donation, medical appointments, or quarantine. The maximum duration of this leave is 27 weeks.

**Leave with Pay:
"...of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages."

Employees who have completed 30 days of continuous employment are entitled to the first three days of their medical leave with pay at their regular rate of wages.

**Benefits Continuation:
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division accumulate during the entire period of the medical leave of absence."

During a medical leave, employees continue to accrue benefits such as pension, health, and disability benefits, as well as maintain their seniority.

### Reserve Force Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation."

Employees are entitled to a leave of absence for various reasons, including caring for family members, attending to family education, addressing urgent family matters, attending citizenship ceremonies, or other reasons specified by regulation. The maximum duration of this leave is five days per calendar year.

**Leave with Pay:
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages."

Employees who have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment are entitled to the first three days of their reserve force leave with pay at their regular rate of wages.

### Personal Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation."

This section mirrors the reasons for reserve force leave, granting employees up to five days of personal leave per calendar year for various reasons, including family care, education, urgent matters, citizenship ceremonies, or other reasons specified by regulation.

**Documentation:
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it."

Employers can request documentation to support the reason for the leave, but only if it is reasonably practicable for the employee to provide it.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides employees with various types of leave of absence, including medical leave (up to 27 weeks), reserve force leave (up to five days per year), and personal leave (up to five days per year). The specific circumstances and duration of each leave are outlined in the legislation.

question: What are the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 207 of the Canada Labour Code: Employee Obligations Regarding Leave of Absence

### Notification Requirements

Section 207 outlines the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under sections 206.3 to 206.9 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This indicates that the primary obligation is to provide the employer with advance notice. Specifically, the employee must provide at least four weeks' written notice before the leave commences. This requirement exists unless the employee has a valid reason for not providing such notice. 

### Notification of Changes to Leave Length

Furthermore, the employee is obligated to inform the employer of any changes to the length of the leave.
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This obligation applies even during the leave period, ensuring the employer is aware of any adjustments to the planned duration.

### Notice for Longer Leaves

For leaves exceeding four weeks, the notice requirement is extended.
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done."

This ensures the employer has adequate time to make arrangements for the employee's absence when the leave is extended.

question: What are the requirements for an employee who needs to interrupt their leave of absence for certain reasons, such as a work-related illness or injury, or other specified reasons?
answer:
## Interrupting a Leave of Absence

### General Requirements for Interrupting Leave

The documents outline specific requirements for employees who need to interrupt their leave of absence for reasons such as work-related illness or injury.
"It is possible for you to interrupt your compassionate care leave in order to take:  medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave..." This indicates that employees on compassionate care leave can interrupt it for other qualifying leaves.

To do so, the employee must follow these steps:

*   **Written Notice:
"You must give your employer a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as you are able after it begins." This emphasizes the importance of providing timely written notification to the employer.
*   **Resumption of Leave:
"Compassionate care leave is to resume immediately after the other leave ends." This clarifies that the compassionate care leave automatically resumes once the other leave concludes.
*   **Maximum Duration:
"However, it cannot extend beyond 52 weeks after the day on which the leave started." This sets a clear time limit for the entire compassionate care leave period, including any interruptions.

### Specific Requirements for Critical Illness Leave

For employees on leave related to critical illness, the requirements are similar:
"If you intend to interrupt the leave related to critical illness, you must give your employer a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins. You must also give your employer a written notice of the day on which leave related to critical illness will resume, before or as soon as possible after that day."

This reinforces the need for written notification, including a specific date for the resumption of the leave.

### Additional Considerations

The documents also mention that employees who take a leave of more than 4 weeks but request to end the leave earlier without giving at least 4 weeks’ written notice may have their return to work postponed.
"...postpone your return to work for a period of up to 4 weeks after the day on which you inform them of the new date. In that case, your employer must inform you of this decision and the period of postponement is considered as part of the leave." This highlights the employer's right to postpone the return to work in such cases.

question: What are the notice and documentation requirements for employees taking a leave of absence under sections 206.3 to 206.9 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Notice Requirements for Leave of Absence (Sections 206.3 to 206.9)

Section 207.3(1) states:
"Every employee who takes a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of the reasons for the leave and the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This indicates that employees must provide written notice to their employer as soon as possible when taking a leave of absence under these sections. The notice should include the reason for the leave and the intended duration.

Section 207.3(2) further clarifies that
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This means that if an employee's leave is extended or shortened, they must inform the employer in writing as soon as possible.

## Documentation Requirements for Leave of Absence (Sections 206.3 to 206.9)

Section 207.3(4) outlines the documentation requirements, stating:
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

This means that the employer has the right to request supporting documentation. This documentation could be related to the reason for the leave or to verify any changes in the leave's duration.

## Additional Requirements for Leaves Longer Than Four Weeks

Section 207.3(3) specifies the notice requirement for leaves exceeding four weeks:
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done."

This highlights that if an employee is taking a leave of absence for more than four weeks, they must provide at least four weeks' notice for any changes to the leave's duration, unless a valid reason prevents them from doing so.

## Employer's Right to Postpone Return to Work

Section 207.3(5) details the employer's right to postpone an employee's return to work if the employee fails to provide the required notice for a leave longer than four weeks:
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave. If the employer informs the employee that their return to work is postponed, the employee is not entitled to return to work until the day that is indicated by the employer."

This provision allows the employer to postpone the employee's return to work for up to four weeks if the employee doesn't provide the required notice for a leave exceeding four weeks. The postponed period is considered part of the leave.

question: Under what circumstances can an employer require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from work?
answer:
## Employer Requirements for Leave of Absence During Pregnancy

### Section 208(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"An employer may require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from employment if the employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job and no appropriate alternative job is available for that employee."

This section outlines the specific circumstances under which an employer can necessitate a leave of absence for a pregnant employee. The key conditions are:

1.  **Inability to Perform Essential Functions:** The employee must be unable to perform the essential duties of her job due to her pregnancy.
2.  **Lack of Suitable Alternative Job:** There must not be a suitable alternative job available for the employee that she could perform.

This provision ensures that the requirement for a leave of absence is directly linked to the employee's health and safety during pregnancy and that the employer has explored options to accommodate the employee within the workplace.

### Section 208(3)
"A pregnant employee who is unable to perform an essential function of her job and for whom no appropriate alternative job is available may be required to take a leave of absence from employment only for such time as she is unable to perform that essential function."

This section clarifies the duration of the leave. The leave is limited to the period during which the employee is unable to perform the essential functions of her job. This ensures that the leave is not indefinite and is tied to the medical necessity arising from the pregnancy.

### Section 208(4)
"The burden of proving that a pregnant employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job rests with the employer."

This section places the responsibility on the employer to demonstrate that the employee's inability to perform her job is directly related to her pregnancy. This protects the employee's rights and ensures that the employer has a valid reason for requiring a leave of absence.

question: What are the rights of an employee who takes a leave of absence from employment under the Canada Labour Code regarding their job and benefits when they return to work?
answer:
## Employee Rights Upon Return from Leave of Absence - Canada Labour Code

### Reinstatement to Former Position

Upon returning from a leave of absence, an employee has the right to be reinstated to their former position or a comparable position. The Canada Labour Code states: "**Upon your return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits.**" This means the employer cannot simply deny the employee's previous role; they must provide an equivalent one.

### Protection Against Wage and Benefit Reduction

The law also protects employees from reduced wages and benefits during a leave period. The text specifies:
"...if you are reinstated in that group you will receive no more than the wages and benefits that you would have received if you had been at work during the reorganization." This ensures that if an employer reduces wages and benefits for a group of employees during a reorganization, the employee will receive the same compensation upon their return as they would have if they had remained employed. Conversely, if wages and benefits are increased for the group during the leave, the employee is entitled to those increases upon return.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Changes to Wages and Benefits

Employers are legally obligated to inform employees of any changes to wages and benefits resulting from a reorganization. The text states:
"Your employer must inform you of any change to wages and benefits resulting from a reorganization by sending you a notice to your last known address." This ensures transparency and allows employees to be aware of any changes affecting their compensation.

### Considerations for Extended Leaves and Return to Work

If an employee takes a leave of more than four weeks and requests to end it early without providing at least four weeks' written notice, the employer may postpone the employee's return to work for up to four weeks. The employer must inform the employee of this decision, and the postponement period is considered part of the leave.

### Continued Seniority and Opportunities During Leave

Even while on leave, employees retain their seniority and are entitled to be informed of any employment or training opportunities or promotions that arise during their absence. The text notes:
"On your written request, your employers must inform you of every employment and training opportunity or promotion that arise while you are away on leave. You also continue to accumulate seniority during your absence." This ensures employees are not disadvantaged in terms of career progression while on leave.

answer:
## Pension, Health, and Disability Benefits and Seniority During Leave of Absence

### General Accumulation of Benefits
"Section 209.2 (1) The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave."

This section clearly states that during a leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code, an employee's pension, health, and disability benefits, as well as their seniority, continue to accumulate. This means that the time spent on leave is considered as if the employee were still actively working, and benefits are not lost.

### Employer Contributions During Leave
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (1), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any leave of absence under this Division unless, before taking leave or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period."
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (1) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s leave of absence under this Division in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not on leave unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time."

These passages clarify the employer's responsibility regarding contributions to pension, health, and disability benefits during a leave. The employer is obligated to continue making contributions at least at the same level as if the employee were not on leave, unless the employee opts to discontinue contributions. The employee is responsible for any outstanding contributions within a reasonable timeframe.

### Seniority Accumulation
"Section 247.91 (1) For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave. Marginal note: Seniority..."
"(2) The seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall accumulate during the leave."

These sections explicitly state that an employee's seniority accumulates during the leave of absence. This means that upon returning to work, the employee retains the same seniority they had before the leave began.

### Benefits Upon Return to Work
"...return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits. If you are no longer able to perform the function of the original position, or those of a comparable position, your employer may assign you to a different position with different terms and conditions of employment.  If, during a leave period, your employer reduces the wages and benefits of a group of employees as part of a reorganization plan and if you are reinstated in that group you will receive no more than the wages and benefits that you would have received if you had been at work during the..."

These passages outline the employer's obligation to reinstate the employee to their former position or a comparable one upon their return. It also specifies that if wages and benefits were reduced during the leave period due to a reorganization, the employee will receive no less than what they would have received had they remained at work.

question: What protections are afforded to employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence under the Code, in terms of their employment status and benefits?
answer:
## Protections for Pregnant and Nursing Employees under the Canada Labour Code

### Job Security and Termination

The Canada Labour Code provides significant protections for employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence.
"Subject to subsection (2), no employer shall require an employee to take a leave of absence from employment because the employee is pregnant." This means an employer cannot *require* a pregnant employee to take leave. However, there is an exception.
"An employer may require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from employment if the employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job and no appropriate alternative job is available for that employee." This protects the employer's need to ensure safety and functionality within the workplace, but it is a narrow exception.

Furthermore, the Code prohibits employers from taking adverse action against employees due to pregnancy or taking leave.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division or take into account the pregnancy of an employee or the intention of an employee to take leave of absence from employment under this Division in any decision to promote or train the employee." This is a broad protection covering various employment actions.

### Leave of Absence and Benefits

The Code guarantees a leave of absence for pregnant and nursing employees.
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability." This establishes the entitlement to leave and the requirement for a medical certificate.
"Notwithstanding the provisions of any income-replacement scheme or any insurance plan in force at the workplace, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan on the same terms as any employee who is absent from work for health-related reasons and is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan." This ensures that employees on leave are entitled to the same benefits as other employees on health-related leave, regardless of existing insurance plans.

The employee is also protected in terms of maintaining their employment status during the leave.
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job." This ensures that the employee retains their job and benefits for the duration of the leave.

### Reassignment

The Code also provides for the possibility of reassignment to a less risky job.
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This allows for a solution that accommodates both the employee's health and the employer's operational needs.

### Duty to Inform

Employees are required to inform their employer of any changes to the duration of their leave or inability to work.
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." This ensures that the employer is kept informed and can make appropriate arrangements.

question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make in relation to employment leaves and absences under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Regulations Regarding Employment Leaves and Absences

The Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad authority to create regulations concerning employment leaves and absences. This authority is detailed in Section 209.4 and Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code.

### Scope of Regulatory Authority

Section 209.4 outlines a wide range of specific areas where the Governor in Council can enact regulations. These include:

*   **Defining Continuous Employment:** The Governor in Council can specify absences that do not interrupt continuous employment. This is crucial for determining eligibility for various benefits and entitlements.
*   **Maximum Leave Periods:** Regulations can set limits on the number of leave of absence periods an employee can take.
*   **Essential Job Functions:** The regulations can define what constitutes an essential function of a job, impacting leave eligibility.
*   **Reasons for Non-Reinstatement:** The regulations can specify reasons why an employee may not be reinstated to their previous position.
*   **Expanding Definitions:** The regulations can broaden the meaning of terms like "family member" and "critically ill adult" for leave purposes.
*   **Including Additional Family Members:** The regulations can specify other individuals to be included in the definitions of family members and support persons.
*   **Adapting Definitions from the Employment Insurance Act:** The regulations can adapt terminology used in the Employment Insurance Act to align with the definitions of terms in the Canada Labour Code.
*   **Excluding Offences from Crime Definitions:** The regulations can exclude certain offences from the definition of crime, particularly in relation to parental leave.
*   **Shorter Periods of Continuous Employment:** The regulations can establish shorter periods of continuous employment for leave eligibility.
*   **Entitlement to Leave Despite Criminal Charges:** The regulations can specify cases where an employee is entitled to leave even if they are charged with a crime.
*   **Defining Family Violence:** The regulations can define family violence for the purposes of leave.
*   **Documentation Requirements:** The regulations can specify documentation that employers may request under various leave provisions.
*   **Circumstances Interrupting Leave:** The regulations can define circumstances under which a leave under the division may be interrupted.
*   **Extending Leave Periods:** The regulations can extend the period for which a leave under the division may be taken.

### Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 265 specifies that the Governor in Council can direct that Part of the Canada Labour Code applies to employment, or classes of employment, related to a work or undertaking that is part of a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Exclusion from Application

Section 266 allows the Governor in Council to exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, employment or classes of employment related to a work or undertaking that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1) of Section 265.

In summary, the Governor in Council has extensive power to create regulations that shape the application of employment leaves and absences under the Canada Labour Code, with specific provisions also allowing for the application of the code to provincial crown corporations and the exclusion of certain employment from its application.

question: What is the relationship between Section 209.5 and Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 209.5 and Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code: Relationship

### Application of Section 189

Section 209.5 explicitly states:
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division."

This means that the provisions of Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code are applicable within the context of the Division of the Canada Labour Code that Section 209.5 is a part of. 

### Context of Section 209.5

Section 209.5 is part of Division X, which deals with "General: Regulations." This indicates that Section 189, as applied through Section 209.5, governs the creation and application of regulations within this specific division. 

### Section 189's Scope

Section 189, as outlined in CLC-209.4, grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations on a wide range of topics related to employment insurance, including:

*   Absences from employment
*   Leaves of absence
*   Essential functions of jobs
*   Reinstatement of employees
*   Family member definitions
*   Documentation requirements

Therefore, Section 209.5 essentially establishes that Section 189 provides the foundational framework for creating and implementing regulations within Division X, ensuring that these regulations are applied consistently and effectively.

question: What are the conditions and entitlements for an employee to take a leave of absence in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member?
answer:
## Bereavement Leave Entitlements under Canadian Labour Law

### General Entitlement and Duration

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 210(1),
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted, in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member in respect of whom the employee is, at the time of the death, on leave under section 206.3 or 206.4, a leave of absence from employment of up to 10 days..." This indicates that an employee is generally entitled to up to 10 days of bereavement leave when a family member dies.

### Definition of "Immediate Family"

Section 210(1) further clarifies the scope of the bereavement leave by referencing "immediate family." While the exact definition is provided for regulations, it generally includes close relatives such as parents, children, siblings, and sometimes grandparents or grandchildren.

### Duration of Leave and Extension
"At the request of the employee, the employer may extend, in writing, the period during which the leave of absence from employment may be taken." This means that the initial 10-day leave can be extended if the employee requests it and the employer agrees.

### Payment During Bereavement Leave
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This specifies that if an employee has worked for the employer for at least three months continuously, the first three days of bereavement leave will be paid at their regular wage rate.

### Notice to Employer
"Every employee who takes the leave of absence shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with written notice of the beginning of any period of leave of absence and of the length of that leave." This highlights the importance of providing timely notification to the employer regarding the start and duration of the bereavement leave.

### Additional Information

It is important to note that the bereavement leave can be taken in one or two periods, with the employer requiring each period to be at least one day long. Also, the leave can be taken during the period that begins on the day the death occurs and ends six weeks after the latest of the days on which any funeral, burial, or memorial service of the deceased person occurs.

question: What are the key terms defined in section 211 of the Canada Labour Code, and what do they relate to?
answer:
## Key Terms Defined in Section 211 of the Canada Labour Code

### Introduction

Section 211 of the Canada Labour Code defines key terms used within Division IX, which specifically addresses group termination of employment. These definitions are crucial for understanding the scope and application of the provisions related to layoffs and group dismissals.

### Definitions Explained

#### Joint Planning Committee
"...joint planning committee means a committee established pursuant to section 214..."

This definition establishes what constitutes a "joint planning committee." It refers to a committee formed according to the stipulations outlined in section 214 of the same division. This committee likely plays a role in the process of group termination, potentially involving discussions and negotiations between the employer and employee representatives.

#### Redundant Employee
"...redundant employee means an employee whose employment is to be terminated pursuant to a notice under section 212..."

This definition is central to the division's focus on group termination. A "redundant employee" is defined as someone whose job is being eliminated due to the group termination process outlined in section 212. This term is fundamental for determining who is eligible for the protections and entitlements provided under this part of the Canada Labour Code.

#### Trade Union
"...trade union means a trade union that is certified under Part I to represent any redundant employee or that is recognized by an employer of any redundant employee as the bargaining agent for that employee."

This definition clarifies the role of a "trade union" in the context of group termination. It specifies that a union must either be officially certified under Part I of the Canada Labour Code to represent redundant employees or be recognized by the employer as the bargaining agent for those employees. This ensures that unions have a formal role in representing the interests of employees affected by group termination.

question: What are the obligations of an employer who plans to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a certain timeframe, and what information must be provided to various parties?
answer:
## Employer Obligations Regarding Group Termination of Employment

### Notification Requirements

According to the Canada Labour Code, an employer who plans to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a particular industrial establishment has specific notification obligations.
"Section 212 (1) Any employer who terminates, either simultaneously or within any period not exceeding four weeks, the employment of a group of 50 or more employees employed by the employer within a particular industrial establishment, or of such lesser number of employees as prescribed by regulations applicable to the employer made under paragraph 227(b), shall, in addition to any notice required to be given under section 230, give notice to the Head, in writing, of his intention to so terminate at least 16 weeks before the date of termination of the employment of the employee in the group whose employment is first to be terminated."

This indicates that the employer must provide written notice to the Head of the relevant labour program at least 16 weeks before the termination takes effect. This applies whether the terminations occur simultaneously or within a period of four weeks.

### Information to be Provided

The notice provided to the Head must include specific information.
"A notice referred to in subsection (1) shall set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations." This means the employer must specify the date(s) of termination, the number of employees in each occupational classification affected, and any other information required by regulations.

Furthermore, the employer has a responsibility to disseminate this information to various parties.
"A copy of any notice given to the Head under subsection (1) must be given immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed."

### Additional Requirements and Waivers

Beyond the initial notification, employers are required to fulfill additional obligations.
"As an employer, when a group termination of employment occurs, you are required to:  establish a joint planning committee with an employee representative cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and  provide affected employees with a statement of benefits, which includes information on the employee’s:             wages vacation pay severance pay, if applicable, and any other benefits and pay arising from employment..."

Employers can also request waivers from certain requirements.
"As an employer, you may request that the Minister of Labour waive certain requirements. Three types of waivers may be granted, including the requirement to:  give 16 weeks’ notice provide employees with a written statement of benefits, and/or establish a joint planning committee when you can show that:             it would be unduly prejudicial to your interests or of the affected employees it would be seriously detrimental to the operation of the industrial establishment similar measures are already in place..."

### Posting the Notice

The employer must also ensure the notice is readily accessible to affected employees.
"...or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed." This ensures transparency and allows employees to be informed of the impending changes.

question: What are the key responsibilities of an employer who gives notice of termination to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code, particularly in relation to redundant employees and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission?
answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Upon Notifying the Head of Group Termination (Section 212)

### Notification Requirements

An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 has several key responsibilities. First, they must provide a comprehensive notice that includes specific information. This notice must
"...set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations."

Furthermore, the employer is obligated to provide copies of this notice to various entities.  The notice must be given
"...immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed." This ensures that relevant stakeholders are informed about the impending layoffs.

### Cooperation with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission (CEIC)

The employer has a responsibility to cooperate with the CEIC to assist redundant employees. Section 213 states that the employer
"...must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee." This implies a proactive role in providing necessary information and working with the CEIC to support the affected employees' transition to new employment.

### Providing Information to Redundant Employees

The employer is required to provide redundant employees with a detailed statement in writing. This statement must be provided
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee..." The statement must detail
"...his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer." This ensures transparency and provides redundant employees with essential information regarding their entitlements.



### Establishing a Joint Planning Committee

The employer has a responsibility to establish a joint planning committee. Section 214 states that
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee..." This committee will be composed of representatives from both the employer and the redundant employees. The employer must also provide the committee with
"...such personal information relating to any redundant employee as the committee may reasonably require for its work." This collaborative approach aims to facilitate a smoother transition for the affected employees.

question: What are the requirements for the composition of a joint planning committee that an employer must establish after giving notice to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Requirements for Joint Planning Committee Composition

### Establishment Requirement
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217."

This indicates that establishing a joint planning committee is a mandatory step for employers after providing notice of group termination under section 212. The employer must do so "as soon as possible" following the notice. The composition of the committee is governed by sections 215 and 217 of the Canada Labour Code.

### Minimum Membership
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members."

This specifies the minimum number of members required for the joint planning committee. The committee cannot be formed with fewer than four individuals.

### Representation of Employees and Employer
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer."

This section details the required representation on the committee. Specifically, "at least half" of the members must be representatives of the employees who are being terminated. The remaining members must be representatives of the employer. The specific procedures for appointing these representatives are outlined in subsections 215(1), (2) and (3) for employee representatives and subsection 215(5) for employer representatives. This ensures that both the interests of the employees and the employer are considered during the development of an adjustment program.

question: How are redundant employees represented on a joint planning committee, especially when some or all of them are represented by a trade union?
answer:
## Redundant Employee Representation on Joint Planning Committees

### Section 215: Employee Representatives
"Where all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of the joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents."

This indicates that when all redundant employees are covered by a trade union, each union gets to nominate at least one representative to the joint planning committee. This ensures that the interests of the entire group are considered.
"Where no redundant employees are represented by a trade union, the employees are entitled to appoint all the members of a joint planning committee who are to be their representatives."

In the absence of a trade union, the redundant employees themselves have the right to select all the members who will represent them on the committee. This empowers the employees directly affected by the group termination to have a voice in the planning process.
"Where some but not all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, (a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents; and (b) the employees that are not represented by a trade union are entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as their representative."

This addresses situations where not all redundant employees are covered by a union. It states that unions representing some of the redundant employees are entitled to appoint at least one member. Simultaneously, the employees not covered by a union retain the right to appoint at least one member to represent their interests. This ensures that all redundant employees have a voice, regardless of union affiliation.
"Each person appointed as a member of a joint planning committee pursuant to subsection (2) or paragraph (3)(b) shall be elected by the redundant employees entitled to appoint the member."

This clarifies the process by which redundant employees select their representatives. It mandates that the representatives are elected by the redundant employees who are eligible to make such an appointment. This ensures that the representatives are accountable to the employees they are meant to serve.

### Section 214: Establishment of Joint Planning Committee
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer."

This section reinforces the principle of having at least half of the committee members representing the redundant employees. It specifies that these representatives are appointed according to the rules outlined in section 215, ensuring a balanced representation on the committee. This structure ensures that the interests of the redundant employees are adequately considered during the planning process.

question: What are the requirements for the appointment and first sitting of the members of a joint planning committee under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Appointment of Joint Planning Committee Members

### Requirements for Appointment

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific requirements for the appointment of members to a joint planning committee.
"Section 214 (1) An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This indicates that an employer is obligated to establish a joint planning committee promptly after providing notice of group termination.
"(2) A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This establishes the minimum number of members required for the committee's formation.
"(3) At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This section details the composition of the committee, requiring at least half of the members to represent the redundant employees and the remaining half to represent the employer. It also specifies the method of appointment for each group – employee representatives are appointed according to sections 215(1), (2) and (3), while employer representatives are appointed according to section 215(5).

### Time for First Sitting
"Section 216 The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212." This clearly states that the committee members must be appointed and the committee must hold its first meeting within two weeks of the employer providing notice to the Head about the group termination.

question: What happens if a trade union or redundant employees fail to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as required, and how can the issue be resolved?
answer:
## Failure to Appoint a Member to a Joint Planning Committee

### Section 217: Head's Appointment in Lieu of Failure
"If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

This section of the Canada Labour Code addresses the scenario where a trade union or the redundant employees themselves fail to appoint a representative to the joint planning committee as mandated by the Code. 

The solution provided is that
"...the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees..." This means that if neither the union nor the employees manage to appoint a representative, the government (represented by the "Head") has the authority to step in and make the appointment. 

Furthermore, the appointed member will represent either the redundant employees who were supposed to be represented by the trade union, or the redundant employees who failed to appoint a representative. This ensures that the interests of the redundant employees are still represented on the committee, even in the absence of a union or employee-led appointment.

question: What are the key aspects of how a joint planning committee is structured and operates according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Structure and Operation of a Joint Planning Committee under the Canada Labour Code

### Establishment of the Committee

Section 214 outlines the initial formation of a joint planning committee. It states that
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This indicates that the employer is obligated to form the committee promptly after providing notice of group termination.

Furthermore, Section 214(2) specifies the minimum size of the committee:
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This ensures a minimum level of representation for effective deliberation.

Section 214(3) details the composition of the committee, requiring a balance of representation:
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This ensures that the interests of both the employees and the employer are considered.

### Appointment of Members

Section 215 provides the details on the appointment of members. It states that
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This means that the employee representatives are selected according to specific rules outlined in the code, while the employer representatives are also appointed following a defined process.

### Operational Aspects

Section 219 outlines the operational aspects of the joint planning committee. It states that
"Subject to this Division, a joint planning committee may determine its own procedure." This gives the committee flexibility in how it conducts its business.

Section 219(2) specifies the election of co-chairpersons:
"The members of a joint planning committee shall elect from among themselves two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees selected by their representatives and the other being a representative of the employer selected by his representatives." This ensures leadership and facilitates effective decision-making.

Section 219(3) details the process for setting meeting times and locations:
"The co-chairpersons of a joint planning committee may, after consultation with the other members of the committee, fix the time and place of its sittings and shall notify the members of the time and place so fixed." This ensures transparency and allows all members to participate.

Section 219(4) addresses quorum requirements:
"A majority of the members of a joint planning committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum, but the members shall not proceed in the absence of any member of the committee at any sitting unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting." This ensures that there is sufficient representation present for the committee to function effectively.

### Objectives of the Committee

Section 221(1) clearly states the primary objective of the joint planning committee:
"It is the object of a joint planning committee to develop an adjustment program to (a) eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment." This highlights the committee's role in mitigating the negative consequences of group termination.

### Member Entitlements

Section 220 addresses the entitlements of committee members, stating:
"A member of a joint planning committee is entitled to such time from work as is necessary to attend sittings of the committee or to carry out any other functions as such a member, and any time spent by the member in carrying out any functions as a member shall, for the purpose of calculating wages owing to the member, be deemed to have been spent at his work." This ensures that members are not penalized for their participation in the committee's work.

question: What are the protections and considerations given to members of a joint planning committee in terms of their work and compensation?
answer:
## Protections and Considerations for Joint Planning Committee Members

### Time Off Work

Section 220 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the time commitment required of joint planning committee members.
"A member of a joint planning committee is entitled to such time from work as is necessary to attend sittings of the committee or to carry out any other functions as such a member, and any time spent by the member in carrying out any functions as a member shall, for the purpose of calculating wages owing to the member, be deemed to have been spent at his work."

This indicates that employees are entitled to time off their regular work duties to participate in the committee's activities. Furthermore, any time spent fulfilling responsibilities as a committee member is considered time worked for wage calculation purposes. This ensures that members are not penalized financially for their participation and dedication to the committee's work.

### Compensation

Section 220 also directly addresses compensation for members of the joint planning committee.
"...any time spent by the member in carrying out any functions as a member shall, for the purpose of calculating wages owing to the member, be deemed to have been spent at his work."

This means that time spent on committee duties is considered work time, and therefore, is included when calculating wages. This ensures that members are compensated for their time and effort dedicated to the committee, without a reduction in their earnings.

### Other Considerations

Section 219 outlines several other considerations for joint planning committee members.
"...a joint planning committee may determine its own procedure." This suggests that the committee has autonomy in how it operates, which can be beneficial for members as it allows for a more efficient and effective working environment.
"A majority of the members of a joint planning committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum, but the members shall not proceed in the absence of any member of the committee at any sitting unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting." This ensures that the committee can function effectively even with some members absent, while also protecting the rights of absent members to be informed of meetings.
"A vacancy in the membership of a joint planning committee does not invalidate the constitution of the committee or impair the right of the members of the committee in office to act, if the number of those members is not less than a quorum." This ensures the committee can continue to function even if members leave, as long as a quorum is maintained.

question: What is the main objective of a joint planning committee when developing an adjustment program in the context of employment termination?
answer:
## Main Objective of a Joint Planning Committee

### Section 221(1) - Object of the Committee

The primary objective of a joint planning committee is clearly stated in Section 221(1) of the Canada Labour Code. It outlines two key goals:
"It is the object of a joint planning committee to develop an adjustment program to (a) eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment."

This indicates that the committee's efforts are directed towards either preventing layoffs altogether or, if layoffs are unavoidable, mitigating their negative consequences for affected employees. The objective extends beyond simply managing the termination process; it actively seeks to support redundant employees in finding new employment opportunities.

### Section 221(2) - Scope of Matters Considered

Furthermore, Section 221(2) clarifies the scope within which the committee operates. It states:
"In attaining its object under subsection (1), a joint planning committee may, unless the members of the committee agree otherwise, deal only with such matters as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to the termination of employment."

This means the committee's work is generally confined to issues typically addressed in collective agreements concerning layoffs, ensuring that the adjustment program aligns with existing labour practices and agreements.

### Section 221(3) - Effort and Cooperation

Finally, Section 221(3) emphasizes the importance of proactive effort and collaboration:
"The members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible."

This highlights the expectation that the committee members will work together diligently and efficiently to achieve the stated objectives. The cooperative spirit is further reinforced by Section 221(4), which mandates cooperation between the employer, trade union, and redundant employees in developing the adjustment program.

question: What kind of support and assistance can a joint planning committee expect to receive in its establishment and operation, and who can provide it?
answer:
## Support and Assistance for Joint Planning Committees

### Role of the Head (Minister)

The Head (Minister) has a role in the establishment and operation of joint planning committees. Section 222(2) states that
"The Head may (a) monitor and, on request, assist in the establishment and operation of a joint planning committee; and (b) attend any sittings of a joint planning committee as an observer." 

This indicates that the Head can provide assistance in getting the committee started and ongoing. The Head can also observe the committee's meetings. This support is available "on request," suggesting that the committee needs to actively ask for this assistance.

### Cooperation from Employer, Union, and Redundant Employees

Section 214(1) outlines the responsibility of the employer:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee..." This highlights the employer's obligation to establish the committee promptly after providing notice to the Head.

Furthermore, Section 222(1) specifies who must provide the committee with information:
"The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee shall, on request of any member of the committee, forthwith provide the committee with such personal information relating to any redundant employee as the committee may reasonably require for its work." This demonstrates the commitment of the employer, union, and redundant employees to provide necessary information to the committee.

Section 214(3) also emphasizes the cooperative nature of the committee's formation:
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This indicates that the committee is designed to be a collaborative body with representation from both the employer and the redundant employees.

### Cooperative Effort and Reasonable Effort

Section 221(3) emphasizes the importance of cooperation:
"The members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible." This highlights the expectation that committee members will work together effectively.

Section 221(2) further clarifies the scope of the committee's work:
"In attaining its object under subsection (1), a joint planning committee may, unless the members of the committee agree otherwise, deal only with such matters as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to the termination of employment." This ensures that the committee focuses on relevant issues and avoids unnecessary distractions.

question: Under what circumstances can members of a joint planning committee apply for the appointment of an arbitrator in relation to the development of an adjustment program for redundant employees?
answer:
## Application for Arbitrator Appointment

### Circumstances for Application

Members of a joint planning committee can apply to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator under specific circumstances. These circumstances are outlined in Section 223(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Agreement and Time Limit:
"Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator..."

This indicates that the application can be made if there is agreement among the committee members, either those representing redundant employees or those representing the employer. This agreement must occur after a six-week period has passed since the Minister was notified under section 212.

**Reasons for Application:**

The application can be made under two primary reasons:

**(a) Uncompleted Adjustment Program:
"...if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program..."

This means the application can be made if the joint planning committee has not yet finished developing an adjustment program for the redundant employees.

**(b) Dissatisfaction with the Program:
"...or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This allows for an application if the adjustment program has been completed, but the members of the committee are not satisfied with the program's content. This suggests a disagreement or dispute regarding the terms of the adjustment program.



### Matters in Dispute

Section 223(2) specifies the information that must be included in the application:
"An application under subsection (1) shall be in writing and signed by the members making the application and shall set out the matters, if any, in dispute respecting the adjustment program."

This means the application must detail the specific issues or disagreements regarding the adjustment program that are prompting the request for an arbitrator. This ensures the arbitrator is aware of the specific issues that need to be addressed.

question: What is the role of an arbitrator appointed under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code, and what are their powers in relation to resolving disputes and assisting in the development of an adjustment program?
answer:
## Role of an Arbitrator Appointed Under Section 224

Section 224 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the role of an arbitrator appointed to assist a joint planning committee in group termination of employment situations. 

### Assistance in Development of Adjustment Program
"The Minister may, on application under subsection 223(1), appoint an arbitrator to assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to resolve any matters in dispute respecting the adjustment program."

This indicates the primary role of the appointed arbitrator is to aid the joint planning committee in creating an adjustment program. This assistance encompasses both the development of the program itself and the resolution of any disagreements or disputes that may arise during this process.

### Powers of the Arbitrator

The arbitrator possesses a range of powers to fulfill this role, as detailed in Section 224(6):

*   **Procedure:** "determine the procedure to be followed;" The arbitrator has the authority to establish the rules and processes for the arbitration proceedings.
*   **Oaths and Affirmations:** "administer oaths and solemn aﬃrmations;" The arbitrator can ensure the reliability of information provided by witnesses through sworn statements.
*   **Evidence:
"...and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the arbitrator sees fit, whether or not the evidence is admissible in a court of law..." The arbitrator can consider various forms of evidence to make informed decisions.
*   **Document Examination:
"...make such examination of documents containing personal information relating to any redundant employee and such inquiries relating to any redundant employee as the arbitrator deems necessary..." The arbitrator can review relevant documents and conduct inquiries to gather necessary information.
*   **Notices:
"...require an employer to post and keep posted in appropriate places any notice that the arbitrator considers necessary to bring to the attention of any redundant employees any matter relating to the proceeding..." The arbitrator can mandate the dissemination of information to affected employees.
*   **Authorization:
"...authorize any person to do anything described in paragraph (b) or (d) that the arbitrator may do and to report to the arbitrator thereon." The arbitrator can delegate tasks to others to facilitate the arbitration process.

Furthermore, the arbitrator has specific restrictions to ensure fairness and prevent undue delays.
"An arbitrator may not (a) review the decision of the employer to terminate the employment of the redundant employees; or (b) delay the termination of employment of the redundant employees." This ensures the arbitrator's role is focused on the adjustment program and does not interfere with the employer's decision to terminate employment.

### Decision-Making
"...the arbitrator, if sent a statement pursuant to subsection (2), shall, within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify, (a) consider the matters set out in the statement; (b) render a decision thereon; and (c) send a copy of the decision with the reasons therefor to the joint planning committee and to the Minister."

The arbitrator is required to consider any matters in dispute that are formally presented to them and must render a decision on those matters within a specified timeframe. The decision must be accompanied by a clear explanation of the reasoning behind it, which is then communicated to both the joint planning committee and the Minister. This ensures transparency and accountability in the arbitration process.

question: How do sections 58 and 66 apply to a decision made by an arbitrator under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Application of Sections 58 and 66 to Arbitrator Decisions under Section 224

### Section 225: General Applicability of Sections 58 and 66
"Sections 58 and 66 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of a decision of an arbitrator under section 224 as though it were a decision referred to in those sections."

This statement from Section 225 establishes the fundamental principle. It clarifies that the procedures and rules outlined in Sections 58 and 66 of the Canada Labour Code are applicable to decisions made by an arbitrator appointed under Section 224. The phrase "with such modifications as the circumstances require" indicates that these sections may need to be adapted to fit the specific context of a group termination of employment case involving an arbitrator.

### Section 58: Finality of Arbitrator Decisions
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This section is crucial because it emphasizes the finality of an arbitrator's decision.  The quote
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." directly addresses the question. It means that a decision made by an arbitrator under Section 224 is generally not subject to judicial review. This provides a degree of certainty and stability to the dispute resolution process.

### Section 66: Filing of Orders and Decisions in Federal Court
"Any person or organization affected by any order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board may, after fourteen days from the date on which the order or decision is made or given, or from the date provided in it for compliance, whichever is the later date, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of the reasons therefor. Marginal note: Idem (2) On filing an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board in the Federal Court under subsection (1), the order or decision shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order or decision were a judgment obtained in the Court."

Section 66 outlines the process for making an arbitrator's decision legally binding. The quote
"On filing an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board in the Federal Court under subsection (1), the order or decision shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order or decision were a judgment obtained in the Court." is important. It means that by filing the decision in Federal Court, it gains the force of a judgment, allowing for enforcement and further legal action if necessary. This ensures the decision is not merely a recommendation but a legally enforceable outcome.
