question: What recourse do employees have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities?
answer:
## Recourse for Employees Facing Disciplinary Action

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition against employers taking disciplinary action against employees for engaging in certain protected activities.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section explicitly protects employees from disciplinary actions like dismissal, suspension, or penalties if those actions are taken because the employee has engaged in activities protected under the Canada Labour Code. These protected activities include testifying in legal proceedings, providing information regarding workplace health and safety, or exercising their rights under the Code.

### Section 147.1: Abuse of Rights

Section 147.1 addresses situations where an employee may have wilfully abused their rights under sections 128 and 129. However, it also stipulates that even in such cases, an employer must provide the employee with written reasons for any disciplinary action taken.
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights. Marginal note: Written reasons (2) The employer must provide the employee with written reasons for any disciplinary action within fifteen working days after receiving a request from the employee to do so."

This provision ensures transparency and fairness, requiring employers to justify any disciplinary action taken against an employee who has exercised their rights, even if those rights were ultimately deemed to have been abused.

### Section 246.1: Filing a Complaint and Protection from Retaliation

Section 246.1 outlines the process for employees who believe their employer has taken action against them in retaliation for exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code.
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention..."

This section empowers employees to formally report any retaliatory actions taken by their employer to the Canada Labour Board. The Board then has the authority to investigate the complaint and order the employer to cease the retaliatory actions and potentially provide remedies to the employee.

### Section 134: Board Orders and Remedies

Section 134 of the Canada Labour Code details the remedies available to employees when the Board determines that an employer has contravened the Code.
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This section provides a range of remedies, including reinstatement, compensation for lost wages, and rescinding disciplinary actions. The Board has the power to order the employer to take corrective action and compensate the employee for any losses suffered as a result of the retaliatory actions.

In summary, employees in Canada have several avenues for recourse if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action in response to protected activities. They can file a complaint with the Canada Labour Board under Section 246.1, seek remedies through a Board order under Section 134, and potentially challenge any disciplinary actions taken under Section 147.1 if they can demonstrate a wilful abuse of their rights.

{"id": "IPG-082_6", "type": "Interpretations, Policies and Guidelines", "title": "Rejection of complaint - IPG-082", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Other means available to the employee to resolve the complaint that should be pursued [subparagraph 251.05(1)(a)(iv)]** A complaint may be rejected if it is determined that other means are available to the complainant. For example, another government body, such as the Canadian Human Rights Commission, has the authority to deal with the complaint, or the complainant is subject to a collective agreement. Prior to the rejection of a complaint on this ground, suspension of the complaint under section 251.02 of the Code should be considered as the primary option until the other means available to the complainant have been pursued and concluded. In order to reject a complaint, it is necessary to demonstrate that other means are not only available, but that those other means are appropriate for resolving the complaint. An example of this would include a complaint regarding a third-party disclosing the results of an employee’s genetic test without consent. Although this is prohibited under the Code, complainants cannot file these complaints with the Labour Program. Instead, they must file these complaints with a provincial Privacy Commissioner or the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, as appropriate. The Head should examine beyond the initial allegations of a complaint and assess the underlying subject-matter. If the underlying subject-matter is related to a dismissal of an employee subject to a collective agreement, it is possible in some cases that the dismissal may have an impact on monetary complaint allegations (such as termination and severance pay). If the employee has been dismissed and the collective agreement contains provisions to challenge the dismissal, the employee should be informed about filing a grievance with their union if they have not already done so. The monetary complaint allegations related to the dismissal should be rejected pursuant to subparagraph 251.05(1)(a)(iv) when the Head is satisfied that there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the complaint that they should pursue.  Example: An employee subject to a collective agreement files a complaint for termination and severance pay. Upon investigation, the employer alleges that the employee was dismissed. There was no termination such as a lack of work or discontinuance of a function. It appears that in reality the employee is challenging the dismissal by filing a complaint for termination and severance pay. Since the underlying subject-matter of the complaint is to challenge the dismissal, the allegations related to termination and severance pay should be rejected pursuant to subparagraph 251.05(1)(a)(iv). This is because there are other means available to the employee to resolve the real subject-matter of the complaint. The complainant has recourse to challenge the dismissal through their collective agreement. If other monetary allegations exist that are not related to the dismissal and the rights and benefits in the collective agreement for those allegations are not as favourable as the rights and benefits provided by the Code, an investigation of the allegations should be conducted. In the event that the union does not pursue the complainant’s dismissal grievance, the complainant should be advised to pursue the matter with the Canada Industrial Relations Board."

question: What can the Board do if it believes an employee needs to take certain actions before it can continue to handle their complaint, and what information must it provide to the employee in this situation?
answer:
## Board Action Regarding Required Actions by Employee

### Suspension of Complaint

The Board has the authority to
"...at any time, in whole or in part, pursuant to subsection 251.02(1) if the Head is satisfied that the complainant must take certain measures within a specific time period before the complaint can be dealt with." This indicates that the Board can temporarily halt the processing of a complaint if it deems it necessary for the employee to fulfill certain requirements.

### Rejection of Complaint Due to Failure to Take Required Measures

If the employee fails to take the required measures within the specified timeframe, the complaint can be rejected. The text states:
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee did not take the required measures within the specified time period, the complaint can be rejected." This highlights the consequence of not meeting the pre-requisite actions.

### Information to the Employee

The text specifies that if a complaint is suspended, the Head must be satisfied that the employee must take certain measures within a specific time period before the complaint can be dealt with. This implies that the employee should be informed about the required measures and the timeframe within which they must be completed. 

Furthermore, the text mentions that
"Prior to the rejection of a complaint on this ground, suspension of the complaint under section 251.02 of the Code should be considered as the primary option until the other means available to the complainant have been pursued and concluded." This suggests that the employee should be informed about the possibility of suspension and the available options for resolving the complaint before it is ultimately rejected.

question: Under what circumstances can the Board reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Rejection of Complaints Under Section 246.1(1)

### Circumstances for Rejection

Section 246.3 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the circumstances under which the Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1). These circumstances are detailed in subsection (1) of the section.

The Board may reject a complaint if any of the following conditions are met:

*   **(i) The complaint is not within its jurisdiction.** This means the Board lacks the authority to hear the specific complaint.
*   **(ii) The complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith.** This refers to complaints that are made with the intention to harass or mislead, or that are without a reasonable basis.
*   **(iii) The complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee.** If the parties have reached a written agreement resolving the issue, the Board may reject the complaint.
*   **(iv) There are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued.** This suggests that the employee has alternative avenues for resolving the issue, such as through a court or other tribunal.
*   **(v) The subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator.** If the issue has already been resolved through other legal or quasi-legal processes, the Board may reject the complaint.
*   **(vi) In respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process.** This indicates that the collective agreement provides a mechanism for resolving the complaint, and the Board may reject the complaint in such cases.

The Board must notify the employee in writing if it rejects a complaint, and the notification must include the reasons for the rejection.

Marginal note: No review by certiorari , etc. (2) No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Division. 2017, c. 20, s. 356 Marginal note: Enforcement of orders"

question: What can the Board do if it determines that a complaint of reprisal by an employer against an employee is justified, and what is the status of the Board's decisions?
answer:
## Board Actions Upon Justified Reprisal Complaint

### Section 246.4: Employer Remedial Actions
"If the Board determines that a complaint under subsection 246.1(1) is justified, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal and, if applicable, to (a) permit the employee who has made the complaint to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate the employee; (c) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the reprisal, have been paid by the employer to the employee; (d) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer; and (e) do any other thing that the Board considers equitable for the employer to do to remedy or counteract any consequence of the reprisal."

This section outlines the specific actions the Board can order an employer to take if a reprisal complaint is found to be justified. These actions are designed to remedy the harm caused to the employee. The Board can order the employer to
"...permit the employee who has made the complaint to return to the duties of their employment..." and to "reinstate the employee." Furthermore, the Board can order the employer to provide financial compensation to the employee, up to the amount equivalent to lost wages and any penalties imposed. The Board also has the discretion to order other equitable actions to address the consequences of the reprisal.

### Section 246.5: Finality of Board Decisions
"Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Division."

These passages from Section 246.5 establish the finality of the Board's decisions regarding reprisal complaints.
"Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This means that once the Board issues a decision on a reprisal complaint, that decision cannot be challenged in court.  The subsequent passage reinforces this by stating that no court can intervene to question, review, or restrain the Board's decisions. This ensures the stability and enforceability of the Board's rulings in reprisal cases.

question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
answer:
## Enforcement of Board Orders in the Federal Court

### Section 156
"Section 156 (1) Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This section establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions. It explicitly states that such orders cannot be challenged or reviewed in any court. This means that once an order is issued by the Board, it is generally binding and cannot be overturned through legal proceedings.

### Section 244
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This section outlines the process for enforcing a Board order in the Federal Court. It states that
"...file in the Federal Court a copy of the order..." This indicates that individuals or entities impacted by a Board order have the right to file a copy of that order with the Federal Court. The filing must occur within 14 days of the order being made or the compliance date, whichever is later.

### Section 246.6
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under section 246.4, or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons. Marginal note: Registration (2) On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

This section reinforces the process described in Section 244 and adds the crucial detail that upon filing in the Federal Court, the order is
"...registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This means that the order gains the full legal weight of a judgment, allowing for enforcement through the standard legal processes available in the Federal Court.

### Section 22
"Section 23 (1) The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This section details the Board's obligation to file an order or decision in the Federal Court upon request. It states that
"...a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court..." This obligation is subject to certain exceptions, such as if there is no indication of non-compliance or if filing would serve no useful purpose.

### Section 23
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding. Marginal note: Effect of registration of order or decision (3) When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court."

This section further clarifies the process and consequences of filing an order in the Federal Court. It emphasizes that the order becomes a judgment upon registration, allowing for enforcement through the Federal Court system. It also specifies that the filing must be done with a written notice to the court stating that the filing is pursuant to this section.

Where the basis of your pay is not time (for example, you may be paid an  annual salary or in accordance with a mileage rate), the Minister of Labour may  fix a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is  determined by dividing the amount of salary you received (excluding any  vacation pay, general holiday pay, and overtime pay) by the number of hours  worked you performed.  **Reporting to work at the call of your employer** If you report to work at the call of your employer, you must receive wages for at least 3 hours at your regular rate of wages. This applies whether or not your employer asks you to do any work after reporting to work.  **Exemptions for apprentices and employees receiving room and/or board** If you are registered under and paid according to a provincial apprenticeship act, your employer is exempt from the application of the minimum wage. If your employer provides you with room and/or board, and you accept that arrangement, your employer may reduce your wages below minimum wage. Your employer cannot reduce your wages more than:  50 cents, for each meal, and 60 cents, per day, for living quarters  **Getting paid for work** Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work."

question: What are the requirements for an employer to pay wages to an employee according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Wage Payment Requirements Under the Canada Labour Code

### Regular Payday and Vacation Pay
"Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work."

This indicates that employers are legally obligated to establish a regular payday for wage payments. Furthermore, vacation pay must be provided when the employee takes their vacation. If employment ends, any accrued vacation pay must be paid out within 30 days of the employee's last day of work. This ensures employees receive their earned vacation benefits in a timely manner.

### Pay for Work at the Call of the Employer
"If you report to work at the call of your employer, you must receive wages for at least 3 hours at your regular rate of wages. This applies whether or not your employer asks you to do any work after reporting to work."

This section specifies that if an employee is required to report to work, they are entitled to wages for at least three hours at their regular rate of pay. This provision ensures that employees are compensated for their time and availability, even if they are not immediately assigned work.

### Pay for Non-Hourly Employees
"Where the basis of your pay is not time (for example, you may be paid an  annual salary or in accordance with a mileage rate), the Minister of Labour may  fix a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is  determined by dividing the amount of salary you received (excluding any  vacation pay, general holiday pay, and overtime pay) by the number of hours  worked you performed."

For employees who are not paid on an hourly basis, such as those with annual salaries or mileage-based pay, the Minister of Labour has the authority to determine a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is calculated by dividing the total salary received by the number of hours worked, excluding vacation pay, holiday pay, and overtime. This ensures that non-hourly employees receive a fair wage equivalent to the minimum wage.

### Minimum Wage Exemptions
"If you are registered under and paid according to a provincial apprenticeship act, your employer is exempt from the application of the minimum wage. If your employer provides you with room and/or board, and you accept that arrangement, your employer may reduce your wages below minimum wage. Your employer cannot reduce your wages more than:  50 cents, for each meal, and 60 cents, per day, for living quarters..."

There are specific exemptions to the minimum wage requirement. Employees registered under a provincial apprenticeship act are exempt. Additionally, if an employer provides room and/or board and the employee accepts, the employer may reduce wages below the minimum wage, but with limitations. The reduction cannot exceed 50 cents per meal and 60 cents per day for living quarters.

### Repealed

Sections 247.1, 247.2, 247.3, and 247.4 of the Canada Labour Code have been repealed. 

The text explicitly states:
"Section 247.1 [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 16] Section 247.2 [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 16] Section 247.3 [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 16] Section 247.4 [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 16]..."

This indicates that these sections were removed from the Canada Labour Code by the enactment of the *2018, c. 22* legislation, specifically through section 16. Therefore, they are no longer in effect.

question: What are the circumstances under which an employee who is a member of the reserve force is entitled to a leave of absence from their employment?
answer:
## Entitlement to Leave of Absence for Reserve Force Members

### Section 247.5: Entitlement to Leave

Section 247.5 outlines the conditions under which an employee who is a member of the reserve force is entitled to a leave of absence.
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities..."

This indicates that the primary condition for entitlement is a minimum of three consecutive months of continuous employment. The duration of employment can be shorter if a specific period is prescribed for the employee's class.

### Types of Operations and Activities

The section further specifies the types of operations and activities for which an employee can receive a leave of absence:

(a)
"...an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..." "an activity set out in the regulations;"
(c) "Canadian Armed Forces military skills training;"
(d)
"...training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act..."
"...duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act..."
"...service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or..."
"...treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

These points detail the various scenarios that qualify for a leave of absence, ranging from active operations and training to service in civil emergencies and recovery from service-related health issues.

### Maximum Duration of Leave
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period."

This limits the total duration of leaves taken for operations, training, and civil duties to a maximum of 24 months within any 60-month period. This provision aims to balance the employee's commitment to the reserve force with their employment.

### Exception to the Maximum Duration
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..."

This exception indicates that the 24-month limit does not apply to leaves taken due to emergencies as defined by the Emergencies Act.

### Designation of Operations
"The Minister of National Defence may designate an operation for the purposes of paragraph (1)(a) or may authorize another person to do so."

This clarifies that the Minister of National Defence has the authority to designate operations that qualify for a leave of absence.

### Employee's Right to Leave
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave."

This provision allows the Head to deny a leave of absence if it would negatively impact public health or safety or create undue hardship for the employer. This ensures that the employee's leave does not unduly compromise essential services.

question: What are the notice and communication requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Notice and Communication Requirements for an Employee Taking a Leave of Absence

This analysis details the notice and communication requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence under the relevant sections of the Canada Labour Code, as outlined in the provided documents.

### Section 207

Section 207 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the requirements for employees taking a leave of absence.

#### Initial Notice
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This indicates that an employee must provide the employer with at least four weeks' written notice before the leave commences. This notice must also specify the intended duration of the leave. The exception to this rule is if there is a valid reason for not providing the notice.

#### Change in Length of Leave
"Every employee who intends to take or who is on a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall provide the employer with notice in writing of at least four weeks of any change in the length of leave intended to be taken, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, in which case the employee shall provide the employer with notice in writing as soon as possible."

This section specifies that any change to the duration of the leave must be communicated to the employer in writing, with at least four weeks' notice, unless a valid reason prevents this. If a valid reason exists, the employee must notify the employer as soon as possible.

### Section 207.3

Section 207.3 further elaborates on the notice requirements, particularly concerning leaves exceeding four weeks.

#### Notice for Leaves Longer Than Four Weeks
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be..."

This reinforces the requirement for a minimum of four weeks' notice for any changes to a leave of absence that extends beyond four weeks.

### Section 247.6

Section 247.6, specifically addressing leaves for members of the Reserve Force, also outlines similar requirements.

#### Initial Notice
"An employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks’ notice to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer of the length of the leave."

This mirrors the requirements outlined in Section 207, emphasizing the need for at least four weeks' written notice before the leave begins and a clear statement of the leave's duration.

#### Change in Length of Leave
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall notify the employer of any change in the length of the leave at least four weeks before (a) the new day on which the leave is to end, if the employee is taking a shorter leave; or (b) the day that was most recently indicated for the leave to end, if the employee is taking a longer leave."

This section reiterates the requirement for at least four weeks' notice for any changes to the leave's duration, providing specific guidance on when the notice should be given depending on whether the leave is being shortened or extended.

In summary, the consistent requirement across these sections is that employees must provide their employer with at least four weeks' written notice before the start of a leave of absence, and any subsequent changes to the leave's duration must also be communicated in writing with at least four weeks' notice, unless a valid reason prevents this.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who takes a leave of absence for military purposes in terms of providing documentation to their employer and notifying them of their return to work?
answer:
## Employee Responsibilities for Military Leave of Absence

### Documentation Requirements

According to the Canada Labour Code, specifically Section 247.7, an employee taking a leave of absence for military purposes has specific documentation responsibilities.
"Subject to subsection (2), if the employer requests proof that a leave of absence is taken under this Division, the employee shall provide the employer with the prescribed document, if any, or with a document that is approved by the Chief of the Defence Staff who was appointed under subsection 18(1) of the National Defence Act..."

This indicates that the employee must provide documentation to their employer if requested, either a prescribed document or one approved by the Chief of the Defence Staff. 

Furthermore, the employee is required to provide this documentation within a specific timeframe.
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, the employee shall provide the document referred to in subsection (1) or (2) within three weeks after the day on which the leave begins." This sets a clear deadline for submitting the required documentation.

### Notification of Return to Work

The Canada Labour Code outlines the employee's responsibility to notify their employer of their return to work.
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, the employee shall provide the document referred to in subsection (1) or (2) within three weeks after the day on which the leave begins."

This implies that the employee must inform their employer of their intended return to work, and if they anticipate a delay, they must do so with at least four weeks' notice.
"...you must give at least 4 weeks’ notice before the new date on which it would end..."

### Additional Considerations

It is important to note that the employee's obligation to provide documentation and notify their employer of their return is subject to certain exceptions. For example, if the employee notifies the employer in accordance with paragraph 247.6(1)(b) before the leave begins and the length of the leave is not changed after the leave begins, the requirement to provide documentation may not apply.

question: What happens to an employee's employment status and position when they return to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division?
answer:
## Reinstatement After Leave of Absence

### Section 247.91: Continuous Employment and Benefits
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave."

This section clarifies that an employee's continuous employment is maintained during the leave of absence. This is crucial for benefit calculations, ensuring that the employee's seniority and benefits are not negatively impacted by the time spent on leave.
"The seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall accumulate during the leave."

This further reinforces the continuity of employment, stating that the employee's seniority continues to accrue while on leave. This ensures that upon return, the employee's seniority is not diminished, which can have implications for future benefits and career progression.

### Section 247.93: Return to Original Position
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins."

This section explicitly states the employer's obligation to reinstate the employee to their original position upon return. This is a fundamental aspect of the leave provision, ensuring that the employee is not disadvantaged by taking leave.
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location."

This provides a fallback option if the original position is no longer available. The employee must be reinstated to a comparable position with equivalent terms and conditions, ensuring that they are not penalized for taking leave.

### Section 247.92: Application of Section 189
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division."

Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code deals with the continuation of employment terms during a leave of absence. By referencing Section 189, this section ensures that the employee's employment terms are maintained during the leave and upon return.

In summary, upon returning from a leave of absence under this Division, an employee is entitled to be reinstated to their original position. If that is not possible, they are entitled to a comparable position with the same wages, benefits, and location. Their seniority continues to accumulate during the leave, and their employment is considered continuous for benefit purposes.

question: What protections are provided to employees who are members of the reserve force and take a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Protections for Reserve Force Members Taking Leave of Absence under the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code provides several protections for employees who are members of the reserve force and take a leave of absence. These protections cover reinstatement rights, continuity of employment benefits, and prohibitions against discriminatory actions.

### Entitlement to Leave

Section 247.5 outlines the conditions under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence. It states that an employee who has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer is entitled to a leave for various operations and activities. These include:

>
"...an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This demonstrates that the leave is specifically intended to accommodate the demands of military service.

### Reinstatement and Continuity of Employment

Section 247.91 addresses the continuity of employment benefits during a leave of absence. It states:

>
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave."

This means that the employee's time in the reserve force is considered as part of their overall employment history when calculating benefits. Furthermore, Section 247.92 reinforces this by stating that the employee's seniority accumulates during the leave.

Upon returning from leave, the employer is obligated to reinstate the employee in their former position or a comparable one. Section 247.91 also specifies:

>
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins."

If the original position is no longer available, the employee is entitled to a comparable position with the same wages and benefits.

### Protection Against Discrimination

Section 247.95 prohibits employers from taking adverse action against employees because of their reserve force membership or their intention to take or having taken a leave of absence. It explicitly states:

>
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them."

This ensures that employees are not penalized for fulfilling their military obligations. Additionally, Section 247.96 further reinforces this protection by prohibiting employers from refusing to hire someone solely because they are a member of the reserve force.

### Wage and Benefits Protection During Reorganization

Section 247.95 also provides protection regarding wages and benefits during a reorganization. It states:

>
"If, during a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the wages or benefits of the group of employees of which an employee is a member are changed as part of a plan to reorganize the industrial establishment in which that group is employed, the employee is entitled, on reinstatement under this section, to receive the wages and benefits in respect of that employment that that employee would have been entitled to receive had that employee been working when the reorganization took place."

This ensures that employees returning from leave are not disadvantaged by changes to wages or benefits that occur during their absence due to reorganization. The employer is also required to notify the employee of any changes to wages or benefits resulting from a reorganization.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides significant protections for employees who are members of the reserve force, ensuring their right to take leave, maintain their employment benefits, and be free from discrimination related to their military service.

question: What is the purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Purpose of Regulations under Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of Division XV.2, which pertains to Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force. 

### Key Objectives of the Regulations

The regulations aim to define and clarify various aspects related to leave of absence for members of the Reserve Force. Specifically, they cover:

**1. Defining Continuity of Employment:
"...specifying the absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment for the purpose of subsection 247.5(1)..."
This indicates that the regulations will specify which absences are considered as not disrupting an employee's continuous employment status when it comes to taking leave for Reserve Force duties.

**2. Defining Operations and Activities:
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute an operation for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(a); (c) setting out the activities for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(b)..."
These provisions suggest that the regulations will provide clarity on what constitutes an operation and what activities are considered part of the Reserve Force duties for which an employee may take leave.

**3. Defining Military Skills Training:
"...defining “military skills training” for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(c)..."
This regulation will provide a precise definition of "military skills training" to determine eligibility for leave.

**4. Limiting Treatment, Recovery, and Rehabilitation:
"...limiting the duration of the treatment, recovery or rehabilitation referred to in paragraph 247.5(1)(g) or setting out the terms or conditions for the application of that paragraph..."
This indicates that the regulations will establish limitations or conditions related to the duration of treatment, recovery, or rehabilitation that an employee can take leave for.

**5. Defining Undue Hardship:
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute undue hardship for the purposes of subsection 247.5(4)..."
The regulations will define what constitutes undue hardship for employers when an employee requests a leave of absence for Reserve Force duties.

**6. Specifying Valid Reasons for Leave:
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute a valid reason for the purposes of subsection 247.6(1), (2), (3) or (4), 247.7(3) or 247.93(2)..."
This regulation will outline the specific reasons for which an employee is eligible to take a leave of absence.

**7. Circumstances Where Sections Do Not Apply:
"...specifying the circumstances in which section 247.7, subsection 247.8(1) or subsection 247.91(2) does not apply..."
The regulations will clarify situations where certain sections of the Canada Labour Code regarding leave of absence may not be applicable.

**8. Restrictions on Employment Terms:
"...specifying the circumstances in which an employer may not assign an employee to a position with different terms or conditions of employment for the purposes of section 247.94..."
This regulation will address situations where employers may not be able to change an employee's terms or conditions of employment when they are on leave.

**9. Classes of Employees Not Entitled to Leave:
"...prescribing the classes of employees that are not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if the Governor in Council is satisfied that the fact of taking leave would cause unreasonable consequences; and (m) prescribing the circumstances in which classes of employees are not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to specify classes of employees who may not be entitled to a leave of absence if it would cause unreasonable consequences.



In summary, the regulations under section 247.97 are designed to provide a comprehensive framework for the implementation of leave of absence provisions for members of the Reserve Force, addressing various aspects from eligibility and duration to employer obligations and potential restrictions.

question: What protections does the Canada Labour Code provide to employees regarding genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results?
answer:
## Protections Regarding Genetic Testing and Disclosure of Results in the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) provides significant protections to employees concerning genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results. These protections are primarily outlined in Division XV.3, specifically section 247.98 and related sections.

### Right to Refuse Genetic Testing

Section 247.98(2) explicitly states:
"Every employee is entitled not to undergo or be required to undergo a genetic test." This means an employer cannot mandate an employee to take a genetic test as a condition of employment or continued employment. This protection is fundamental, ensuring employees retain control over their personal genetic information.

### Right Not to Disclose Genetic Test Results

Section 247.98(3) further protects employees by stating:
"Every employee is entitled not to disclose or be required to disclose the results of a genetic test." This is a crucial provision, preventing employers from demanding that employees reveal the results of genetic tests they have undergone. This safeguard is designed to prevent discrimination based on genetic predispositions.

### Prohibition Against Discriminatory Actions

Section 247.98(4) prohibits employers from taking adverse action against an employee based on genetic testing. This includes:

*   Dismissal
*   Suspension
*   Layoff
*   Demotion
*   Imposing financial or other penalties
*   Refusing to pay remuneration

The section clarifies that these actions are prohibited
"...because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee." This demonstrates a clear commitment to preventing discrimination based on genetic information.

### Restrictions on Disclosure by Third Parties

Section 247.98(5) prohibits anyone from disclosing to an employer that an employee has undergone a genetic test, or disclosing the results of a genetic test, without the employee's written consent. This provision is designed to protect the employee's privacy and prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive genetic information.

### Restrictions on Collection and Use of Genetic Test Results

Section 247.98(6) states that employers are prohibited from collecting or using the results of a genetic test without the employee's written consent. This reinforces the employee's right to control their genetic information and prevents employers from using this information for discriminatory purposes.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides comprehensive protections to employees regarding genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results. These protections are designed to prevent discrimination, safeguard privacy, and ensure employees retain control over their personal genetic information.

question: What steps can an employee take if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of subsection 247.98(4), and what is the role of the Head and the Board in handling the complaint?
answer:
## Employee Recourse for Violations of Section 247.98(4)

### Employer Actions Prohibited by Section 247.98(4)

Section 247.98(4) of the Canada Labour Code prohibits employers from taking disciplinary action against employees
"...because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee." This means an employee who believes they have been disciplined (e.g., dismissed, suspended, or penalized) for refusing a genetic test, refusing to disclose test results, or due to the results of a genetic test, has grounds for a complaint.

### Steps an Employee Can Take

According to the text, an employee who believes their employer has violated Section 247.98(4) has the following recourse:

1.  **Complaint to the Board:
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them..." This indicates that the primary avenue for an employee to address a violation of Section 247.98(4) is by filing a formal complaint with the Canada Labour Board.

2.  **Judicial Review:
"If your concerns are not resolved, you may be able to  request a judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court, within 30  days of receiving the investigator’s report." This provides an additional option for the employee if the Board does not resolve the complaint to their satisfaction.

### Role of the Head and the Board

The text outlines the roles of the Head and the Board in handling complaints related to Section 247.98(4):

*   **The Head's Role:** The Head is responsible for examining the underlying subject-matter of a complaint and assessing whether other means are available to resolve the complaint. The Head should also consider whether the dismissal of an employee subject to a collective agreement may have an impact on monetary complaint allegations.
*   **The Board's Role:** The Board is the body to which an employee can file a complaint. The Board will investigate the complaint and determine whether the employer has violated Section 247.98(4). If the Board finds that a violation has occurred, it can order the employer to take corrective action. The Board also provides a mechanism for judicial review if the employee is not satisfied with the Board's decision.

The text states,
"A complaint made under subsection (1) is itself evidence that the reprisal was actually taken and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the reprisal was not taken, the burden of proof is on that party." This highlights the importance of filing a complaint with the Board, as it provides evidence of the employer's actions and shifts the burden of proof to the employer to demonstrate that no violation occurred.

question: What is the effect of an order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code, and how does it interact with the court system?
answer:
## Effect of an Order Under Section 247.99

Section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code establishes that
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This means that once the Board issues an order under this section, it is binding and cannot be challenged in the courts. 

This is further reinforced in Section 247.991, which states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." The marginal note "No review by certiorari, etc." emphasizes the lack of appeal options.

## Interaction with the Court System

Despite the finality of the order, the Canada Labour Code provides a mechanism for enforcement through the court system. Section 247.991 outlines this process:
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 247.99(8), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file a copy of the order in the Federal Court, exclusive of reasons."

This indicates that while the order itself is final and not subject to review, it can be registered in the Federal Court. Once registered, the order has the
"...same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This allows for the enforcement of the order through the court system, similar to a regular judgment.

Furthermore, Section 247.991 clarifies that
"The making of a complaint under subsection 247.99(1) does not suspend or affect an employee’s civil remedies against their employer." This means that even after the Board issues an order, an employee retains the right to pursue other legal avenues against their employer if they believe further action is necessary.

question: What actions can the Minister take to investigate employment in industrial establishments, and who can be appointed to carry out this investigation?
answer:
## Minister's Authority to Investigate Employment

### Section 12.07: Measures for Investigation

The Minister has several options to initiate an investigation into employment within industrial establishments. These include:

*   **Information Gathering:
"...obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary..." This indicates the Minister can proactively gather information to assess the need for a formal inquiry.
*   **Mediation:
"...refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation..." The Minister can direct the matter to mediation if they believe it's a suitable avenue for resolution.
*   **Governor in Council Inquiry:
"...request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..." The Minister can formally request the Governor in Council to initiate an inquiry.

### Section 12.08: Appointment of Inquirer

When the Governor in Council receives a request for an inquiry, they can appoint an inquirer.
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry." This specifies that a judge of a superior court can be appointed to conduct the inquiry, following a recommendation from the Minister of Justice.

## Powers of the Inquirer

### Section 12.09: Judge's Powers

The judge appointed to conduct the inquiry possesses extensive powers, mirroring those of a superior court.
"The judge has all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court, including the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath." This includes the authority to compel testimony and access to documents.

### Section 12.10: Support for the Inquirer

To assist in conducting the inquiry, the judge can engage support staff.
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses." This allows for the inclusion of experts and legal counsel to aid in the investigation.

## Overall Summary

The Minister has a range of tools at their disposal to investigate employment matters in industrial establishments, ranging from informal information gathering to formally requesting a inquiry from the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council then appoints an inquirer, typically a judge of a superior court, who is granted broad powers to conduct the investigation, including the power to compel testimony and access documents, and can be supported by counsel and other experts.

question: What powers does the Head have to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code, and who can assist or be delegated these powers?
answer:
## Head's Powers to Gather Information and Conduct Inspections

### Inspections

The Canada Labour Code grants the "Head" significant powers regarding workplace inspections.
"If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer."

This indicates that inspections must be conducted with a specific level of representation, ensuring fairness and transparency. The Head also has the discretion to proceed with an inspection even if the designated representatives are not present, provided they choose not to be there.

### Powers Regarding Information Gathering

The Head possesses extensive powers to gather information related to wages, hours of work, and working conditions. These powers are outlined in section 249 of the Canada Labour Code.
"...the Head may (a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee; (b) take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a); (c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment; (c.1) require any employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan that must be insured in accordance with subsection 239.2(1) to furnish proof that the plan is insured in accordance with that subsection; (d) require an employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment; and (e) require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made."

This includes the power to inspect records, take copies, demand statements, and require employees to provide information. The Head can also require parties to a complaint to provide statements regarding the circumstances of the dismissal.

### Delegation of Powers

The Head can delegate their powers to qualified individuals or groups.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part."

This delegation can be subject to specific terms and conditions set by the Minister. The Head is required to provide a certificate of authority to anyone to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated.

### Assistance and Support

The Head can be assisted during inspections and information gathering.
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations."
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary."

This ensures that employers and employees provide reasonable assistance to facilitate inspections and information gathering. The Head can also bring along additional personnel to aid in these tasks.

### Limitations on Delegation and Testimony

There are limitations on who can receive delegated powers and who can be compelled to testify regarding information obtained during inspections or assistance provided.
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), and no person who has accompanied or assisted such a person or the Head in carrying out their duties and functions, shall be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions or in accompanying or assisting the person, except with the written permission of the Head."

This protects individuals who assist the Head from being compelled to testify about information they learned during the course of their assistance, unless the Head provides written permission.

While Section 250 directly addresses oaths, affidavits, and statutory declarations, it is important to note its connection to other sections. For example, Section 249 details the Head's inspection powers, and Section 271 outlines the Head's ability to establish forms of notices of violation. question: What happens if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this impact potential prosecution?
answer:
## Employer Failure to Pay Wages and Potential Prosecution under the Canada Labour Code

### Findings of Non-Compliance and Written Notification
"The Labour Program may find that your employer does not owe you wages or other amounts under the Code." This indicates that if the Labour Program investigates and determines an employer has not met their obligations regarding wages or other entitlements, the employee will receive written notification of this finding. This notification may also include a "Notice of Unfounded Complaint," which explains the reasons for the determination of compliance and provides an opportunity for the employee to request a review.

### Administrative Fees and Director Liability
"The following administrative fee will be added to the Payment Order when issued to the employer:  a fee of $200, or a fee of 15% of the total amount owed..." This highlights that even if an employer is found to be in violation, there may be additional costs associated with the recovery of unpaid wages. Furthermore, the Labour Program has the authority to hold corporate directors liable for unpaid wages.
"Corporate directors are jointly and individually liable for employees’ wages and other amounts to which employees are entitled, up to a limit equivalent to 6 months’ wages." This means that directors can be held personally responsible for ensuring employees receive their rightful compensation.

### Potential Prosecution for Continued Non-Compliance
"If the Labour Program finds a pattern of non-compliance during an investigation, it will advise the employer on their responsibilities under the Code. If the employer does not comply with the Code, they may be subject to enforcement action up to and including an administrative monetary penalty." This passage outlines the consequences for employers who fail to rectify violations after being informed. The Labour Program can issue administrative monetary penalties, which are financial fines.
"If you do not correct a contravention with the Code or Regulations, the Labour Program may choose to prosecute you. The Labour Program may also take this route if you are fully aware of your legal obligations and still willfully break the law. Repeat contraventions indicate an intentional or willful action." This indicates that in cases of persistent or intentional violations, the Labour Program can pursue legal action against the employer.

### Public Naming of Employers
"The Labour Program will publish information about employers who violate the Code, including:         all payment orders of $5000 or greater filed in federal court administrative monetary penalties (some exceptions apply for category “A” violations), and  prosecutions..." This demonstrates that employers found to be in violation, particularly those with significant unpaid wages or who have been prosecuted, may be publicly named by the Labour Program. This serves as a deterrent to other employers and provides transparency to the public.

question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records, and what information must be included in the report?
answer:
## Internal Audit Order by the Head

### Circumstances for Ordering an Internal Audit

Section 251.001(1) states that the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit
"...for the purpose of verifying compliance or preventing non-compliance with this Part..." This indicates that the Head can initiate an internal audit when there is a need to either confirm that the employer is adhering to the requirements of the Canada Labour Code or to proactively address potential violations.

### Information Required in the Report

Section 251.001(2) outlines the specific information that must be included in the internal audit report. This includes:

*   **(a) Scope:** The order must specify
"...any industrial establishment and class of employees to which it applies..." This defines the specific workplaces and employee groups that are subject to the audit.
*   **(b) Time Period:** The report must cover
"...the period of time to be covered by the internal audit..." This clarifies the timeframe for the audit's scope.
*   **(c) Provisions Reviewed:** The order must identify
"...the provisions of this Part or the regulations with respect to which the internal audit was ordered..." This specifies the particular aspects of the law that the audit should focus on.
*   **(d) Report Deadline:** The order must state
"...the date by which the employer is to provide the report..." This sets a clear deadline for the submission of the audit findings.
*   **(e) Report Format:** The order must specify "the form of the report." This ensures that the report is presented in a standardized and usable format.

Section 251.001(3) further clarifies that the Head may also specify "any information that the Head considers appropriate" to be included in the report, allowing for flexibility in the audit's scope and content.

### Additional Reporting Requirements

Section 251.001(5) details the requirements for a certificate confirming the delivery of the audit order. It states that a certificate
"...is admissible in evidence and is proof of the statements contained in the certificate, without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate." This ensures that the employer can demonstrate that they received the order.

Section 251.001(6) mandates that if the employer determines they have not complied with any provision, the report must
"...set out in the report the nature of the employer’s non-compliance and the steps that have been or will be taken by the employer to comply with the provision." This ensures transparency and accountability.

Section 251.001(7) requires the employer to include information about any unpaid wages or other amounts owed to employees, including the amount owed, the method used to determine the amount, and any payments made.

Finally, Section 251.001(9) prohibits employers from making "a false or misleading statement in a report," ensuring the integrity and reliability of the audit findings.

question: What is the process and timeframe for employees to make complaints about potential contraventions of the Canada Labour Code by their employer?
answer:
## Process and Timeframe for Employee Complaints under the Canada Labour Code

### General Process for Making a Complaint

The Canada Labour Code outlines a process for employees to make complaints to the Board regarding potential contraventions by their employer.
"...any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96."

This indicates that complaints can be made by employees, trade unions, or individuals acting on their behalf. The complaint must be in writing and detail a contravention of specific sections of the Canada Labour Code.

### Timeframe for Making a Complaint

The timeframe for making a complaint depends on the nature of the complaint.

**Monetary Complaints:
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you."

This means that if the complaint involves unpaid wages or other amounts owed under the Canada Labour Code, the complaint must be filed within six months from the last day the employer was obligated to make those payments.

**Non-Monetary Complaints:
"...months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose."

For complaints not related to monetary issues, the deadline is six months from the date the issue occurred.

**Unjust Dismissal Complaints:
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal."

This is a shorter timeframe, requiring the complaint to be filed within 90 days of the dismissal.

### Extension of Time
"The Head may, subject to the regulations, extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; (b) in any circumstances prescribed by regulation; or (c) in the conditions prescribed by regulation."

In certain circumstances, the Head of the Labour Program may extend the deadline for filing a complaint. This can occur if the initial complaint was made to an individual who lacked the authority to handle the matter, and the complainant reasonably believed they had the authority.

### Suspension of Complaints
"For greater certainty, a complaint is not permitted under this section if it relates to a disagreement whose settlement is governed exclusively by a collective agreement under subsection 168(1.1)."

This indicates that if a collective agreement already governs the resolution of the issue, a complaint under the Canada Labour Code may not be permitted.

question: Under what circumstances can the Head suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee, and what are the requirements for the Head's decision to be implemented?
answer:
## Circumstances for Suspending Consideration of a Complaint

The Head can suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee if they are satisfied that the employee must take certain measures before the Head can continue to deal with the complaint. This is outlined in Section 251.02(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This indicates that the suspension can occur at any point in time when the Head believes the employee needs to fulfill specific requirements before the complaint can be addressed.

## Requirements for Implementing the Head's Decision to Suspend

Section 251.02 outlines the requirements for the Head's decision to suspend consideration of a complaint to be implemented.

**Notification to the Employee:
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

This means the employee must receive a written notification detailing the specific actions they need to take and the timeframe within which they must complete those actions.

**End of Suspension:
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

The suspension of the complaint is lifted once the Head is satisfied that the employee has fulfilled the required measures within the specified timeframe.

**Extension of Time:
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice."

The Head has the discretion to grant an extension to the timeframe provided in the initial notification, should the employee require more time to fulfill the necessary measures.

question: What happens when an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this affect potential prosecution?
answer:
## Settlement of Wage Claims under the Canada Labour Code

### Agreement and Payment
"If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process when an employer and employee agree on a settlement for unpaid wages or other amounts. The key takeaway is that the employer can choose to either pay the agreed-upon amount directly to the employee or remit the funds to the "Head," which refers to the Labour Program.

### Impact on Prosecution
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head."

This is a crucial point regarding potential legal action.  The law explicitly states that an employer cannot be prosecuted for failing to pay wages if they have fulfilled the settlement agreement by paying the agreed amount to either the employee or the Labour Program. However, this requires the written consent of the Minister to avoid prosecution. This provision encourages settlements and provides a pathway for employers to resolve wage disputes without facing legal repercussions.



### Additional Considerations
"If an employer pays the amounts to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving them, pay them over to the employee who is entitled to the amounts."

This clarifies the role of the Labour Program when the settlement is made out to the "Head." The Labour Program is obligated to promptly forward the funds to the employee who is rightfully entitled to them. This ensures that the employee receives the compensation they are owed.
